## 4 Alternative routes of adjustment of saving to investment in the long period

*Man-Seop Park*

Heinz Kurz is a prolific writer – one, among many, of his aspects that I admire. I came to chew on a small corner of his literature when I was reading for my PhD on a long-period theory of effective demand. Kurz (1985) and Kurz (1986) were inspirations for part of the thesis. His work on capital accumulation and economic growth, among others, has continued to give me the pleasure of reading and the benefit of getting insights for research. What is presented in the present chapter is concordant with his work along the lines of the ‘Keynesian Hypothesis’ (Kurz, 1990, 1992, 1994) – the kind of work that was enthusiastically pursued by the ‘Sraffian Keynesians’ in the 1980s (see, for example, papers collected in Bharadwaj and Schefold, 1990; Kurz, 1990, is one of them) but since then have attracted none of the attention they deserve except sporadically (Serrano, 1995; Trezzini, 1995, 1998; Park, 1997a, 2000; Palumbo and Trezzini, 2003).<sup>1</sup>

### **Introduction**

The recent period has witnessed a surge in the analysis of economic growth and development on neoclassical lines. New Growth Theory (Romer, 1987, 1990; Lucas, 1988) has proved influential both in theory and in practice (see e.g. Bardhan, 1995). One of its distinct differences from Old Growth Theory (Solow, 1956) is that in New Growth Theory different saving ratios affect the *rate* of output growth while in Old Growth Theory they do not influence anything other than the *level* of the accumulated capital stock relative to labour. By this is strengthened a typically neoclassical conclusion that the path of growth of an economy is causally affected by the saving behaviour of the constituent members of that economy; investment does not have a causal impact on economic growth and development, for investment is to adjust to saving for macroeconomic equilibrium. Economic growth is basically supply-led.<sup>2</sup>

In stark contrast, the Keynesian conception reverses the causality of economic growth and development: in the *long period* as well as in the short period, it is saving that adjusts to investment, not the other way around: investment is determined autonomously, that is, independently of the saving corresponding to the capacity output; then, macroeconomic equilibrium requires saving to adjust to investment. Economic growth is demand-led (Setterfield, 2002).

{33}------------------------------------------------

The Keynesian conception, however, has identified several alternative routes through which saving is generated to match investment in the long period. Two such routes are widely known, in reference to which different Keynesian positions are distinguished. The first position is usually called ‘Neo-Keynesian’, with Kaldor, Robinson and Pasinetti as its early representatives. This position holds that, in the long period, saving is brought into line with investment through *variations in the state of income distribution*. A higher level of investment causes a rise in the general price level so that wage earners, who are paid at a fixed money wage rate and have a lower propensity to save than profit earners, find themselves with a lower real wage rate while profit earners are consequently remunerated at a higher rate of profits; the resulting level of saving is higher corresponding to the higher level of investment. The second position is commonly called ‘Kaleckian’ and its early inspirations include Kalecki, Steindl, and Baran and Sweezy.<sup>3</sup> The source of saving required to match varying levels of investment is varying levels of output ensuing from *variations in the equilibrium degree of capacity utilization*; in the long period, the degree of capacity utilization tends to settle at a certain level which is usually different from the given ‘planned’ or ‘normal’ level.<sup>4</sup> In this adjustment, the real wage need not, if it may, change while the rate of profits changes in accordance with the degree of utilization. This route of adjustment closely resembles the short period adjustment of saving to investment.

There is, however, a third ‘Keynesian route’ of adjustment, which was identified some time ago but has not attracted as much attention as it deserves. This route is *variations in the size of productive capacity* and, consequently, in the volume of output (and, in principle, without changes in the relation between the real wage rate and the rate of profits). This route was brought to attention first by Garegnani (1962, 1979, 1982a, 1982b, 1992) and later elaborated by Ciccone (1984, 1986), Vianello (1985), Kurz (1990, 1994), Park (1997a), Palumbo and Trezzini (2003), and others. The present chapter aims to make an explanatory and constructive contribution along these lines. The next two sections provide brief criticisms of the two well-known Keynesian routes of adjustment of saving to investment. The following sections expound the third alternative route and provide a simple model which accords with that route. The final section concludes with a short comment.

### **The Neo-Keynesian position**

The Neo-Keynesian mechanism of adjustment of saving to investment – the adjustment through changes in the distribution of income – is based on three characteristic assumptions.

One is the differentiated propensities to save out of profits and out of wages.<sup>5</sup> It is due to this differentiation in the propensities to save (such that the propensity to save out of profits is higher than that out of wages) that changes in the distribution of income manifest themselves in the form of the corresponding changes in the level of aggregate saving.

Another assumption is that, in the long-period equilibrium the available labour force is fully employed and/or productive equipment is utilized at the normal

{34}------------------------------------------------

level.<sup>6</sup> It is implied, then, that the relationship among output, labour and the material means of production in the long-period equilibrium will be as specified by the dominant technique in use (see, e.g., Robinson, 1962, p. 11). Thus, except in the case of normal utilization of productive capacity alone (Joan Robinson's 'Limping Golden Age' growth), the theory does not intend to explain the existence of the long-period, structural unemployment, i.e. unemployment due to the shortage of productive equipment to which labour is applied.

A third assumption states that what is autonomous is the rate of accumulation rather than the level of investment in value terms. Whether to take the hypothesis of the autonomy of the rate of accumulation or the hypothesis of the autonomy of the level of investment is a matter of economic perspective. But, as Garegnani (1982a, 1982b, 1992) first pointed out, the two hypotheses are in general very different things to be clearly distinguished from each other. For, if we take the value of investment as autonomous, then the value of the stock, which constitutes the denominator of the rate of accumulation, is a dependent variable in the long period, being determined by a series of autonomously undertaken investments; this implies that the rate of accumulation is, in general, also a dependent variable in the long-period analysis. On the other hand, taking the rate of accumulation as autonomous amounts to leaving the value of investment (and, in the long period, the value of the stock) as a dependent variable. This difference proves substantial in the case where accumulation is, as in an actual economy, not effected along a steady-state growth path but goes through a tortuous process of ups and downs. In this case, it is certain that the annual proportionate rate of accumulation cannot be considered constant through time. It is, however, precisely this constancy of the rate of accumulation with the constant normal utilization of productive capacity that lies behind the Neo-Keynesian conception of autonomous changes in the rate of accumulation and accompanying changes in the state of income distribution. Thus, the respective hypotheses can lend themselves to the formulation of alternative long-period theories of income distribution and capital accumulation. It is a fact that the Neo-Keynesians in general tend to consider the autonomy of the rate of accumulation to be firmly based on, if not the same thing as, the autonomy of investment (e.g. Robinson, 1962, pp. 82–3; Pasinetti, 1962, p. 103; and, implicitly, Kaldor, 1956, pp. 94–5) without making clear the difference between the two hypotheses.

Given the equilibrium condition of the equality of saving and investment, and on the assumption that profit earners save a fraction  $s_r$  of their income while wage-earners spend their whole income, we have the following well-known version of the Cambridge equation for an economy where there are  $n$  industries and  $n$  commodities (the aggregate rate of accumulation is expressed in its defining ratio on the right-hand side):

$$s_r r = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n g_i [x_i \mathbf{A}_i \mathbf{p}(r)]}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \mathbf{A}_i \mathbf{p}(r)} \quad (4.1)$$

{35}------------------------------------------------

where  $r =$  the normal rate of profits;  $g_i =$  the rate of accumulation of the  $i$ -th industry;<sup>7</sup>  $x_i =$  the activity level of the  $i$ -th industry;  $\mathbf{A}_i =$  the  $i$ -th row of the material input coefficient matrix  $\mathbf{A}$ ;  $\mathbf{p}(r) =$  the column price vector (as a function of  $r$ ). Given the technique in use and the rates of accumulation in the respective industries, equation (4.1) consists of two groups of unknowns:  $r$  and the set of  $n$   $x_i$ 's. Now, for a set of given industrial rates of accumulation, an appropriately defined quantity system for a given technique with an appropriate normalization rule (e.g. Abraham-Frois and Berrebi, 1979; Pasinetti, 1977) will determine the set of  $n$   $x_i$ 's.<sup>8</sup> Equation (4.1) is, thus, effectively a single equation with one unknown,  $r$ . Any given vector of industrial rates of accumulation – within the limits set by the condition of the non-negativity of both the real wage rate and the normal rate of profits – causes the normal rate of profits and, thus, the system of relative prices to be such that the aggregate value of saving equals the aggregate value of investment. Also determined accordingly are the scale and composition and the value of investment. This is the general Neo-Keynesian long-period model of growth, combined with the Sraffa system as has been suggested by various writers (e.g. Schefold, 1976, pp. 204ff.; Pasinetti, 1977, p. 128).

But equation (4.1), with its right-hand side being a ratio between two polynomial functions of  $r$ , in general has multiple solutions: there can be at most  $n$  economically meaningful rates of profits. It is self-explanatory that this multiplicity renders doubtful the general applicability, if not the validity, of the procedure just followed. Being, as it were, not equipped with additional relations in reference to which to choose among the  $n$  solutions for  $r$ , we do not know which result will be brought about by the investments undertaken.

There is a case in which this multiplicity disappears outright. In the case of balanced growth, where the industrial rates of accumulation are uniform across the industries ( $g_i = g$  for all  $i$ ), the right-hand side of equation (4.1) boils down to that uniform rate ( $g$ ); hence, a unique determination of the rate of profits.<sup>9</sup> Indeed, it seems that it is by implicitly assuming the case of balanced growth that the Neo-Keynesians say a given rate of accumulation ‘determines’ the rate of profits. This conjecture is strengthened by the fact that the case of balanced growth is one in which the two aforementioned hypotheses coincide at the aggregate level: the vector of aggregate physical investments being a uniform fraction of the given vector of aggregate physical stocks, the exogenous determination of the (common) ratio of those levels of investments to the corresponding levels of the stocks amounts, *in the long- as well as in the short-run*, to the exogenous determination of the levels of investment.

#### **The Kaleckian position**

The Kaleckians put forward a different mechanism of adjustment between saving and investment. For them, as for Keynes and unlike the Neo-Keynesians, it is the level of investment that is autonomous.<sup>10</sup> The autonomy is represented by the exogeneity of the ‘structural coefficients’ (that is, parameters) appearing in the investment function. With the aid of other behavioural functions, which have their own ‘structural coefficients’, and some identities, it is shown that the

{36}------------------------------------------------

economy tends to utilize productive capacity at a certain level, probably different from the normal level, yielding a corresponding rate of profits. If the ‘structural coefficients’ are such as to bring about a higher (lower) long-run degree of utilization, the rate of profits will correspondingly be higher (lower). This gives a picture of adjustment of saving to investment very different from the Neo-Keynesian one. The contrast between these two Keynesian views is well remarked by Steindl (1952, p. 211):

[The model for the case of constant utilization] presumes that utilization, though variable in the short-run, is re-established at a given level by the process of squeezing out any ‘excess’ capital equipment which may tend to appear. Taken as a moving average over *n* years utilization may be considered constant. The corollary of this assumption is that the profit function is variable. . . . In other words the profit rate at a given utilization will adjust itself in response to changes in the rate of growth of capital.

But we can hardly maintain that this case is an adequate model embodying even the most essential features only, because the underlying hypothesis of a prompt re-establishment of a given degree of utilization is not realistic. It is natural, then, to go a step further, to allow the degree of utilization to vary. . . . The most obvious way is to go, as it were, to the other extreme: instead of making utilization constant, and the profit function variable, we shall make utilization variable, and assume the profit function rigid.

Then, for the Kaleckians, it is mainly variations in output due to variations in the degree of utilization that align the level of saving to the level of investment. A higher rate of profits need not be accompanied by a lower real wage rate. If we assume that the real wage rate is constant, the higher (lower) rate of profits – due to the now larger (smaller) volume of output – is the source for the higher (lower) level of saving corresponding to the higher (lower) level of investment. Thus, the models conceived in the Kaleckian literature are differentiated from those of the long-period equilibrium conceived by the Classical (Ricardian) economists – and also by the Neo-Keynesians – in which the rate of profits always moves in the opposite direction to the real wage rate.

However, one crucial criticism has been proposed to the Kaleckian position: permanent utilization of productive equipment at an other-than-normal level is contradictory to economic rationality in the following sense. The Kaleckian result is due mainly to the constancy of the given ‘structural coefficients’, especially those of the investment function. If, however, entrepreneurs ‘wish to establish a planned degree of utilization over a number of years (boom and slump)’ (Steindl, 1952, p. xiv), why will they not adjust these ‘structural coefficients’ in the long period of time in such a way that, through these changes in the pattern of investment and other connected economic behaviours, the scale and composition of productive equipment becomes appropriate to the scale and composition of demand? (As a matter of fact, what we can observe in reality is only the tendency towards such a situation, so often interrupted by disappointed expectations, short-period rigidities of various economic variables, changes in the forces themselves which determine

{37}------------------------------------------------

the trend, etc.) Due emphasis on the *flexibility of investment behaviour* in entrepreneurs' eagerness to establish a normal degree of utilization may induce one to conceive of a situation in which the size and the composition of productive capacity are, in the long period, fully adjusted to demand. This flexibility is effected by the *autonomy of short-period investment*: the entrepreneurs, rather than being led by the constancy of 'structural coefficients' to install that size of productive equipment which will be utilized permanently below its planned level, will undertake investment autonomously period by period in their eager attempt to adjust productive capacity to the state of demand.

As will be implied by our argument below, the Kaleckian view would be similar to ours if it were carried out in terms of 'averages' over  $\tau$  periods ( $\tau$  being sufficiently large). Then the long-run equilibrium degree of utilization should be conceived as the average degree of utilization over the periods covered, and the rate of profits corresponding to this degree of utilization as the average rate of profits over the same periods. This way, the 'structural coefficients' of an investment function, now representing the average degree of activity over  $\tau$  periods, would be *post factum* a proxy for the autonomy of investment.<sup>11</sup>

#### **An alternative position**

On the one hand, we reject the Kaleckian conception of permanent utilization of productive capacity at an other-than-normal level and, consequently, conceive of the long-period equilibrium in which productive capacity is so adjusted to demand that it is utilized at its normal level. On the other, we do not take the Neo-Keynesian hypothesis of the autonomy of the rate of accumulation but, instead, follow Keynes in his *General Theory* by taking the level of investment in value terms as autonomous<sup>12</sup> – this allows, as we shall see in what follows, for the constancy of the normal distribution of income in the process of adjustment of saving to investment. Then we have a third possible mechanism of adjustment of saving to investment: adjustment through *variations in the size of productive capacity*. This route is in operation, it must be remarked, also both in the Neo-Keynesian and the Kaleckian analyses; however, the title-role of adjustment in these analyses is given to the other mechanisms. Our position then implies an understanding that the causes of changes in the normal distribution of income or in the equilibrium (normal) degree of utilization must be sought elsewhere than in mere accumulation.<sup>13</sup> We shall start a detailed discussion of our conception by explaining the concept of the long-period equilibrium we hold.

A long-period equilibrium is a situation in which (a) the rate of profits is uniform across the productive processes and (b) the level of saving is equal to the level of investment in the aggregate. Long-period or normal prices are determined by (i) the conditions of reproduction of commodities and (ii) the distribution of the surplus over the wages at a uniform, normal rate of profits on the value of means of production in each productive process; or, alternatively, the determination of the wages as residue remaining after the means of production invested in each production process earn a uniform rate of profits on their value, this rate of profits

{38}------------------------------------------------

being determined by the money rate of interest (Sraffa, 1960, p. 33). (Throughout the present chapter we will take the latter perspective on how the normal distribution of income is determined.)<sup>14</sup> The uniformity of the industrial rates of profit is assumed to be achieved in the long-period equilibrium through free movement of money capital in pursuit of higher returns. Then, for a particular technique employed as dominant, there will in equilibrium be a unique relationship among relative prices, the normal rate of profits and the real wage rate.

Now, the long-period levels of output and of employment are those which are concomitant to the long-period configuration of the rate of profits, the real wage rate and relative prices (Eatwell, 1983). The tendency towards the realization of the uniform rate of profits implies that the scale and composition of output on the one hand and the size and composition of productive capacity on the other tend to be adjusted one to the other. This full adjustment between output and productive capacity in the long-period equilibrium in turn imports – *by the very definition of long-period equilibrium* – that productive capacity will be utilized at the normal level in equilibrium. The size of aggregate productive capacity depends on the level of aggregate net investment taken in the course of ‘gravitation’ towards equilibrium: the higher the level of investment, the larger the size of productive capacity.

A larger size of productive capacity implies a higher level of normal output (i.e. the level of output which would result if actual investment were such as to bring about the normal utilization of that productive capacity), and this higher level of normal output is the basis on which a higher level of saving will be generated corresponding to a higher level of investment. Between two different fully-adjusted positions,<sup>15</sup> which result from different levels of aggregate investment but with the same technique, the same normal rate of profits and the same relative rates of growth of the components of consumption demand, we shall observe – on the assumption of constant returns to scale – the same set of relative prices, the same real wage rate, the same composition of the stock of means of production and the same composition of output, but *different sizes* of the stock and output.<sup>16</sup>

It will be noted that what is autonomous is the volume of aggregate investment in value terms. The fact is, however, that the volume of aggregate investment in a certain period, let alone over a number of periods, is not a matter to be determined by a single decision by a single person or authority: it is merely the sum of individual investments in that period or over a number of periods concerned. But when we are speaking of the volume of aggregate investment being autonomous, we are conceiving that there is, in Keynes’s terms, a general ‘state of long-term expectations’ (Keynes, 1936, Ch. 12) in the economy as a whole; this depends on various – economic, political, institutional, etc. – aspects of the economy (see Eatwell, 1983; Park, 1994), and acts as a general incentive to invest, ‘regulating’ individual, short-period investment; that is, it is autonomous in the particular sense that it is prior to saving. Where the economy settles in a stationary state, the size of productive capacity in equilibrium depends on the general state of long-term expectation: if the latter is for the better, the former will be larger. Where the economy is growing, the average pace of accumulation will be faster if the state

{39}------------------------------------------------

of long-term expectation is for the better. In the case of a stationary economy, the short-period movement of money capital on the path towards equilibrium is such that a sector whose commodity bears a market price higher than its costs of production attracts investment and a sector of the opposite character discourages investment. In the case of a growing economy, a sector with a market price higher than its costs of production attracts more investment than it would do if the market price coincides with the costs of production, and a sector of the opposite character would behave in the opposite way; or, when the demand for one commodity grows faster than that of another, the productive process of the former commodity needs a rate of accumulation of productive equipment relatively higher than that of the latter, an inflow of money capital occurring into the former productive process. This is, of course, the Classical concept, or its extension, of *free competition*, and implies that the composition of investment and, thus, that of the stock are a matter of *endogenous* determination – in accordance with the relative rates of growth of the components of consumption demand and the equilibrium condition of the uniformity of the industrial rates of profit.

It being admitted that the long-period equilibrium or the fully-adjusted position as we conceive it would not be such a situation as will be readily observed in the actual economy, the mechanism of adjustment of saving to investment through variations in the size of productive capacity may be said to be merely a logical possibility. Borrowing Steindl's words, our position may be 'to go . . . to the . . . extreme' (1952, p. 211): we take both utilization and income distribution constant in equilibrium, and then see how saving accommodates itself to investment. But we believe that our conception reflects important aspects of a capitalist economy in its process of creating saving by investment. As we have said just above, we take seriously the flexibility of autonomous short-period investment which is guided, on the one hand, by the general state of long-term expectation and, on the other, by the eagerness on the part of the entrepreneurs to adjust productive capacity to demand; this has led us to assume the state of full adjustment in the long period in which productive capacity is tailored to demand and utilized at the planned level. What bears vital importance in the process of adjustment is varying capacity utilisation in the *short period*: during the transition period from one fully-adjusted position to another, the degree of utilization varies with the level of short-period investment, and the size of productive capacity in the new fully-adjusted position depends on the average degree of utilization during the transition period. This implies in turn that the notion of a steady-state growth path in which the initial stock is constantly utilized at the normal level must be subject to re-consideration. (In the formal models in the following pages, we do use the notion of a steady-state growth, but from a perspective quite different from the usual ones.)

To take the normal distribution of income as constant is to reflect the political, institutional and financial aspects of a capitalist economy. When we take the real wage rate as given, we are conceiving the distribution of income as determined by the power balance between the social classes; when we take the rate of profits as determined by the money rate of interest, we are taking account of the monetary

{40}------------------------------------------------

impacts on the real economy. As has been well noted, the latter conception is suggested by Sraffa (1960, p. 33). We are able to follow this suggestion by following Keynes closely by taking the value of investment as autonomous and thus by rejecting the Neo-Keynesian position of taking the rate of accumulation as autonomous. For in the long-period equilibrium, where productive capacity is utilized at the normal level, the exogeneity of the rate of accumulation precludes the possibility of the exogeneity of the rate of profits (or the real wage rate).<sup>17</sup>

#### A conceptual framework for the alternative position

This section will present a conceptual framework which would allow the third Keynesian route to be given analytic treatment. Throughout the argument, constant returns to scale are assumed.

Let  $K_0$  stand for the size of the initial stock at period 0,  $v$  for the technical stock to output ratio,  $r$  for the normal rate of profits and  $s_r$  for the propensities to save out of profits (saving out of wages is assumed to be nil).<sup>18</sup> If the stock  $K_0$  is utilized at the normal level so as to produce the *normal level of output* ( $Y_0^*$ ), then

$$Y_0^* = v^{-1}K_0 \quad (4.2)$$

and the level of net saving accruing from  $Y_0^*$ , which is called the *normal level of net saving*, will be

$$S_0^* = s_r Y_0^* \quad (4.3)$$

In equilibrium, the level of investment and that of saving coincide; the level of net investment ( $I_0^*$ ) which corresponds to  $S_0^*$  in equilibrium will be called the *normal level of net investment* at period 0. Then the ratio, denoted by  $g^*$ , which the normal level of net investment bears to the value of the stock will be

$$g^* \equiv \frac{I_0^*}{K_0} = s_r r \quad (4.4)$$

This rate, christened the *normal rate of net accumulation*, depends on the following:<sup>19</sup>

- (a) the dominant technique in use, represented here by  $v$ ;
- (b) the state of normal income distribution, which is determined in turn with reference to the dominant technique ( $v$  and the labour to output ratio), once the normal rate of profits is determined by the money rates of interest; and
- (c) saving behaviour ( $s_r$ ).

All the variables listed above from (a) to (c), which we shall call the *normal variables*, are taken as given in the following arguments (it being thus implied that technical changes, among others, are exogenous). It immediately follows that the normal rate of net accumulation is determined *prior* to the size of the stock and the

{41}------------------------------------------------

level of investment, and that the normal level of net investment at a certain period is that amount which is required in order to utilize a given stock at the normal capacity—thus it is not an autonomous quantity. The normal rate of net accumulation is therefore such a ratio that, if net investment is taken at that ratio in relation to a certain given stock, then this stock will be utilized at the normal capacity to generate saving corresponding to that investment.

If the initial stock  $K_0$  is constantly utilized at the normal level period by period so that the annual proportionate rate of net accumulation is constantly at the given normal level, we shall have the size of the stock after  $\tau$  periods as

$$K_\tau^* = (1 + g^*)^\tau K_0 \tag{4.5}$$

The sum of net investments undertaken to achieve this size of the stock is then

$$I^* \equiv \sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} (1 + g^*)^t I_0^* = \left[ \frac{(1 + g^*)^\tau - 1}{g^*} \right] I_0^* \tag{4.6}$$

We now consider autonomous investment. It is more convenient, as will become apparent below, to consider the autonomy of investment in terms of *gross*, rather than net, investment. We shall adopt a simplifying (though problematic from a theoretical point of view) assumption that the stock of capital equipment depreciates at an annual proportionate rate of  $\delta$ . Then, the normal level of gross investment at period 0 is  $J_0^* = (\delta + g^*)K_0$ , and the gross investment counterpart to (4.6) is

$$J^* \equiv \sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} (1 + g^*)^t J_0^* = \left[ \frac{(1 + g^*)^\tau - 1}{g^*} \right] J_0^* \tag{4.6'}$$

Keynes's principle of effective demand is to the effect that the autonomy of investment prevents it from being necessarily of the level equal to the normal level of saving so as to guarantee the normal utilization of the stock period by period. If actual gross investments are autonomously undertaken at the levels of  $J_0, J_1, \dots, J_{\tau-1}$  up to period  $\tau - 1$  so that the corresponding annual proportionate rates of net accumulation are  $g_0, g_1, \dots, g_{\tau-1}$ , the size of the actual stock at period  $\tau$  will be

$$K_\tau = \left[ \prod_{t=0}^{\tau-1} (1 + g_t) \right] K_0 \tag{4.7}$$

As has been argued earlier, we conceive the levels of short-period autonomous investment as undertaken in the light of a given state of 'long-term expectation' (LTE). Combined with the eagerness of the entrepreneurs to adjust productive capacity to demand, the state of LTE comes to reveal itself as a series of actual gross investments such as  $J_0, J_1, \dots, J_{\tau-1}$ . However, the series of actual gross investments will take various levels and compositions from situation to situation,

{42}------------------------------------------------

making its consistent analysis extremely difficult (see Palumbo and Trezzini, 2003). The following is designed as a device of ‘taming’ the state of LTE as analytically manageable in the framework of a long-period analysis.

Let us assume that a fully-adjusted position has been reached at period  $T$ . Denoting by  $J$  the sum of actual gross investments up to period  $T-1$ , we can find the value of  $\tilde{J}_0$  such that

$$J \equiv \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} J_t = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} (1+g^*)^t \tilde{J}_0 \text{ ; that is, } \tilde{J}_0 = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} J_t \Bigg/ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} (1+g^*)^t \tag{4.8}$$

$\tilde{J}_0$  stands with regard to  $J_0^*$  at the same ratio as  $J$  stands with regard to  $J^*$ ; thus, to compare  $\tilde{J}_0$  and  $J_0^*$  is equivalent to comparing  $J$  and  $J^*$ . Since  $J$  is the manifestation of a given state of LTE,  $\tilde{J}_0$  is also its manifestation. It follows that we shall have a ground for speaking of  $\tilde{J}_0$  as ‘representing’ the given state of LTE. Whenever there is a change in the state of LTE, there will be a corresponding change in the level of  $\tilde{J}_0$ .<sup>20</sup>

We have been arguing as if  $\tilde{J}_0$  could be calculated from a series of actual investments. But this is practically impossible, for while its calculation requires a definite knowledge of  $T$ , a fully-adjusted position is practically never observable in reality (and, in theory, the common case would be  $T = \infty$ ). Still, the argument has given us some insight and provides some ground for *reversing* the procedure of our understanding. Entrepreneurs have, at period 0, long-term expectations (LTE) of demand for the coming future and thus of the volume of output (or volumes of output over time) that will satisfy the demand. This means that, given the technique in use, they have an idea of a stock of productive equipment at period 0, denoted by  $\tilde{K}_0$ , which would, if utilized to the normal degree, generate that volume (or volumes over time) of output. One can then calculate a level of investment which would bring about the normal utilization of that stock; this level of ‘normal’ gross investment is obtained as  $(\delta + g^*)\tilde{K}_0$  and we may take this as  $\tilde{J}_0$  referred to above.

Now, if the state of LTE is for worse than the current one, the equilibrium stock of productive equipment will be smaller than the existing one (or smaller than the one which would be installed if entrepreneurs would be expecting for the better), and the corresponding level of normal gross investment would be lower than otherwise. It can then be reasoned that *different states of LTE will be represented outright by different levels of  $\tilde{J}_0$  at the initial period*. There is, of course, the following relationship between  $\tilde{J}_0$  and the stock of productive equipment that corresponds to it:

$$\tilde{K}_0 = \tilde{J}_0 / (\delta + g^*) \tag{4.9}$$

This stock is one which, being utilized at the normal degree, would have yielded the level(s) of output estimated on the basis of LTE. In this sense, this stock can be called the (long-term) *equilibrium* stock of productive equipment.<sup>21, 22, 23</sup>

{43}------------------------------------------------

Recall that  $g^*$ , the normal rate of net accumulation, is determined in reference to what we have called normal variables – the variables which represent the persistent forces of the economy: the technique, the saving behaviour of the income groups and the normal rate of profits. Then, the series of investments  $(1 + g^*)^t \tilde{J}_0$  for each period  $t$  starting from period 0 can be conceived as the path of normal gross investments which accords with a given state of LTE.

If the state of LTE is for the better and thus  $\tilde{J}_0$  is larger than otherwise, it is reasonable to assume that actual investment is, on average, accordingly higher than otherwise. The initial actual stock  $K_0$  will then grow more rapidly than otherwise (on the assumption of availability of labour force, which is normally granted for a capitalist economy, thanks to the permanent existence of the industrial reserve army). As Garegnani observes, the capitalist economy shows a high elasticity to the stimuli for a more rapid accumulation – the ‘elasticity in erasing any visible trace of the losses in output and in productive capacity due to the absence of such stimuli’ (1982a, p. 6; also 1962, pp. 74–88; 1982b, p. 33; 1992). This elasticity is sufficient to preclude the necessity for a change in the relation between the real wage and the rate of profits in order to bring saving into line with any change in investment. If the stimuli for accumulation are such that the state of LTE is represented by  $\tilde{J}_0 (< J_0^*)$ , then, after the lapse of  $t$  periods, the economy will have lost productive capacity by the amount of

$$I^* - \tilde{I} = \left[ \frac{(1 + g^*)^t - 1}{g^*} \right] (I_0^* - \tilde{I}_0) \tag{4.10}$$

where  $I_0^* = J_0^* - \delta K_0$  and  $\tilde{I}_0 = \tilde{J}_0 - \delta \tilde{K}_0$ ; similarly,  $I^*$  is the sum of net investments that would bring about the normal utilization of the initial actual stock ( $K_0$ ) continuously from period 0 to period  $t$ , and  $\tilde{I}$  is the sum of net investments that would result in the normal utilization of the initial equilibrium stock ( $\tilde{K}_0$ ) for the same span of time. Of course, this amount is also that amount of saving which will have failed to accrue due to the loss of output by

$$v^{-1} \left[ \frac{(1 + g^*)^t - 1}{g^*} \right] (I_0^* - \tilde{I}_0) \tag{4.11)$$

Even if gross investment should be undertaken along the path of  $(1 + g^*)^t \tilde{J}_0$ , the degree of utilization of the *actual* capital stock would fluctuate over periods. If we average the degree of utilization over  $t$  periods, the average has a higher value as the state of LTE is for the better, and so does the average rate of accumulation (see Appendix and also Park, 1997a). It goes without saying, however, that actual investments diverge from the path of ‘normal (gross) investments’,  $(1 + g^*)^t \tilde{J}_0$ ; even if the normal variables and the state of LTE remain constant over time, what we observe in an actual economy is a fluctuating degree of utilization and rate of accumulation. This fluctuation is aggravated by changes in the normal variables and/or in the state of LTE themselves in the course of economic growth. But, for a given set of the normal variables and the state of

{44}------------------------------------------------

![Graph showing Output versus Time with curves for Actual output, Normal output from actual capacity, and paths (1 + g*)^t Y_0^* and (1 + g*)^t \tilde{Y}_0.](78fcfedad60b6dd255b4cc3c69d02c62_img.jpg)

Graph showing Output versus Time with curves for Actual output, Normal output from actual capacity, and paths (1 + g\*)^t Y\_0^\* and (1 + g\*)^t \tilde{Y}\_0.

*Figure 4.1* The paths of output.

LTE, the series of what we have called the path of normal investments would be a path round which actual investment fluctuates. Then the path of the stock which corresponds to the path of normal investments would also be a path round which the size of actual stock fluctuates; the volume of actual output would fluctuate round the path of normal output corresponding to the path of equilibrium stock for the given state of LTE (see Figure 4.1).<sup>24</sup> Hence

the outstanding feature of our actual experiences; – namely, that we oscillate, avoiding the gravest extremes of fluctuation in employment . . . in both directions, round an intermediate position appreciably below full employment and appreciably above the minimum employment a decline below which would endanger life.

(Keynes, 1936, p. 254)

#### **An aggregate model for the alternative position**

We shall here present a model for an aggregate economy that incorporates the conceptual framework elaborated above.<sup>25</sup>

There is first an equation (a set of equations for a disaggregated economy) that represents the equilibrium condition for the value side: the equality between the value of aggregate output and the sum of the value of replacement, profits and

{45}------------------------------------------------

wages. Assuming constant returns to scale and circulating capital, the following relationship should hold:

$$(1 + r)a + wl = 1 \tag{4.12}$$

where  $a$  = material input coefficient;  $l$  = labour input coefficient;  $r$  = the rate of profits;  $w$  = the wage rate. The equation describes the relationship that should be established if the stock of productive equipment is utilized at the normal level – that is, when the economy is in a fully-adjusted position. The equation determines  $w$  for a given level of  $r$ , given the technique  $(a, l)$ .

There is another set of equations which represents the equilibrium state of the quantity side *on the assumption that, over time, productive capacity is utilized at the normal level and labour fully employed continuously*: the case of Golden Age Growth (GAG). For our aggregate economy, it consists of two equations: one expresses the equilibrium condition that output is used as replacement, net investment and consumption, and the other sets up the condition of full employment of labour (which also serves as the normalization of quantities):

$$(1 + g^*)x^*a + h^* = x^* \tag{4.13)$$

$$x^*l = \bar{L} \tag{4.14}$$

where  $x^*$  = the level of output corresponding to the normal utilization of capacity and full employment of labour;  $h^*$  = the level of consumption when output is at the capacity level;  $\bar{L}$  = the available labour force (which will usually grow over time). The level of output is determined (normalized) in accordance with equation (4.14); this leaves two variables,  $g^*$  and  $h^*$ , to be determined.

The two sets of equations are connected through the saving behaviour of the two income groups, profit-earners and wage-earners. The saving propensity of profit-earners is  $s_r$  ( $0 < s_r \le 1$ ) and we assume for simplicity that the saving propensity of wage-earners is zero. Thus, we have

$$h^* = (1 - s_r)rx^*a + wx^*l \tag{4.15}$$

The system consisting of equations (4.12) to (4.15), sometimes generalized for a disaggregated economy, has been extensively studied (e.g. Kurz and Salvadori, 1995). One of the final results is the following ‘Cambridge equation’:

$$g^* = s_r r \tag{4.16}$$

As  $r$  is given exogenously,  $g^*$  is endogenoulsy determined;  $g^*$ , determined in reference to the normal variables, is the normal rate of net accumulation.

For an effective-demand-constrained (EDC) economy, we need a different system of equations. Even if constrained by effective demand, the economy we consider is in a fully-adjusted position; therefore, equation (4.12) continues to stand as the equation expressing the value side equilibrium. Now, similarly

{46}------------------------------------------------

to (4.13), equilibrium on the quantity side requires that output be equal to the sum of replacement, net investment and consumption; however, for our economy, *gross investment is autonomously given*. We are dealing with a growing economy (including a stationary one), and for this kind of economy, a volume of investment that is given at an absolute level makes little sense. This is where the system for GAG comes in to play the role. The system consisting of (4.13) and (4.14) describes a growing economy (if  $g^* > 0$ ) in which there is *no* constraint of effective demand: productive capacity is utilized at the normal level and labour employed at the full level continuously *over time*. Our theoretical intention is to analyse effects of the constraint of effective demand in a growing economy. Thus, the state of effective demand is best represented if analysis is carried out in terms of *comparison* with the GAG economy.

For GAG to be possible, gross investment is required to be realized at the level of  $J^* = (1 + g^*)x^*a$ . In contrast, in an economy where effective demand is a binding force, the state of effective demand is best represented by a ratio that gross investment in the economy bears to its counterpart in the GAG economy. Let us denote that ratio by  $z$ ,<sup>26</sup> that is, the level of gross investment in an EDC economy is  $zJ^*$ . Then the counterpart of (4.13) for the EDC economy is

$$zJ^* + h = x \quad (4.13')$$

The value and the quantity sides are connected, precisely in the same way as in the GAG economy, through the saving behaviour of income groups: a fraction  $s_r$  of profits and no fraction of wages are saved, so that one has

$$h = (1 - s_r)rx a + wxl \quad (4.15')$$

The system of equations for analysing an EDC economy in the long period consists of equations (4.12), (4.13') and (4.15').

For a given value of  $z$ , one obtains the level of output as<sup>27</sup>

$$x = \frac{zJ^*}{(1 + s_r)r} = zx^* \quad (4.16)$$

One thus observes that higher investment (a higher value of  $z$ ) leads to higher output ( $zx^*$ ). Productive equipment ( $zx^*a$ ) is utilized at the normal level to produce the normal level of gross saving ( $(1 + s_r)zx^*a$ ) that matches the autonomously given, higher gross investment. The level of consumption is also higher ( $h = zh^*$ ). The employment of labour also moves in step with effective demand ( $zx^*l$ ).<sup>28</sup> The principle of effective demand is in full operation. One will also note that a higher saving propensity out of profits is associated with a lower level of output and thus a lower level of saving – the paradox of saving. Despite differences in these variables, the rate of profits and the wage rate remain the same.

As is seen in equation (4.16), the ratio that the exogenously given (gross) investment bears to the endogenously determined stock of means of production is

{47}------------------------------------------------

the same as the normal rate of (gross) accumulation. This is simply a reflection of the fact that the system, even though for an EDC economy, represents a *fully-adjusted position*. The capacity output that will ensue from the EDC economy bears a ratio  $z$  to the GAG counterpart; as was discussed in the previous section, one can take this ratio as the *average* degree of utilization over the process of full adjustment.

The system of equations consisting of equations (4.12), (4.13') and (4.15') – to be appropriately generalized for a disaggregated economy – thus offers a model, designed for a ‘long-period analysis’ (Kurz and Salvadori, 1995), in which the principle of effective demand is fully at work and the third route of adjustment of saving to investment is in exclusive operation. Different states of effective demand manifest themselves not in the form of different states of normal income distribution (and, thus, different normal rates of accumulation) but in the form of different sizes of the equilibrium stock of means of production and different levels of capacity output that would accrue from the full utilization of that stock. Accordingly generated are different levels of capacity saving matching different levels of investment.

### Concluding remarks

The recent surge in the analysis of economic growth and development along neoclassical lines has proved influential both in theory and in practice. According to these lines, economic growth is supply-led and investment does not have any substantial causal power in determining the path of economic growth, since it should passively adjust to saving, which is determined in accordance with supply-side situations.

In contrast, the Keynesian conception construes economic growth and development basically as a demand-side matter; especially, investment is understood to be the engine of economic growth – saving is generated in accordance with autonomously undertaken investment. But several routes of adjustment of saving to investment along Keynesian lines have been identified. The two well-known routes – the ‘Neo-Keynesian’ and the ‘Kaleckian’ ones – are subject to some theoretical problems. There is a third Keynesian route which has attracted relatively less attention. The present chapter has expounded this third route, by way of criticizing the two well-known Keynesian routes and presenting a framework and a model which can be used to show that variations in the level of investment generate corresponding changes in saving through variations in the size of productive capacity. A smaller amount of investment will result in a smaller size of productive capacity, which implies a smaller capacity to absorb labour: the long-period unemployment is a result of wiping out productive capacity which has been caused by a lower utilization of the existing productive capacity – that is, a lower level of investment (Garegnani, 1982a, 1982b, 1992; Kurz, 1990, 1992; Park, 1997a).

### Appendix

We start from period 0. Let us have  $\tilde{K}_t$  stand for the size of the equilibrium stock corresponding to the long-period level of investment  $\tilde{I}_t$  at period  $t\ (>0)$ : that is,  $\tilde{K}_t$

{48}------------------------------------------------

is that part of the actual stock  $K_t$  at period  $t$  which would be utilized at the normal level when the investment at period  $t$  is  $\tilde{I}_t = (1 + g^*)^t \tilde{I}_0$ . Then the degree of utilization at period  $t$ , where  $t$  is sufficiently large, is

$$\begin{aligned}
\tilde{u}_t &\equiv \frac{\tilde{K}_t}{K_t} = \frac{(1 + g^*)^t \tilde{K}_0}{K_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} I_k} & (4.\mathrm{A}1) \\
&\approx \frac{(1 + g^*)^t \tilde{K}_0}{K_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \tilde{I}_k} = \frac{(1 + g^*)^t}{(1 + g^*)^t + \left( \left. K_0 \middle/ \tilde{K}_0 \right. - 1 \right)}
\end{aligned}$$

and the annual proportionate rate of accumulation

$$\tilde{g}_t \equiv \frac{\tilde{I}_t}{K_t} = \tilde{u}_t g^* \tag{4.A2}$$

Then

$$\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{u}_t = 1 \text{ and } \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{g}_t = g^* \tag{4.A3}$$

The ‘long-period average degree of utilization’ over  $\tau$  periods is defined as

$$\bar{u}(\tau) \equiv \tau^{-1} \sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \tilde{u}_t \tag{4.A4}$$

the first approximation of which for a sufficiently large  $\tau$  is

$$\bar{u}(\tau) = 1 - \tau^{-1} \left( \frac{\ln(K_0^*/\tilde{K}_0)}{\ln(1 + g^*)} \right) \tag{4.A5)$$

The state of LTE for the better is represented by a higher level of  $\tilde{I}_0$ , which implies a higher level of  $\tilde{K}_0$ . Thus as the state of LTE is for the better, the average degree of utilization  $\bar{u}(\tau)$  is higher. The long-period average rate of accumulation is defined as

$$\bar{g}(\tau) \equiv \tau^{-1} \sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \tilde{g}_t = \bar{u}(\tau) g^* \tag{4.A6}$$

Thus, the state of LTE for the better will be associated with a higher average rate of accumulation.

We proceed to our argument on the assumption that the normal degree of utilization has already been determined and remains unchanged.
- 5 This version of saving propensities is due to Kaldor (1956). Pasinetti (1962) considers saving behaviour in reference to capitalists and workers, and Kaldor (1966) in reference to corporations and households. These different versions thus have been given the names of, respectively, the ‘functional’, ‘social’ and ‘institutional’ theories of income distribution.
- 6 The state of growth with full employment/normal utilisation is, for (the early) Kaldor, the normal lot of a capitalist economy towards which it actually gravitates; for Robinson, a logical construction designed to show that the opposite is true in reality; for Pasinetti, a normative target which a capitalist economy must try to achieve.
- 7 The assumption of a given technique implies that each industry will vary the stock of its respective means of production at a uniform rate ( $\gamma_i$ ); thus the industrial rate of accumulation ( $g_i$ ), which must be a ratio of two value terms (the value of investment and the value of capital stock), is outright the same as the uniform material rate of change.
- 8 We shall assume that this quantity system has a unique solution for  $x_i$ ’s for a given set of industrial rates of accumulation.
- 9 Another case is one in which the labour theory of value applies; that is, when the proportions between the amount of labour directly employed and the value of the means of production in terms of prices of production are identical in all the production processes. In this case, the value of each commodity is uniquely proportional to the amount of labour embodied in that commodity so that both the numerator and the denominator of the right-hand side of equation (4.1) can be uniquely expressed in terms of a homogeneous quantity, i.e. labour (the heterogeneity of labour itself being assumed to have been resolved); therefrom follows a unique determination of  $r$ .
- 10 In contrast, later Kaleckian protagonists take the rate of accumulation as autonomous, mostly in terms of the ‘accumulation function’ where the rate of accumulation is a given function of some endogenous variables such as the degree of utilization and the rate of profits. The critique of the Kaleckian position expounded in the following pages applies equally to the position of the later Kaleckians.
- 11 Steindl’s argument on the ‘Long-Run Theory of Investment’ in his 1952 book (Ch. 13), which is conducted in terms of moving averages over  $t$  years, is seemingly similar to our argument presented below. For Steindl, however, the relations between the moving averages ‘simply reflect the corresponding relations between annual values, from which we derive them’ (Steindl, 1952, p. 199), save for the propensity to save out of income. His later presentations (1979, 1985) are steps away even from his former one, being carried out entirely in terms of annual flows and stocks.

{50}------------------------------------------------

- 12 Contrary to what has usually been conceived (e.g. Asimakopulos, 1985), the discussion between Keynes and Harrod in terms of the rates of growth on the occasion of the publication of the latter's 'An essay in dynamic theory' does not indicate that Keynes would have considered the rate of accumulation to be autonomous. Referring to Harrod's draft, Keynes argues that both the 'warranted rate of growth' and the 'natural rate of growth' are functions of the level of employment, and the 'normal rate of growth' is determined at the point where the former two rates of growth coincide; the level of employment corresponding to this normal rate of growth is called the 'level of long-period employment', probably less than full employment (Keynes, 1973, vol. 14, pp. 325–36). The level of employment being, as Keynes argues in the *General Theory*, dependent upon the level of investment, it follows that the various rates of growth referred to above are, for Keynes, not autonomous but functions of the level of investment. Also for Harrod, in his published article, the 'actual rate of growth' in a certain period is a function of the level of investment: the denominator of the actual rate of growth is 'the value of the increment of capital per unit increment of output actually produced' (Harrod, 1939, pp. 17–18). It would be redundant to say that his warranted rate of growth and the natural rate of growth are not autonomous in any sense which was given by Keynes to the level of investment.
- 13 The relation between the normal rate of profits and the real wage rate is affected, as Sraffa (1960) has argued, by political or monetary factors and by the technical conditions. As for the dependence of the normal degree of utilization on the distribution of income, see Kurz (1986).
- 14 On the relation between the rate of profits and the rate of interest in the light of Sraffa, see for example Panico (1980, 1988).
- 15 We speak of a particular 'long-period equilibrium' as corresponding to a given state of the dominant technique in use and the state of normal income distribution, regardless of the size and composition of the means of production. The term 'fully-adjusted position' is used to denote different positions of long-period equilibrium according to different sizes and compositions of the means of production. Vianello (1985) uses the term 'fully-adjusted situations' for the same purpose.
- 16 Kurz (1985) argues that an increase in the volume of aggregate investment in value terms accompanied by a different composition could be associated with a decrease in the volume of total output. This is because the respective productive processes produce output in different proportions: the case in question is possible if there is a relatively greater investment in the productive processes in which the unit production of output requires relatively greater productive equipment while there is a relatively smaller investment in the productive process in which the unit production requires relatively smaller productive equipment.
- 17 Thus, Robinson's following remark is partly explained by her Neo-Keynesian hypothesis of the autonomy of the rate of accumulation: '... the suggestion that the rate of profits could be determined by monetary policy seems to be excessively fanciful' (1979, p. 180).
- 18 These differential saving propensities are, however, not essential for our mechanism of adjustment: the constancy of the normal distribution of income makes redundant the role which is assigned to such differentiation of saving propensities.
- 19 In the case of the multi-sector model, it depends also on the composition of consumption demand (which affects the activity levels).
- 20 Changes in the state of LTE will either be induced by changes in the normal variables or reflect autonomous changes in the general 'state of confidence' (Keynes, 1936, Ch. 12). The present chapter does not touch upon the relation of the first type; it needs separate detailed studies. Thus, when we speak of different states of LTE, reference is being restricted to different states of confidence for the same normal variables.
- 21 This concept of the equilibrium stock for a given level of investment is derived by analogy with Harrod's concept of the 'justified' investment, which is 'that addition to capital goods in any period, which producers regard as ideally suited to the output

{51}------------------------------------------------

which they are undertaking in that period' (Harrod, 1939, p. 19). In Harrod, one at the outset has the amount of incremental output in a certain period; then, given the ratio between the 'justified' investment and incremental output (which reflects the technical conditions), one gets the amount of 'justified' investment. In our conception, one at the outset has the amount of planned investment, which determines the level of output from which accrues the saving equal to the given volume of planned investment; then, given the stock to output ratio (that is, the technical conditions), one gets the size of the stock which would be utilized at the normal level for the production of the output just mentioned. The similarity is strengthened by the fact that the stock to output ratio and the ratio between investment and incremental output coincide in the case of steady-state growth. More importantly, both concepts share one characteristic which keeps them away from the neoclassical system; that is, the characteristic that 'the equilibrium stock of means of production is determined by the flow of output' (Robinson, 1962, p. 10).

- 22 Thus, a fully-adjusted position need not be 'realized' in reality at a definite point of time. With the normal variables given, every scale and composition of investment and thus of output has – at any point of time – its corresponding fully-adjusted position, in the form of equilibrium stock. This notion of an equilibrium stock is, in certain respects, similar to Roncaglia's (1978) interpretation of the Sraffa system as a 'photograph' at an instant of time.
- 23 Now one can see the reason why we have adopted gross, not net, investment as the main operating variable. If we had used net investment, the counterpart of equation (4.9) would have been  $\tilde{K}_0 = \tilde{I}_0/g^*$  where  $\tilde{I}_0$  is the net investment counterpart of  $\tilde{J}_0$ . If we consider a stationary economy, in which  $\tilde{I}_0 = 0$ , then we obtain an absurd result:  $\tilde{K}_0 = 0$ . But, proceeding in terms of gross investment,  $J$  and thus  $\tilde{J}_0$  are always positive as far as the economy exists.
- 24 Figure 4.1 is obviously based on the figure of Garegnani (1983); however, the reader will note important differences.
- 25 A generalization into a disaggregated economy requires several additional considerations. With a multiple number of industries, we need determine the quantity of output in the respective industries and this necessitates consideration of investment behaviour at the industry level. A natural accompaniment of this necessity is the need to consider investment financing at the industry level. For fulfilling this need, however, it seems hardly to make sense to refer to saving out of profits and out of wages *à la* Kaldor (1956) or to saving by capitalists and by workers *à la* Pasinetti (1962): aggregate saving is generated that way but there is no sensible way to sort this aggregate saving in order to match each of the sorted part of saving with investment in the respective industries. A sensible way is provided by Kaldor (1966), who refers to corporations financing their investment by means of retained profits (corporate saving) – which will be used for investment in own corporations – and new issue of shares – which will attract part of aggregate household saving into corporations in the respective industries. Despite this, the present chapter has adopted Kaldor's (1956) way, in order to focus on the more fundamental issues. A paper detailing the multiple-industry case is in preparation.

But the conceptual framework is different (and we, unlike Serrano, who follows the accelerator theory of investment, need not rely upon the necessary existence of autonomous investment that is *not* designated for contributing to producing output – such as investment for technical progress).
- 28 Indeed, our EDC economy is simply a replica of the GAG economy scaled to the ratio  $z$ . But this result is limited to the aggregate model. A multi-industry case will have different and more interesting results.

## **Part II**

## **Theory of growth**

{56}------------------------------------------------

### 5 A simple model of path-dependent growth with some Keynesian features

*Amit Bhaduri*

Growth theory which assigns a central role to the evolving stock of long-lived capital goods cannot escape several difficult problems. Aggregate neoclassical models hide them by assuming a one-commodity world in which both capital and output are the stock and flow respectively of the same commodity, while technology is depicted as a smooth production function with the usual properties, and costless, instantaneous substitution between ‘capital’ and labour as the two factors of production. The purpose of such models is to build in assumptions which give the market mechanism an exaggerated role to equilibrate market imbalances under perfect competition, while the accompanying marginal productivity theory brushes aside uncomfortable questions of conflicting class interests and market power over distribution of income. Even more important is the fact that the problem of effective demand is ignored by postulating Say’s law. It presumes that full employment saving is always automatically invested and resources are fully utilized so that the only remaining problem is the allocation rather than under-utilization of resources.

Despite its obvious theoretical as well as empirical limitations, this analytical scheme came to dominate neoclassical academic thinking about growth in the post-war years.<sup>1</sup> In its intellectual defence it was often claimed that growth theory deals with the ‘long run’, when the price mechanism has solved the problem of deficient effective demand as well as that of choice of optimal technology at market clearing factor prices ruling in each period with changing availability of exogenous labour supply and accumulation of capital (through saving being automatically invested). The awkward question is seldom faced as to whether there is any point in discussing such a mythical long-run state when most adjustments are assumed to have worked out satisfactorily. It avoids in particular the problem that adjustments take place through each successive short period to trace the path to (or away from) any long-run equilibrium. In the course of these adjustments the succession of short periods leave their mark on the long-run growth path and create path dependence. This should have been a primary focus of enquiry of any growth process through real time.<sup>2</sup>

Some Keynesian and post-Keynesian models of growth incorporated the problem of effective demand, but hardly succeeded in dealing with the resulting problem of path dependence. Moreover, the problem of changes in relative prices

{57}------------------------------------------------

which arises from changes in the distribution of income during the growth process outside a one commodity world was also not reckoned with in any satisfactory way (Sraffa, 1960). An honest recognition of these problems required restricting Keynesian growth theory mostly to comparisons of properties of steady state growth.<sup>3</sup>

One of the most glaring omissions of the present state of growth theory – neoclassical as well as Keynesian – is an explicit formal analysis of the consequences of path dependence that link successive short periods to the process of growth in historical time. The present chapter makes a modest analytical attempt in this direction. We continue to operate in a one-commodity framework, but try to capture some properties of path dependence through the evolving time structure of capital stock in relation to variations in the state of aggregate demand. Thus this chapter aims to indicate how incorporating the Keynesian problem of effective demand affects the path dependence of the economy.

Our formal analysis is greatly simplified by assuming that investment in the economy over the relevant past had been growing at some steady compound rate  $g$ . This growth rate might even be thought of as some trend or average growth rate with year to year variations around the trend, but incorporating this complication makes the algebra more cumbersome without necessarily adding to our understanding. We assume investment to have a gestation lag of  $\theta$  periods, with investment expenditure uniformly spread over  $\theta$  periods. As a convention for reckoning with discrete time we consider the value of variables the end of each period, e.g. investment of period  $(t - 1)$  is investment undertaken throughout the period  $(t - 1)$ , which is the same as investment maturing at the beginning of period  $t$ . Thus investment maturing at the beginning of period  $t$  is given as,

$$\begin{aligned} I^*(t) &= (1/\theta)[I(t-1) + I(t-2) + \dots + I(t-\theta)] \\ &= (1/\theta)I(t)[\{1/(1+g)\} + \{1/(1+g)^2\} + \dots + \{1/(1+g)^\theta\}] \end{aligned}$$

which reduces to

$$I^*(t)/I(t) = [1/g\theta].[\{(1+g)^\theta - 1\}/(1+g)^\theta] = M, \tag{5.1}$$

where  $M$  is the ‘correcting coefficient’ for gestation lag linking effective investment to investment expenditure at the beginning of period  $t$ .

Linear approximation of (5.1) yields

$$M \approx 1 - (g\theta/2), \tag{5.2}$$

which would be a reasonable approximation if  $g\theta$  is sufficiently small.<sup>4</sup> In approximation (5.2),  $\theta/2$  would be recognized as the Austrian ‘average period of production’, which is the first moment of the time distribution of investment resources locked during gestation. However, when higher moments are powerful enough this approximation might become misleading. It has been shown to play

{58}------------------------------------------------

havoc with many received wisdoms by opening up possibilities of re-switching of techniques of production, and making nonsense of the idea of the rate of profit or interest as the ‘reward for waiting’.<sup>5</sup>

When this linear approximation (5.2) is reasonable for parameter values, a further approximation may be useful through a parameter  $z$  to correct for non-uniform time distribution of investment. Using this approximation,

$$\text{M} \approx 1 - (zg\theta/2), \tag{5.3}$$

so that  $z = 2$  implies all costs concentrated in the first period of production;  $2 > z > 1$  implies costs are more concentrated in the earlier periods of production;  $z = 1$  corresponds to the case of uniformly distributed investment costs, while  $1 > z > 0$  implies costs concentrated towards the later periods of production.

If we assume the average working life of capital goods to be  $n$ , then the capital stock effective for production at the beginning of period  $t$  is given as the sum of effective investments of the previous  $n$  periods,<sup>6</sup> i.e.

$$K^*(t) = \sum I^*(t-j), j = 1, \dots n,$$

yielding a relation between the effective stock of capital and the flow of investment at the beginning of period  $t$  as

$$\begin{aligned} K^*(t) &= M.[\{(1+g)^n - 1\}/g(1+g)^n].I(t) \\ &= M.N.I(t), \text{ where } N = [\{(1+g)^n - 1\}/g(1+g)^n]. \tag{5.4} \end{aligned}$$

For instance, if the uniform gestation period  $\theta = 3$  years,  $n = 12$  years and  $g = 0.15$ , from equation (5.4),  $K^*(t)$  is about 4.12 times  $I(t)$ . Given the same values of the other parameters, for  $g = 0.10$ ,  $K^*(t)$  increases to 5.66 times  $I(t)$ , and 8.06 times for  $g = 0.05$ .

The impact of exogenous technical progress on the time profile of past investments and output capacity can be captured by assuming that the increase in output capacity per unit of investment, or the incremental output to investment ratio is given as  $x(t)$  for each period  $t$ . Therefore, the total capacity for producing output created through investments of various periods from the supply side  $Y_s(t)$  at the beginning of period  $t$  is given as,

$$Y_s = x(t-1).I^*(t-1) + x(t-2)I^*(t-2) + \dots + x(t-n)I^*(t-n). \tag{5.5}$$

Without any technical progress,  $x$  is constant through time, and

$$Y_s = x \sum I^*(t-j), j = 1, \dots, n,$$

which yields from (5.4),

$$Y_s = x.K^*(t) = x.M.N.I(t). \tag{5.6}$$

{59}------------------------------------------------

Incremental output to investment ratio  $x(t)$  for each time period can be decomposed into output per worker  $a(t)$  working with capital goods made at time  $t$  divided by investment cost to build those capital goods per worker at time  $t$ ,  $b(t)$ . For example, at time  $(t - 1)$ ,

$$x(t - 1) = [\Delta Y(t - 1)/\Delta L(t - 1)]/[I(t - 1)/\Delta L(t - 1)] = a(t - 1)/b(t - 1).$$

Assuming labour productivity and investment cost increase at compound rates  $\lambda$  and  $\mu$  respectively, we have in general for period  $j$ ,

$$x(t - j) = (a/b)[(1 + \lambda)/(1 + \mu)]^j \tag{5.7}$$

Using (5.7) in (5.5) and summing we obtain the level of existing capacity for producing output at the beginning of period  $t$  as

$$Y(t) = (a/b).M.[1/(p - 1)].[1 - (1/p)^n], p = [((1 + \lambda)(1 + g)/(1 + \mu)], p > 1. \tag{5.8}$$

Unless  $\lambda > \mu$ , rate of increase in cost per worker would outweigh productivity gain per worker, making technical progress economically unviable. Therefore we restrict the value to  $p > 1$ . In the borderline case of  $\lambda = \mu$ , the two effects of productivity and cost increase neutralize each other, leaving incremental output to investment ratio unchanged over time.<sup>7</sup>

As numerical illustration assume,  $\theta = 2$ ,  $g = 0.05$ ,  $a = 0.12$ ,  $b = 0.4$ ,  $\lambda = 0.04$ ,  $\mu = 0.02$ . We compute from (5.8) the level of output from the supply side (e.g. potential GDP) as a multiple of investment of that period for different assumed values of the life time of capital goods:

$$n = 5\text{ yrs} \qquad 8\text{ yrs} \qquad 9\text{ yrs} \qquad 12\text{ yrs} \qquad 16\text{ yrs} \qquad 20\text{ yrs}$$

$$Y_s = (1.175)\cdot I \quad (1.724)\cdot I \quad (1.99)\cdot I \quad (2.260)\cdot I \quad (2.747)\cdot I \quad (3.077)\cdot I.$$

Given the values of the relevant parameters, we may consider the supply potential of the economy in relation to demand in the current short period. Suppose that the multiplier operating on investment to generate demand is 2, so that  $Y_d = 2.I$ . Let the operating life time of machines  $n = 16$  years, implying  $Y_s = 2.747$ . The economy suffers in this case from excess capacity due to lack of demand, which as a percentage of existing capacity is  $(Y_s - Y_d)/Y_s = 27$  per cent. On the other hand, if  $n = 8$  years, there would be excess demand of 16 per cent of existing capacity.

The model demonstrates how in case of an arbitrary departure from the trend rate of investment an economy would typically tend to have either excess capacity or excess demand in each short period in relation to its inherited capacity from the past.

It remains a matter of speculation how the economy would adjust in response to such short-period mismatch between demand or supply. On the supply side, the rate of obsolescence determined by the depreciation and replacement policies of firms would gradually affect the average lifetime of capital goods. For instance, in

{60}------------------------------------------------

the above numerical example a lowering of average lifetime from 16 to about 9 years would eliminate an excess capacity of 27 per cent. However, for this to be possible demand has to persist at that particular level for a sufficiently long time, and expectations about the level of demand have to be firm enough to pursue such depreciation and replacement policy over a sufficiently long time. This makes clear why practical policies have to operate mostly on the demand side by stimulating investment, rather than relying on the supply-side adjustments. Moreover, persistent excess demand or supply might also certainly affect the pace of adoption of technical progress, which has been assumed to be an exogenous constant in this model. For instance, persistence of serious unemployment would usually mean less opportunities for on-the-job training and skill formation to reduce the future growth rate of labour productivity (e.g. less of ‘learning by doing’).<sup>8</sup>

The introduction of effective demand through an arbitrarily given level of investment as the consequence of an independent investment function in the current period has interesting implications on how the growth path would be affected . First, consider the stability of the growth path. If lack of demand resulting in significant excess capacity persists for a while, low capacity utilization will affect negatively the climate for investment (acceleration-like effect), and might depress private investment. In turn, this would further reduce effective demand and capacity utilization, pushing the private enterprise economy along an unstable path towards depression. In the opposite case of high investment and over-utilization of capacity the economy would also move towards higher accelerating growth and inflation. In short, feedbacks between investment and capacity utilization reinforces Harrod’s (1939) original formulation arguing that the growth process of an unregulated market economy is placed on a knife edge.<sup>9</sup>

Consider next the role of the price mechanism in correcting imbalances. While the present model resembles standard ‘vintage models’ in many ways, it differs in one significant way. Standard vintage models followed the Ricardian closure rule according to which the marginal machine satisfies the zero profit (rent) condition to determine the life time of machines in use.<sup>10</sup> By introducing the role of effective demand the present model shows how the binding constraint of demand might make the profit maximizing obsolescence policy inoperative.<sup>11</sup> However, this model suggests that even if the profit maximizing solution holds, it may exacerbate instead of correcting the economic imbalances through factor substitution. A vintage model of this kind allows for substitution at extensive rather than intensive margin through variation in the lifetime of capital goods. Consider again a situation of persisting excess capacity and unemployment which, in a standard neoclassical view of the world, would result in lower real wages and lower unit cost of production leading to longer average life of machines. From the above numerical examples, it means increasing potential productive capacity of the economy. Consequently, the problem of excess capacity is aggravated in so far as substitution induced by the price mechanism affects the average lifetime of capital works in the wrong direction.<sup>12</sup>

The consequence of changes in the class distribution of income due to a lower real wage rate caused by excess capacity and unemployment could be analysed further by considering its effect on different components of aggregate demand.

{61}------------------------------------------------

A lower real wage is likely to reduce aggregate consumption in the economy because of the higher consumption propensity of the working class. However, it is also likely to increase both the profitability of investment and international export competitiveness, whereas the excess capacity accompanying a lower real wage would have a depressing effect on investment. These counteracting tendencies result either in a wage-led or in a profit- (or export-) led regime depending on the relative quantitative importance of these tendencies (Bhaduri and Marglin, 1990). In the former case aggregate demand contracts but in the latter case it expands due to a lower rate and share of wage in income. Thus in the wage-led regime, lower wage by reducing demand but expanding potential productive capacity through longer average life of capital goods widens the gap between capacity to produce and actual production. The price mechanism in this case of a wage-led regime would be sending the wrong signals for capacity utilization. However, in the profit- or export-led regime, the opposite would happen as demand and potential capacity expands at a lower real wage.<sup>13</sup>

It should be clear by now why the mythical world of an aggregate production function which allows for smooth capital labour substitution with no complication due to deficient demand or path dependence turns out to be a favourite model of mainstream neoclassical economics. It is not merely a convenient pedagogic model that hides the logical inconsistencies of neoclassical capital and distribution theory. By banishing inconvenient questions, it also serves as a convenient device to inculcate faith in the equilibrating demand supply mechanism of the market system.
