## **Part III****Sraffa**

{97}------------------------------------------------

## 8 Sraffa and Trinity<sup>1</sup>

*Jonathan Smith*

Piero Sraffa was a fellow of Trinity College Cambridge for forty three years – a little more than half of his life. In that time the college was both his home and his employer. For nineteen of those years Sraffa directed the studies of its students studying for the Economics tripos. On its part, Trinity provided him with collegiate hospitality, making him part of a community of scholars of all disciplines with whom he could interact; and it gave him a base to work outside the faculty of Economics. On the more prosaic side, the college also offered him elegant accommodation, three square meals a day and the assistance of members of the college staff when he required it. Even in the case of a man such as Sraffa, who could be fiercely independent, the association with Trinity over such a long period of time had a significant impact on his life and work. This association is, however, an aspect of his biography that emerges only in passing from the literature produced on him since his death.

It may now be time to make an attempt to document and contextualize the relationship between Sraffa and Trinity as I believe this will help to illuminate aspects of his intellectual life. In many ways it is not an easy task. Sraffa was certainly an extremely complex figure, a man who was quite secretive about many things and who rarely made any sort of record or gave any written opinion of his work for the college, while, on the other hand, the college's administrative record is bald and matter-of-fact. Occasionally a little light is shed on the relationship by comments in his correspondence with friends such as Joan Robinson and Maurice Dobb, but these are few and far between. Other friends are, of course, still alive and may well be able to give details beyond the written record. With this in mind I submit this piece as a contribution to the biography of an extraordinary man.

### **Admission to Trinity**

On 5 October 1939 Sraffa took part in a brief ceremony in the chapel at Trinity by which he was made a fellow of the college. Alongside him was Ludwig Wittgenstein, his friend and the recently-appointed Professor of Philosophy at the University of Cambridge.<sup>2</sup> Sraffa had, in effect, been pre-elected to the fellowship. When Dennis Robertson left Trinity to become Professor at LSE it created a vacancy in the college staff for someone to teach Economics to its students. Sraffa

{98}------------------------------------------------

had certainly been approached about the post, at least informally, by 1 December 1938, as Wittgenstein wrote to him with advice about the matter on this date (McGuinness 2008: 288). However, it was not until a meeting of 10 February the following year that the college council decided by a majority to offer Sraffa a lectureship in Economics to be held from 1 October 1939, with the promise that he would be elected Fellow in that month. He must have had some misgivings in leaving King's, the College of his sponsor Keynes, where he had held certain privileges but not a fellowship since his arrival in Cambridge. He also had misgivings about joining Trinity, not least because his friend Maurice Dobb, despite having supervised students in Economics there since 1926 when he had been forced out of Pembroke, had yet to be made a fellow. If by declining the position Sraffa could have engineered the post for Dobb, he would certainly have done so. He did discuss this possibility with both Dobb and Robertson but they indicated that there was no chance of Dobb being appointed at that time – Dobb himself insisting that he would prefer the appointment of Sraffa rather than any alternative candidate.

Sraffa canvassed opinion regarding his prospective migration among his friends. Keynes and Kahn gave no advice. Pigou advised against the move because of 'dislocation' while Wittgenstein was in favour for similar reasons (McGuinness 2008: 228). Dennis Robertson did encourage him to accept as he thought he would like 'both the work and the society' (TCL: SRAFFA B11/1). Closer to Sraffa than all of these, with the exception of Keynes, was Joan Robinson, in whom he confided his concerns in a remarkable letter of 15 February (KCMAC: JVR 7/431/27–32), citing in addition to his relationship with Dobb a low self-esteem and a dislike of the way in which fellowships were lauded in Cambridge far beyond their value. This letter in the King's College Modern Archive Centre is by far our best source for the background to Sraffa's move to Trinity.

Sraffa replied to the offer of a lectureship from the Master of Trinity, Sir J. J. Thomson, with a request to be given time to consider the matter, but ultimately accepted. Although he thought it would make little difference from his personal point of view whether he moved to Trinity or not, he seems to have been persuaded by two considerations. The first was that, all things being equal, a change was to be preferred. The second, more concrete, reason was that he felt that he was 'fairly idle' and was in danger of becoming completely so once the Ricardo edition was published.<sup>3</sup> He calculated that the moderate amount of compulsory work that a college lectureship entailed might act as a stimulus and encourage him to do some research work of his own.

Though younger than King's, the college he was entering was certainly an eminent one, perhaps the pre-eminent one in Cambridge. Founded in 1546 by Henry VIII on the site of a number of medieval institutions, the college's main task in the first half of its existence was to provide learned clergy for the church, occasionally producing great scholars such as Isaac Barrow, John Ray and, of course, Isaac Newton. It was not until the latter part of the eighteenth century that aspects that we would recognize as belonging to a modern university began to appear. At the same time Mathematics became the dominant subject in examinations

{99}------------------------------------------------

for the bachelor's degree. By the early part of the nineteenth century Trinity had usurped the position of St John's as the largest college within the university, and so it was 'the undisputed giant . . . a university within the university' as Christopher Brooke would have it (Brooke 1993: 69). The second half of the nineteenth century saw a rapid increase in new disciplines that students could study for honours at Cambridge, including Economics, though for a time the subject was yoked with Law in the Moral Sciences Tripos. Indeed, it was not until 1905 that Cambridge University first allowed its students to take an honours degree purely in Economics. Coincidentally, the previous year Lord Rayleigh became the first Trinity man to be awarded the Nobel Prize. He was part of a group of remarkable scientists who increased the college's fame further by carrying off what still seems a remarkable number of Nobel Prizes for a single college (though at no time could the college justifiably uphold the oft-heard claim that it had produced more Nobel laureates than France). Nonetheless, when Sraffa was admitted to the fellowship the Master, Sir J. J. Thomson, was a laureate as were five other men of the status of fellow or honorary fellow. Thus Sraffa could not fail to be aware of the historical significance and the academic prowess of the college that he was joining.

#### **Friends, colleagues and collaborators**

To help ease him into his new surroundings, Sraffa was made a member of high table six months before his fellowship began. Much of the social life for senior members was based around the communal aspects of college life, many of which could be traced back to the cloistered origins of such institutions. Chief among the communal areas for senior members were the high table, where they met to eat, the combination room, where they retired after eating, and the parlour. The interaction between fellows that these common areas encouraged could be most fruitful. Here friendships could be made and academic and political alliances forged. Whereas in the faculties academics from similar subjects congregated together, at high table many subjects were represented and physicists might socialize with classicists and economists with linguists. Thus it was possible to discuss one's work with academics of different disciplines and to find men prepared to help with research, leading to a cross-fertilization of ideas. Although Sraffa tended to play his cards close to his chest, even with his friends, when discussing his research, because of this mix of social and academic interaction, it is not surprising that when Sraffa required advice and assistance for his work he turned to other Trinity men.

Sraffa already had friends at Trinity. Though not a fellow, Maurice Dobb was a member of high table and Dennis Robertson would also dine there on his return to Cambridge. Amartya Sen has commented that the fact that three such different economists were able to peacefully co-exist in Trinity in the 1950s was one of the reasons he chose the college over others when he first came to Cambridge (Frangmyr 1999). For people who had studied outwith the Oxbridge system, the communal aspects of college life at a senior level could provoke different reactions. We have already noted Sraffa's suspicion of the excess weight given to college

{100}------------------------------------------------

fellowships, but he does admit that this feeling may have been exaggerated by the fact that, coming from the Italian academic system, such positions were alien to him. Wittgenstein, it would appear, did not particularly care for what he saw as the typical Cambridge don. Abram Besicovitch, on the other hand, ‘organised his family life so that he could dine in the masculine setting of high table each evening, and drink port after dinner with the bachelors G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood and other Trinity intellectuals’ (Domb 2004: 509–11).

Wittgenstein was, of course, one of the fellows of Trinity that Sraffa had known before he was admitted to the college and with whom he had for some time enjoyed good relations, although the philosopher’s style of reasoning did begin to tell on the Italian economist. In fact, although in 1938 Sraffa had given Wittgenstein extremely good advice on the situation in Austria and persuaded him not to return to his homeland for fear of his not being able to leave, once they became members of the same college their relationship deteriorated as they seemed to grow apart. It is not surprising as Wittgenstein accused Sraffa of having a narrow intellectual outlook (McGuinness 2008: 301). When Wittgenstein decided to resign his chair and leave Cambridge he wrote to Sraffa to discuss the breakdown in their relationship from 1940 onwards and chose to describe it in the following terms: ‘For, gradually’, he said, ‘you seemed to me to become a Trinity Don: stiff, stand-offish and unfriendly’ (McGuinness 2008: 416). But if Wittgenstein grew distant, other friendships were to be made. In addition to Dobb and Robertson he became friendly with Abram Besicovitch, who would play a crucial part in assisting Sraffa with the equations for *Production of Commodities*. Soon G. M. Trevelyan and his wife Janet, who had played an instrumental role in ensuring Sraffa could enter Britain in the 1920s, would take possession of the Master’s lodge and later E. H. Carr, author of a vast multi-volume history of the Soviet Union, was saved from the intellectual wilderness by the college, which appointed him to a senior research fellowship. In addition to these established academics, younger men, in whose college education Sraffa had played a part, such as Robert Neild, Amartya Sen and, later, Pierangelo Garegnani, would be elected to the fellowship.

One aspect of the Trinity Fellowship was that because of its large size – it consisted of 74 members in 1939 – it could not be homogeneous and could accommodate people, like Sraffa, who had become dislocated, whether geographically, as a cause of religious or political persecution or intellectually, because of their academic or social views. Wittgenstein, of course, became such an individual after the annexation by Germany of Austria, but Dobb too was at times shunned for both his political views and his decision to divorce his first wife, while Carr became isolated by his decision to make the early Soviet Union the subject of his researches. There were others: Otto Frisch, who became a fellow in 1948, had been dismissed from his academic post in Hamburg when Hitler came to power and Walter Ullman, the Austrian lawyer and historian, forced to flee to Britain by the Anschluss, became a fellow in 1959.

With seniority came responsibility. It was, and still is, a part of college life for each fellow to help share the administrative burden of running the college. Although there was no formal rota, it was expected that fellows who stayed at

{101}------------------------------------------------

Trinity for some time would take their turn on the college council or on the various college committees. Some fellows, of course, are keener on this aspect of college life than others and Sraffa clearly was not. It is, perhaps, something of a black mark against him that he was never a member of the college council and rarely of its committees. This might partly be explained by his reticent nature, but he managed to conquer this sufficiently to take part in faculty administration and politics, which in the post-war Cambridge Economics Faculty could be rather a dangerous business. What does seem to be the case is that he does not seem to have shared with his colleagues what might be termed an Anglo-Saxon sense of duty, the absence of which he explained in a letter to Joan Robinson when considering the offer of a Trinity fellowship: ‘I find that if I had been properly educated,’ he writes, ‘my first consideration would be “my duty” to somebody or other, say to the world’ (KCMAC: JVR 7/431/27–32). Thus his contribution to college life was essentially an academic rather than an administrative one.

#### College lecturer in Economics

Sraffa’s appointment at Trinity was no sinecure. He was a ‘Title C’ Fellow, a college officer with the duties of a lecturer in Economics (TCL: SRAFFA B11/1). However, the responsibilities of the post were quite different from those in the faculty as they centred around the direction of studies and the supervision of students singly, or in small groups, so Sraffa’s well-known fear of lecturing was not an issue. It was the collegiate system of supervisions – developed initially by reformers in Trinity in the 1870s – that set Cambridge apart and was at the heart of the university’s dualistic system of teaching. So while the faculties organized lecture series on various aspects of their subjects – the very type of lectures that Sraffa had to withdraw from because of his strong dislike of giving them – the colleges provided a more personal form of teaching in parallel. In the context of students studying Economics, Keith Tribe describes the situation succinctly:

All faculty members were permitted a maximum of 40 lecture hours a year. . . . The lecture list was published in *The Reporter*<sup>4</sup> and students went to whichever lectures they saw fit. They also attended, singly or in pairs, a weekly college supervision which was the principal source of guidance for their studies. A weekly essay was usually prepared for and discussed in each supervision, placing a premium on the rapid assimilation of material and the construction of arguments. [Very much appreciated by able and motivated students, but less effective in the less able or poorly motivated.]

(Tribe 2000: 226)

An arrangement between the University and the colleges directed that, as Sraffa had faculty responsibility for directing research studies, he was unable to undertake a full quota of college instruction of 12 hours per week, but did six hours at half stipend. His sole colleague in teaching Economics to Trinity students at this time was Dobb.

{102}------------------------------------------------

However, soon after acquiring Sraffa's services the College nearly lost them again, as following the outbreak of German attacks on Britain, the authorities responded by interning all German and Italian aliens. While Wittgenstein had recently taken British citizenship, Sraffa proudly retained his Italian passport, and, though Keynes tried to delay his internment by insisting he remain in hospital, where he was being treated for an attack of shingles, he was soon taken to a camp on the Isle of Man. He was not the only Trinity man so treated; Hans Heilbronn, the German-Jewish mathematical Fellow of Trinity and F G Friedlander,<sup>5</sup> who was then of BA status, were also interned. A meeting of the college council on 19 June decided to appeal to the War Office in an attempt to free all three of them, but ultimately, after informal discussion with the authorities, no such appeal was made. With transportation to a colonial destination, probably Canada, in the offing, Sraffa considered a move to the New School in New York, which seems to have acted as a conduit into the USA for academic refugees, though he clearly wished to stay in Cambridge. In the end it was Keynes who proved to be the hero, using his influence within Whitehall to ensure Sraffa's release. A. S. F. Gow, a long-standing Fellow of Trinity, gave notice to his students engaged in military duties of Sraffa's return thus:

The Home Office, after 5 months' shameful bungling, has begun to release respectable aliens. Our Italian economist is back; our German mathematician is released but has joined the Pioneer Corps; and a German engineer whom we elected to a Fellowship while in a concentration camp in Canada is to be let out.  
(Gow 1945: 61)

On his return to college, Sraffa was faced with the problem of diminishing student numbers, with so many Trinity men in uniform. The number of Economics students was further affected by the fact that it was not regarded by the government as a reserved subject, so would-be students could not put off their call-up into the forces by two years in order to undertake studies in Economics as was possible with technical and medical subjects. In 1940/1 there were only four men in Trinity taking Part I of the Economics Tripos and three taking Part II, and it was a matter of discussion whether the college could afford to employ two lecturers in the subject in wartime, putting Dobb's position in the college at risk. For, although Dobb had taught for the college since the 1920s, Sraffa as a Fellow was now the senior of the two. The council had already reduced Sraffa's stipend to payment on a pro-rata basis, which reduced his income from teaching at Trinity to between £30 and £40. Discussions between John Burnaby, the Senior Tutor, and Sraffa on the subject of whether the college should continue to employ Dobb revealed that Sraffa would prefer an arrangement 'which preserved Mr Dobb's connection with the college' (Senior Tutor's Report, 9 January 1941). Ultimately a decision was reached in January 1941. Dobb was to be paid £50 a year to retain his services with the understanding that he would also receive payment if he was required to supervise any students for Part I of the tripos. When the situation was reviewed in the long vacation 1942 it was decided that the arrangement might still prove

{103}------------------------------------------------

expensive, but Sraffa once again interceded on Dobb's behalf, insisting the college should continue to employ him, both in recognition of his services to Trinity and in order to give it a lien upon him at the end of the war (Senior Tutor's Report, Long Vacation 1942). The arrangement seems to have been amenable to both men and continued in operation for the duration of the War. Sraffa is to be commended for his advocacy on behalf of his friend and colleague and in saving Dobb for Trinity and perhaps for Cambridge. He must have felt vindicated when Trinity finally rewarded Dobb for his services to the college by electing him to a fellowship in 1948.

Perhaps encouraged by the lack of students to teach, as well as the progress of the Ricardo Edition before the discovery of the Mill–Ricardo papers, Sraffa turned once again to the intellectual concepts he had begun to develop in the late 1920s and which were to culminate in *Production of Commodities*. He had originally enlisted the help of Frank Ramsey of King's College to assist him in formulating his equations, but with Ramsey dead it seemed natural to ask the help of a mathematician from among the Fellowship of Trinity. The choice fell on Abram Besicovitch, who was to provide so much assistance, especially in the latter stages of bringing Sraffa's equations together in the late 1950s. Whether Besicovitch was the best man in Cambridge to attack Sraffa's problems is unclear, though he was certainly able to produce the equations Sraffa wanted. It seems to me that the important factor was that Sraffa had come to know him through Trinity, clearly got on with him; and he was at hand, which made it easier for both parties. By 1942 meetings with Besicovitch are regularly noted in Sraffa's diaries (see Kurz and Salvadori 2000), and by 1943, with the help of the mathematician, Sraffa had achieved the important breakthrough in the problem that he was experiencing with regard to fixed capital (Kurz and Salvadori 2008). Their academic relationship continued, on and off, until publication in 1960.

Following the cessation of hostilities, normality gradually returned to the college and the number of students reading economics began to rise, as did the workload of Sraffa and Dobb. From 14 economics students resident in 1947, numbers leapt to 43 the following year and fluctuated between 40 and 60 throughout most of the 1950s. In the early post-war period, the burden seems to have been shared between the two men reasonably equally, given the fact that Dobb was required by Trinity to work for twice as many hours a week as Sraffa. However, as numbers reading economics gradually increased it appears that Sraffa took on fewer men to supervise. The basic division of labour between the two men saw Dobb take on those reading for Part I while Sraffa took most, but not all, of them intending to work for Part II, who were fewer in number. Students attempting the preliminary examination were shared. Details of Sraffa's weekly appointments with his students – generally three-quarters of an hour each – can be found in his diaries. Originally it may have seemed sensible that Dobb take on the larger numbers that Part I involved. However, this was not only because Dobb was required to supervise for more hours a week than Sraffa, but because Sraffa was, in many ways, unsuited to teach a type of economics of which he was critical to students to whom the subject was comparatively new in order to help them pass

{104}------------------------------------------------

the tripos. Sraffa really came into his own with more advanced students, with whom he could engage in real debate. Given Tribe's assertion that the supervision system motivated the better students while demotivating the less able, this might be the reason we get such inconsistent assessments of Sraffa's abilities as a teacher.

Tribe also gives ample statistical evidence to back up the assertion by Harry Johnson, who was a student and lecturer in the decade after World War II, that many students saw Part I as being a soft option, with only those committed to studying economics taking Part II. Consequently most Cambridge Economists spent a great deal of time in supervisions with students who would only manage a third class in Part I. This is a fate which Sraffa would no doubt have hated. A good percentage of students who took Part I opted to change subject for their third year to history or law. The latter was an especially popular strategy, being a convenient way of avoiding the study of Roman Law by avoiding Law Part I (Tribe 2000: 226). Thus the ratio of Trinity men taking Part I Economics compared with those studying for Part II increased. In 1950 18 Trinity men took Part I, with nine taking Part II, while in 1958 the comparative numbers were 37 and 13. But as numbers taking Part I increased, Sraffa supervised a lower proportion of Trinity men studying Economics while Dobb shouldered most of the burden. Of course, since 1948 Dobb had been assisting Sraffa in preparing the Ricardo edition for publication and he may have considered that taking a greater number of Trinity students was a way of helping his friend, who was finding writing difficult. Nevertheless, as student numbers grew, it seemed likely that the college would be forced to recruit more staff.

As senior fellow responsible for college teaching in Economics, Sraffa was able to exert considerable influence on the choice of personnel who supervised students in the subject at Trinity. We have already seen that Dobb finally became a fellow of Trinity after more than 20 years' work for the college: this was not without Sraffa's assistance. Lectureships and assistant lectureships were awarded by the College Council on the advice of the Education Committee, but before reporting to the Council the Education Committee itself took advice from fellows teaching the relevant subject. When the committee met in 1948, Sraffa gave a verbal report on the state of teaching in economics and on the basis of this the committee proposed Dobb for a Lectureship in Economics with the promise of a fellowship. This the Council were happy to approve. From time to time Sraffa was able to request additions to the staff, either to cover for leave of absence or because student numbers were high. Subsequently, such verbal reports by Sraffa resulted in Robert Neild, David Champernowne and Amartya Sen being appointed to college teaching posts held with fellowships.<sup>6</sup>

Both the University and the colleges recognized the need to grant teaching staff periods of sabbatical leave in order to pursue their researches. To coincide with a sabbatical allowed by the Economics Faculty, Sraffa applied for leave of absence from Trinity for the academic year 1954–5. As Sraffa had been a teaching fellow since 1939 and had thus served for many more than the 21 terms required by statute to qualify for leave of absence, the Senior Tutor was able to recommend to the College Council that the application for leave be granted; particularly as at the

{105}------------------------------------------------

same time they appointed K. E. Burrill, a member of the college but fellow of St Catharine's, as lector in Economics for 1952–35 with the expectation that he would also cover for Sraffa while he was absent. However, as he too took sabbatical leave, Aubrey Silberston was drafted in to augment Dobb's college teaching. When applying, Sraffa clearly indicated that his intention was to pursue research while on leave, presumably with the intention of picking up again his notes for *Production of Commodities*. In fact, he spent the first term of his sabbatical in China and Russia before returning to his work. As Dobb wrote to Rudolph Schlesinger, 'Piero is just back from interesting voyagings on the other side of the world; Ricardo Vol X should be out about February and he's now off for a stay in Majorca – hoping to do some work (non-Ricardo) of his own' (Pollitt 1990: 526). As it was, the faculty had difficulties in providing teaching and he was recalled to Cambridge shortly after completing the Majorca draft of the earlier chapters, and the college allowed him also to take leave of absence in the academic year 1956–7. So, in addition to the end of the scholarly work for the Ricardo edition, we might add the withdrawal of college teaching responsibilities in preparing the way for the final push towards the publication of *Production of Commodities*.

Sraffa retired from his college lectureship in Michaelmas Term 1958 as he reached 60. There had been talk within the college of extending the tenure of his lectureship but this came to nothing. He had been the senior fellow responsible for college teaching in Economics for nineteen years, throughout which time he had been ably supported by Maurice Dobb and a number of younger men. Although in this time Trinity was not the outstanding college for the subject, Sraffa had played his part in the education of men such as Robert Neild, Amartya Sen, Charles Goodhart, Michael Bacharach and Pierangelo Garegnani, who all went on to have substantial academic careers. He had, of course, influenced many more young economists from other colleges through his work with the faculty and, in addition to his formal duties, he must also have had an influence in more informal ways.

#### Retired fellow

On retirement, Sraffa was not simply cast out. One of the more endearing aspects of life in the established colleges was that fellows of a certain seniority retained their fellowship for life. This had both social and intellectual benefits. Sraffa could continue with his research and contribute to Trinity's intellectual life, while enjoying the companionship and assistance that collegiate life was able to offer. And as life necessarily became more difficult, there was help at hand in the shape of colleagues for advice and porters, bedders and a works department to help with any problems that might emerge. He was also allowed to retain his splendid set of rooms in Nevile's Court, which owed their grandeur to the necessity of extending the Court westward in order to accommodate Wren's great library and were therefore contemporary with it. When Sraffa became a fellow of Trinity he was offered as accommodation a teaching set in Nevile's Court, close to the Hall, as he was then living with his mother.

{106}------------------------------------------------

However, following the death of Mrs Sraffa he was able to move into grander accommodation just along the court in G1, next to the Library, in the Christmas vacation of 1948/9. According to Dobb, the move took its toll on their work on the Ricardo edition and work was consequently fitful until Autumn 1949 (Pollitt 1990: 523). His rooms were his Cambridge home for the rest of his life, where he held supervisions and entertained friends and colleagues, only moving to the Evelyn Nursing Home at the very end.

Sraffa's rooms were also home to his own outstanding library of works on economic subjects. The annotations in many of the books and notes relating to them in Sraffa's papers witness the fact that this was a scholar's library, not that of a dilettante. As such, he had many items that were rare and not to be found elsewhere in the country. He could thus be of great assistance to his friends working in areas that were then less well covered in academic libraries. One such friend was E. H. Carr, who had embarked on a multi-volume history of the early Soviet Union for which he relied in part on material in private libraries. Although he does not acknowledge Sraffa by name, we know that he allowed Carr to borrow some items from the library, and indeed that he was annoyed at the tardiness of Carr in returning them as this 1973 exchange with Carr shows:

‘Dear Carr’, Sraffa writes. ‘These gaps in my book case literally drive me to madness I do not remember what they are. I do not remember who has them. By the time I find out, I am quite in a state of rage. Could I now please have them back without further delay.’ Carr’s reply is most respectful: ‘Yes, I have *Annali* 1966<sup>7</sup> and a volume not in the Series by Secchio, they have a large number of important letters and papers . . . Please let me keep them for another fortnight. . . . I am extremely grateful to you because *there are no other copies in the country so far as I know.*<sup>8</sup> I am sorry to be so slow’ (TCL: SRAFFA C49a). Carr was at the time working on the third volume of his *Foundations of a Planned Economy*, with which he was to bring to a conclusion his great history.

Surely the most tragic aspect of Sraffa’s retirement was the decline of his mental health, which must have hit hard a man with so acute a mind. For help he turned again to a Trinity colleague, Lord Adrian, former Master and Nobel Laureate, a pioneering neurophysiologist. In a heart-rending letter of June 1974 Sraffa wrote to him:

My physical health is perfect, but my head (my mind) is vanishing – specially in normal erect posture – it is slightly better when I lie down.

I beg you to get a specialist to come and see me.

I am sorry to trouble you. I have not dared to do so for some time, but now I feel I can’t go on. And I have no one else to ask for help.

(TCL: ADRIAN Box 3)

{107}------------------------------------------------

His problems were, however, irreversible and he suffered more and more from lapses of memory, particularly in the case of personal names. As time went on, the lapses became more pronounced. Sometimes he could be found wandering, having forgotten his destination, and more than once he lost his bicycle, on which he enjoyed rides out to the local villages. On these occasions the fellowship rallied round and usually someone from the college, sometimes a younger fellow, would be sent off to collect him or purchase a new bicycle. I do not wish by these examples to chronicle the decline of a great mind, but to record the fact that it was his association with Trinity that allowed him to live as independent a life as he could for so long as was possible.

Sraffa died at the Evelyn Nursing Home on 3 September 1983. He left his personal fortune, his library and his personal archive to Trinity College, with Pierangelo Garegnani, a former fellow of Trinity, as literary executor of the latter. Later a simple brass commemoration plaque with an inscription in Latin was placed in the ante-chapel of the college alongside those of many great nineteenth- and twentieth-century Trinity men.

The relationship between Sraffa and Trinity was a mutually beneficial one and a good example of how collegiate societies should work. For while Sraffa did play his part in educating Trinity students for 19 years, he was not so overburdened with teaching that he could not devote time first to bringing the Ricardo edition to fruition and later developing the ideas that grew into *Production of Commodities*. In each case he was substantially assisted in his efforts by other Trinity men, namely Dobb and Besicovitch. Beyond this, Trinity gave him a home and a community of scholars with whom he could interact on a social basis, where he entertained his friends with witty observations on private and public affairs (*Times*, 6 September 1983).

## 9 Besicovitch, Sraffa and the existence of the Standard commodity

*Neri Salvadori*

### Introduction

At the end of summer 1996 Heinz Kurz, just back from a period of time spent at the Wren Library to work on the Sraffa papers, informed me that there was a lot of material on the relationship between Sraffa and the ‘mathematical friends’ he thanks in the Preface of *Production of Commodities by means of Commodities*. He also proposed to write a joint paper on ‘Sraffa and the mathematicians’, on the basis of this material. Shortly afterwards I went to Cambridge and I agreed with my frequent co-author to write such a paper. The deadline came from a conference to be held at the Fondazione Einaudi at Turin from 15 to 18 October 1998. We committed ourselves to that title and started working.

I remember that first of all we prepared an Excel file to put the material in some order: one field was, obviously, the date (each single day from the 1920s to the 1950s); another field the content of Sraffa’s diaries during that period; other fields were devoted to lists of documents in Sraffa papers which were either written or commented on or amended during the period, either by Sraffa directly or by other scholars. This allowed the material to be read in the appropriate order.

What little material there was concerning Frank Ramsey proved very interesting: we were able to infer the essence of the meeting that the two friends had on 26 June 1928. It was a very fruitful meeting for Sraffa. Similarly, we were able to reconstruct the talks that Sraffa and Alister Watson had on several occasions both during the writing of the book and while correcting the proofs. But we soon realized that it would be impossible to complete our original project since the material concerning Abram S. Besicovitch was enormous. So we added a subtitle to our original title and left the material concerning Besicovitch to another occasion (Kurz and Salvadori, 2001).

That occasion came when the Accademia dei Lincei organized a conference on Sraffa, held on 11 and 12 February 2003. Of the four sessions, one was devoted to ‘*Production of Commodities by means of Commodities and Mathematics*’ and was chaired by the well-known mathematician Edoardo Vesentini, at that time the President of the Academy. We promised the Besicovitch part of our original project. We implemented our database and divided the material concerning Besicovitch into seven items, but we were able to deal with only two of these items (Kurz and Salvadori, 2004). A third item was added when Guglielmo Chiodi and

{110}------------------------------------------------

Leonardo Ditta invited us to another conference on Sraffa (Kurz and Salvadori, 2008). Hence four items are still missing and I hope that Heinz and I will be able to complete our project in the near future.

The present chapter is strongly related to that project, but it is different in spirit. In those contributions Heinz and I tried to reconstruct the talks between Sraffa and his ‘mathematical friends’ and to locate their contributions within the development of Sraffa’s thought. This chapter, instead, has its origin in the fact that the proof of the existence of the Standard commodity contained in Sraffa’s book (§ 37) was recently debated. Lippi (2008) has argued that the algorithm in section 37 of Sraffa’s book is not precisely stated and does not need to converge to the desired eigenvalue and eigenvector. The first part of the proposition has been known since the proofreading stage of Sraffa’s book when it was sustained by Alister Watson (cf. Kurz and Salvadori, 2001, pp. 272–3). But the second part escaped the attention of all commentators before Lippi. Indeed, examples can be found in which an algorithm corresponding to the description provided by Sraffa converges to a vector which is not an eigenvector and it is certainly to Lippi’s credit that he uncovered the problem. In Appendix A I report the example provided in a paper in which I investigated the properties that an algorithm needs to have in order to converge to the desired eigenvalue and eigenvector (cf. Salvadori, 2008). In an appendix to his paper Lippi (2008) provided a complete proof of the existence of the Standard commodity by using a very special algorithm from among all the algorithms corresponding to the description of section 37 and another special algorithm was provided, without proof, by Kurz and Salvadori (2001, p. 284). The fact that Sraffa did not choose a particular algorithm may suggest that he was convinced that any algorithm would do the job. This is wrong but, as I proved elsewhere (Salvadori, 2008), the job can actually be done by any algorithm based on a continuous function which can start from any feasible point.

In this chapter I want to shed some more light on the issue from a historical perspective. Sraffa was provided with a proof of the existence of the Standard commodity by Besicovitch on 21 September 1944. This proof has not yet been discussed in the literature. In Appendix B there is a transcription of the file D3/12/39: 42 that includes it. In this chapter I will also show that the proof by Besicovitch is incomplete, but it can easily be completed. Once complete, this proof concerns a family of algorithms as well, but all the algorithms in question converge to the desired eigenvalue and eigenvector. Why did Sraffa not use this proof in his book? The final section of this chapter tries to provide an answer.

### **Sraffa’s section 37**

Sraffa starts section 37 of his book with the following two paragraphs.

That any actual economic system of the type we have been considering can always be transformed into a Standard system may be shown by an imaginary experiment.

{111}------------------------------------------------

(The experiment involves two types of alternating steps. One type consists in changing the proportions of the industries; the other in reducing in the same ratio the quantities produced by all industries, while leaving unchanged the quantities used as means of production.)

What Sraffa calls an ‘imaginary experiment’ is clearly what mathematicians call an algorithm: given an initial state, a definite list of well-defined instructions is given to proceed through a well-defined sequence of successive states, eventually terminating in an end-state. In order to formally reconstruct Sraffa’s argument, let us introduce the square nonnegative matrix  $\mathbf{A} = [a_{ij}]$  and the positive vector  $\mathbf{l} = [l_1, l_2, \dots, l_n]^T$  as the material input matrix and the labor input vector, on the assumption that the output matrix is the identity matrix  $\mathbf{I}$ . Matrix  $\mathbf{A}$  is assumed to be also indecomposable, that is, all non-basic commodities are explicitly not considered. Let us continue our reading of section 37.

We start by adjusting the proportions of the industries of the system in such a way that of each basic commodity a larger quantity is produced than is strictly necessary for replacement.

Let us next imagine gradually to reduce by means of successive small proportionate cuts the product of all the industries, without interfering with the quantities of labour and means of production that they employ.

As soon as the cuts reduce the production of any one commodity to the minimum level required for replacement, we readjust the proportions of the industries so that there should again be a surplus of each product (while keeping constant the quantity of labour employed in the aggregate).

The initial state of the algorithm is the ‘actual economic system’. This is able to produce a surplus, but does not need to produce a surplus consisting of all (basic) commodities, so the first step consists in determining  $\mathbf{x}_0 \in \{\mathbf{x} > \mathbf{0} \mid \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{l} = \beta, \mathbf{x}^T [\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] > \mathbf{0}^T\}$  and then building up two sequences:  $\{\mathbf{x}_t\}$  and  $\{\lambda_t\}$ , where

$$\lambda_t = \lambda(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}) = \max_j \frac{\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{e}_j}{\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^T \mathbf{e}_j} \quad (9.1)$$

so that  $\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^T [\lambda_t \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] \geq \mathbf{0}^T$  and  $\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^T [\lambda_t \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] \neq \mathbf{0}^T$ , and  $\mathbf{x}_t (t > 0)$  is a vector such that  $\mathbf{x}_t > \mathbf{0}$ ,  $\mathbf{x}_t^T \mathbf{l} = \beta$  and  $\mathbf{x}_t^T [\lambda_t \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] > \mathbf{0}^T$ . Sraffa comments: ‘This is always feasible so long as there is a surplus of some commodities and a deficit of none.’ However, he does not provide a proof of this sentence. As we will see, this proof is an immediate consequence of the first three theorems provided by Besicovitch. Then Sraffa proceeds to the end-state of the algorithm:

{112}------------------------------------------------

We continue with such an alternation of proportionate cuts with the re-establishment of a surplus for each product until we reach the point where the products have been reduced to such an extent that all-round replacement is just possible without leaving anything as surplus product.

The ‘imaginary experiment’ concludes, in Sraffa’s opinion, when  $\mathbf{x}_\infty > \mathbf{0}$ ,  $\mathbf{x}_\infty^T \mathbf{l} = \beta$  and  $\mathbf{x}_\infty^T [\lambda_\infty \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] = \mathbf{0}^T$ . Sraffa never states that the algorithm may need an infinite number of steps, but we know indeed that this is so. Finally, we have the last paragraph of section 37:

Since to reach this position the products of all the industries have been cut in the same proportion we are now able to restore the original conditions of production by increasing the quantity produced in each industry by a uniform rate; we do not, on the other hand, disturb the proportions to which the industries have been brought. The uniform rate which restores the original conditions of production is  $R$  and the proportions attained by the industries are the proportions of the Standard system.

Hence we arrive at the equation

$$\mathbf{x}_\infty^T [\mathbf{I} - (1 + R) \mathbf{A}] = \mathbf{0}^T \quad (9.2)$$

where, obviously,  $1 + R = 1/\lambda_\infty$ . As Alister Watson, Kurz and Salvadori (2001) and Lippi (2008), among others, have remarked, the algorithm is not well defined since there are infinitely many ways to define  $\mathbf{x}_t$ . Completing the definition of the algorithm means defining a function  $\phi(\mathbf{q})$  such that  $\mathbf{x}_t = \phi(\mathbf{x}_{t-1})$ , at each  $t$ . To be more precise, we introduce the sets

$$R = \{ \mathbf{q} \in \mathfrak{R}^n \mid \mathbf{q} \geq \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{q}^T \mathbf{l} = \beta, \mathbf{q}^T [\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] \geq \mathbf{0}^T \} \quad (9.3)$$

$$R^* = \{ \mathbf{q} \in \mathfrak{R}^n \mid \exists \rho \geq 0 : \mathbf{q} \geq \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{q}^T \mathbf{l} = \beta, \mathbf{q}^T [\rho \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] = \mathbf{0}^T \} \quad (9.4)$$

$$S = R - R^* \quad (9.5)$$

and the set of functions

$$Z(S_0) = \{ \phi \mid \phi: S_0 \rightarrow R \mid \forall \mathbf{q} \in S_0 \\ \phi(\mathbf{q}) \in S_0 \cup R^*, \lambda(\mathbf{q})\phi(\mathbf{q}) - \mathbf{A}^T \phi(\mathbf{q}) > \mathbf{0} \} \quad (9.6)$$

where  $S_0$  is any subset of  $S$ . Each function of the set  $\bigcup_{S_0 \subseteq S} Z(S_0)$  defines a different algorithm which corresponds to Sraffa’s description.

If function  $\phi(\mathbf{q})$  has a fixed point in  $S_0$ , then sequence  $\{\mathbf{x}_t\}$  may converge on the fixed point of function  $\phi(\mathbf{q})$ . As a consequence, sequence  $\{\lambda_t\}$  may converge to a number which does not even need to be close to the eigenvalue of

{113}------------------------------------------------

matrix **A**. This cannot hold if function  $\phi(\mathbf{q})$  has the mentioned inequality properties in the whole  $S$ , and therefore the set of functions to be considered must be

$$Z = Z(S) = \left\{ \phi : S \rightarrow R \mid \forall \mathbf{q} \in S : \phi(\mathbf{q}) \geq \mathbf{0}, \lambda(\mathbf{q})\phi(\mathbf{q}) - \mathbf{A}^T \phi(\mathbf{q}) > \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}^T \phi(\mathbf{q}) = \beta \right\} \tag{9.7}$$

and not  $\bigcup_{S_0 \subseteq S} Z(S_0)$ . This is the extra assumption found by Salvadori (2008). The interpretation is close at hand: the function  $\phi(\mathbf{q})$  is such that  $\phi(\mathbf{q}) \geq \mathbf{0}$ ,  $\lambda(\mathbf{q})\phi(\mathbf{q}) - \mathbf{A}^T \phi(\mathbf{q}) > \mathbf{0}$ ,  $\mathbf{1}^T \phi(\mathbf{q}) = \beta$ , whatever is point  $\mathbf{q} \in R$  and not just in the support of sequence  $\{\mathbf{x}_t\}$ , as Sraffa's description may be interpreted. In the following two sections I will show that Besicovitch proposed a better-defined algorithm and proved that the algorithm converges to the desired solution (apart from a small point to be completed).

### **Towards Besicovitch's proof**

Besicovitch's proof is divided into four ‘Theorems’. Only the last is the required proof. The first three prepare the field. In this section we discuss the first three theorems. Besicovitch does not follow the matricial notation we used above to achieve a more compact presentation.

The first theorem of file D3/12/39: 42 reads in plain English: *With positive prices any distribution of the net outputs can be attained*. This theorem starts from the assumption that there is a system with no profits and positive prices and a positive wage rate. The aim is to prove that industries can be operated in such a way that any proportion in which the surplus is distributed among industries is feasible. The no-profit assumption is not necessary, but probably follows the exercise that Sraffa is performing. Obviously the rate of profit must be lower than the maximum one since the wage rate must be positive and this is really what is needed. In modern notation the first theorem states:

$$\exists \mathbf{p} > \mathbf{0}, w > 0 : \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p} + w\mathbf{l} = \mathbf{p} \Rightarrow \exists \mathbf{x} \geq \mathbf{0} : \mathbf{x}^T = \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{y}^T \quad \forall \mathbf{y} \geq \mathbf{0}. \tag{9.8}$$

Obviously the semipositive vector  $\mathbf{y}$  is the vector of what Besicovitch calls ‘the Surplus outputs’ (net outputs in the above). In order to obtain this result it is enough to prove that matrix  $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}$  is invertible and its inverse is positive, and we know that this is the case when matrix **A** is indecomposable and there is a positive vector  $\mathbf{p}$  such that  $[\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}]\mathbf{p} \geq \mathbf{0}$ , because of the Perron-Frobenius Theorem. However, Besicovitch makes no reference to the latter theorem and indeed the proof of the existence of the Standard commodity can be interpreted as a proof of the Perron-Frobenius Theorem (see Kurz and Salvadori, 1993).

The proof provided by Besicovitch is very ingenious, but may need some explanation. Like the Gauss-Jordan elimination way to solve a linear system of equations it is based on consecutive applications of two elementary steps:

{114}------------------------------------------------

(i) multiplication of an equation by a non-zero scalar, and (ii) addition to an equation of non-zero scalar multiples of other equations. Besicovitch proves that since prices are positive the *non-zero* scalar multiplications involved in both steps are indeed *positive* scalar multiplications. Let us follow step by step this recursive proof. In the first step only the last industry,  $n$ , is considered. Since

$$a_{n1}p_1 + \dots + a_{nn}p_n + l_n w = p_n \tag{9.9}$$

and since  $a_{n1}p_1 + \dots + a_{nn-1}p_{n-1} + l_n w > 0$ , then  $1 - a_{nn} > 0$ . Hence it is possible to find a positive  $\lambda_n$  such that  $\lambda_n(1 - a_{nn})$  can take any positive value.

In the second step the last two industries are considered. Taking account of the equations

$$a_{n-1,1}p_1 + \dots + a_{n-1,n-1}p_{n-1} + a_{n-1,n}p_n + l_{n-1}w = p_{n-1} \tag{9.10}$$

$$a_{n1}p_1 + \dots + a_{nn-1}p_{n-1} + a_{nn}p_n + l_n w = p_n \tag{9.11}$$

and using the first step, we can multiply the latter by a  $\lambda_n$  such that  $\lambda_n(1 - a_{nn}) = a_{n-1,n}$  so as to obtain that the surplus of industry  $n$  equals the input of commodity  $n$  into industry  $n - 1$ :

$$a_{n-1,1}p_1 + \dots + a_{n-1,n-1}p_{n-1} + a_{n-1,n}p_n + l_{n-1}w = p_{n-1} \tag{9.12}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}a_{n1}p_1 + \dots + \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}a_{nn-1}p_{n-1} + \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}a_{nn}p_n + \\ \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}l_n w = \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}p_n \end{aligned} \tag{9.13}$$

As a consequence, by summing up the two equations we obtain

$$\begin{aligned} \left( a_{n-1,1} + \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}a_{n1} \right) p_1 + \dots + \left( a_{n-1,n-1} + \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}a_{nn-1} \right) p_{n-1} + \\ \left( l_{n-1} + \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}l_n \right) w = p_{n-1} \end{aligned} \tag{9.14}$$

Once again, since

$$\begin{aligned} \left( a_{n-1,1} + \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}a_{n1} \right) p_1 + \dots + \left( a_{n-1,n-2} + \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}a_{nn-2} \right) p_{n-2} + \\ \left( l_{n-1} + \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}}l_n \right) w > 0 \end{aligned} \tag{9.15}$$

{115}------------------------------------------------

then

$$1 - \left( a_{n-1,n-1} + \frac{a_{n-1,n}}{1 - a_{nn}} a_{n,n-1} \right) = \frac{\det \begin{bmatrix} 1 - a_{n-1,n-1} & -a_{n-1,n} \\ -a_{n,n-1} & 1 - a_{nn} \end{bmatrix}}{1 - a_{nn}} > 0 \tag{9.16}$$

Hence we can find two positive scalars  $\lambda_n$  and  $\lambda_{n-1}$  such that  $\lambda_{n-1} - \lambda_n a_{n,n-1} - \lambda_{n-1} a_{n-1,n-1}$  can take any positive value and  $\lambda_n - \lambda_n a_{nn} - \lambda_{n-1} a_{n-1,n} = 0$ , that is, we can proportion the two equations in such a way that the output of commodity  $n$  equals the sum of the inputs of commodity  $n$  in the last two industries and the output of commodity  $n - 1$  is any desired positive number. In a similar way we can proportion the two equations in such a way that the output of commodity  $n - 1$  equals the sum of the inputs of commodity  $n - 1$  in the last two industries and the output of commodity  $n$  is any desired positive number. Thus the two equations can be so proportioned that there is the desired surplus of the last two commodities.

The third step analyses the last three industries. By using the second step we can proportion the last two equations in such a way that the outputs of the last two commodities equal the sum of their inputs in the last three industries.

$$a_{n-2,1}p_1 + \dots + a_{n-2,n-1}p_{n-1} + a_{n-2,n}p_n + l_{n-2}w = p_{n-2} \tag{9.17}$$

$$\frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} a_{n-1,1}p_1 + \dots + \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} a_{n-1,n-1}p_{n-1} + \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} a_{n-1,n}p_n + \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} l_{n-1}w = \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} p_{n-1} \tag{9.18}$$

$$\frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} a_{n1}p_1 + \dots + \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} a_{nn-1}p_{n-1} + \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} a_{nn}p_n + \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} l_n w = \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} p_n \tag{9.19)$$

where

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta &= \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 - a_{n-1,n-1} & -a_{n-1,n} \\ -a_{n,n-1} & 1 - a_{nn} \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Delta_1 = \det \begin{bmatrix} a_{n-2,n-1} & -a_{n-1,n} \\ a_{n-2,n} & 1 - a_{nn} \end{bmatrix}, \\ \Delta_2 &= \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 - a_{n-1,n-1} & a_{n-2,n-1} \\ -a_{n,n-1} & a_{n-2,n} \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned} \tag{9.20}$$

By adding up, we obtain

$$\begin{aligned} &\left( a_{n-2,1} + \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} a_{n-1,1} + \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} a_{n1} \right) p_1 + \dots \\ &+ \left( a_{n-2,n-2} + \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} a_{n-1,n-2} + \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} a_{n,n-2} \right) p_{n-2} + l_{n-2}w = p_{n-2} \end{aligned} \tag{9.21}$$

{116}------------------------------------------------

since

$$\begin{aligned} a_{n-2,n-1} + \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} a_{n-1,n-1} + \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} a_{n,n-1} &= \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta}, \\ a_{n-2,n} + \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} a_{n-1,n} + \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} a_{n,n} &= \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} \end{aligned} \quad (9.22)$$

Once again, since prices are positive, we obtain that there is a surplus of commodity  $n-2$ , that is,

$$\frac{1 - \left( a_{n-2,n-2} + \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta} a_{n-1,n-2} + \frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} a_{n,n-2} \right) - \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 - a_{n-2,n-2} & -a_{n-2,n-1} & -a_{n-2,n} \\ -a_{n-1,n-2} & 1 - a_{n-1,n-1} & -a_{n-1,n} \\ -a_{n,n-2} & -a_{n,n-1} & 1 - a_{nn} \end{bmatrix}}{\Delta} > 0 \quad (9.23)$$

and that multipliers can be found such that the surplus of commodity  $n-2$  can take any positive value, whereas the outputs of the last two commodities equal the sum of their inputs in the last three industries. This is enough to find multipliers such that there is the desired surplus of commodity  $n-2$ , the desired surplus of commodity  $n-1$ , and the desired surplus of commodity  $n$ . And so on.

The second theorem reads in plain English: *If the wage is positive and prices are positive, then net outputs cannot be all nought and, therefore, there is a surplus of at least one commodity.* In modern notation the second theorem states:

$$\exists \mathbf{p} > \mathbf{0}, w > 0 : \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p} + w\mathbf{l} = \mathbf{p} \Rightarrow \mathbf{x}^T \neq \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \quad \forall \mathbf{x} \geq \mathbf{0} \quad (9.24)$$

If not, we obtain  $\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p} + w\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{l} = \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}$ , and therefore  $w\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{l} = 0$ , which is not possible. The proof by Besicovitch does not need a *reductio ad absurdum*. If, for some  $j$ ,  $\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_i = \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{e}_i$ , each  $i \neq j$ , where  $\mathbf{e}_i$  is the  $i$ -th unit vector, then

$$\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_j (\mathbf{e}_j^T \mathbf{p}) + M + w\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{l} = (\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{e}_j) (\mathbf{e}_j^T \mathbf{p}) + M \quad (9.25)$$

where  $M = \sum_{i \neq j} \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_i (\mathbf{e}_i^T \mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i \neq j} \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{e}_i (\mathbf{e}_i^T \mathbf{p})$  and since  $w\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{l} > 0$ , we have  $\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_j < \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{e}_j$  as required.

The third theorem reads in plain English: *If the surplus of a commodity is positive and that of the others is nought then the prices are positive.* Note that it is always implicit that the wage rate is positive. The aim is to prove that if there is a positive surplus of at least one commodity (and a negative surplus of none), then the wage is positive and prices are positive. Also in this case it is enough to prove that matrix  $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}$  is invertible and its inverse is positive. In modern notation the third theorem states:

{117}------------------------------------------------

$$\exists \mathbf{x} \geq \mathbf{0} : \mathbf{x}^T \geq \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \Rightarrow \exists \mathbf{p} > \mathbf{0} : \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p} + w\mathbf{l} = \mathbf{p} \quad (9.26)$$

However, in document D3/12/39: 42 of 21 September 1944 this theorem is not proven. What is proven is that if there is a surplus in one commodity and no surplus in all the others, then the equations can be proportioned in such a way that a surplus is obtained in every commodity (even this proof is incomplete: if the input matrix were decomposable, the statement would be false; the proof does not show why the statement holds when the input matrix is indecomposable). However, in document D3/12/39: 42 there is a note by Sraffa saying: ‘Refer to blue page’. The reference is no doubt to D3/12/39: 7, which is written on a blue piece of paper and contains a proof by Besicovitch of the fact that if there is a surplus in every commodity, then prices are positive.<sup>1</sup> The transcription of this document is reported below in Appendix C.

Before arguing the proof of the third theorem I will discuss the proof in D3/12/39: 7. The statement in modern notation is:

$$\mathbf{x}^T > (1 + r)\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A}, \quad (1 + r)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{p} + w\mathbf{l} = \mathbf{p}, \quad w > 0 \Rightarrow \mathbf{p} > \mathbf{0} \quad (9.27)$$

where  $\mathbf{x}$  is, that is a vector of 1’s. Note that the equation a positive vector always admits a solution since it is homogeneous in  $(\mathbf{p}, w)$ . However, we are assuming here something more, i.e. that a solution with a positive  $w$  exists. We will deal with this problem in a moment. Suppose that in this solution some price (at least one) is negative or nought, and all the others (possibly none) are positive. With no loss of generality assume that the prices of the first  $h$  commodities are negative or nought,  $1 \leq h \leq n$ , and the last  $n - h$  are positive. Then, with obvious meanings of symbols.

$$(1 + r)\mathbf{A}_{12}\mathbf{p}_2 + w\mathbf{l}_1 = [\mathbf{I} - (1 + r)\mathbf{A}_{11}]\mathbf{p}_1 \quad (9.28)$$

which is impossible since  $\mathbf{x}^T [\mathbf{I} - (1 + r)\mathbf{A}_{11}]\mathbf{p}_1 \leq 0$  whereas  $(1 + r)\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{A}_{12}\mathbf{p}_2 + w\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{l}_1 > 0$ . Note that this proof holds even if matrix  $\mathbf{A}$  is decomposable, and therefore some commodities are non-basic, provided that labor enters directly into the production of all commodities and, therefore,  $\mathbf{l}_1 > \mathbf{0}$  (it still holds if labor enters directly or indirectly into the production of all commodities, but I will not deal with this issue here). But what happens if all solutions to the system  $(1 + r)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{p} + w\mathbf{l} = \mathbf{p}$  have a zero  $w$ ? Indeed, the same proof can be slightly modified to prove that in this case  $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{0}$  and therefore the unique solution would be the trivial one. This being impossible, there are solutions with  $w \neq 0$  and therefore with  $w > 0$ .<sup>2</sup>

Now we can discuss the proof of the third theorem in document D3/12/39: 42. With no loss of generality, assume that the first  $h$  commodities have a positive surplus,  $1 \leq h \leq n$ , whereas the last  $n - h$  have no surplus (and no loss). Therefore  $\mathbf{x}_1^T > \mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{A}_{11} + \mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{A}_{21}$  and  $\mathbf{x}_2^T = \mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{A}_{12} + \mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{A}_{22}$ . Therefore, Besicovitch maintains, if  $u$  is a real number lower than 1, but so close to 1 that  $u\mathbf{x}_1^T > u\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{A}_{11} + \mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{A}_{21}$  still

{118}------------------------------------------------

holds, then by necessity  $\mathbf{x}_2^T > u\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{A}_{12} + \mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{A}_{22}$ . However, this is not necessarily true. Indeed, if matrix  $\mathbf{A}$  is decomposable and  $\mathbf{A}_{12} = \mathbf{0}$ , this is certainly false. It is reasonable to suppose that Besicovitch assumed that all commodities are basic and, therefore, matrix  $\mathbf{A}$  is indecomposable. Even in this case, however, the proof is incomplete ( $\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{A}_{12}$  is semi-positive, but does not need to be positive) since we may need to iterate the process to bring home the result. In fact, if matrix  $\mathbf{A}$  is indecomposable, we are sure that  $\mathbf{x}_2^T \geq u\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{A}_{12} + \mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{A}_{22}$  and therefore the number of commodities with a positive surplus is increased and still no commodity has a negative surplus. Further, since at any iteration of the process the number of products with a positive surplus increases, the number of iterations needed to obtain a surplus in all commodities is certainly finite since it is lower than  $n - h$ .

The first three theorems of file D3/12/39: 42 are intended to support two facts. First, if there is a surplus of any type, industries may be proportioned in such a way as to get the surplus anywhere it is needed. Second, there is a surplus if, and only if, prices are positive and the wage rate is positive. The relationship with section 37 of the book by Sraffa (1960) is obvious. One of the two steps of the algorithm introduced there consists exactly in ‘adjusting the proportions of the industries of the system in such a way that of each basic commodity a larger quantity is produced than is strictly necessary for replacement’. The fourth theorem concerns the existence of the Standard commodity and will be analysed in the next section.

#### Besicovitch’s proof

The fourth theorem reads in plain English: *If prices are positive, then there exist positive multipliers  $q_a, \dots, q_k$  such that the net output is proportional to the total of every kind of raw material.* In modern notation the fourth Theorem states:

$$\exists \mathbf{p} > \mathbf{0}, w > 0 : \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p} + w\mathbf{l} = \mathbf{p} \Rightarrow \exists \mathbf{x} > \mathbf{0}, R > 0 : (1 + R)\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{x}^T \quad (9.29)$$

The proof is similar to that provided by Sraffa, but is more detailed and closer to the description of an algorithm. It starts by assuming that there is a surplus with regard to all commodities. If there were a surplus only in some industries, then we could find a starting point with a surplus in all industries,  $\mathbf{x}_0 \in \{\mathbf{x} > \mathbf{0} \mid \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{l} = \beta, \mathbf{x}^T [\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] > \mathbf{0}^T\}$ , since the assumption of Theorem 1 holds. Then the second step used by Sraffa is applied. That is, it is found that

$$\lambda_1 = \lambda(\mathbf{x}_0) = \max_j \frac{\mathbf{x}_0^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{e}_j}{\mathbf{x}_0^T \mathbf{e}_j} \quad (9.30)$$

so that  $\mathbf{x}_0^T [\lambda_1 \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] \geq \mathbf{0}^T$  and  $\mathbf{x}_0^T [\lambda_1 \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}] \neq \mathbf{0}^T$ . Then all the equations of commodities for which there is a surplus are multiplied by a common scalar lower than 1. Besicovitch thinks this is enough to obtain that all commodities are in surplus, but this does not need to be true since input coefficients are not all positive.

{119}------------------------------------------------

However, since all commodities are assumed to be basic, the input matrix  $\mathbf{A}$  is indecomposable and therefore we can get the desired result by iterating the same procedure, as seen above, in the analysis of the third theorem by Besicovitch. Let us consider the point in a more formal way.

Let  $\mu \in \mathfrak{R}$  and  $\mathbf{x} \in S$  be such that  $\mu \mathbf{x}^T \geq \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A}$  and let us define the set of indices

$$I_{\mu\mathbf{x}} = \left\{ i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\} \,\middle|\, \mu x_i > \sum_{j=1}^n x_j a_{ji} \right\} \tag{9.31}$$

$$\hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} = \left\{ i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\} \,\middle|\, \mu x_i = \sum_{j=1}^n x_j a_{ji} \right\} \tag{9.32)$$

The aim of this step consists in finding an intensity vector  $\phi(\mathbf{x})$  such that  $I_{\mu\phi(\mathbf{x})} = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$  and, as a consequence,  $\hat{I}_{\mu\phi(\mathbf{x})} = \emptyset$ . Besicovitch considers that this can be obtained if  $\phi(\mathbf{x})$  is the function  $\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x})$ , where

$$g_i(\mu, \mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} x_i & \text{if } i \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \\ \eta x_i & \text{if } i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \end{cases} \tag{9.33}$$

where  $\eta$  is a scalar lower than 1, but so close to 1 that

$$\mu(\eta x_i) > \sum_{j \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j a_{ji} + \eta \sum_{j \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j a_{ji} \quad \text{each } i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \tag{9.34}$$

That is,

$$\max_{i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} \frac{\sum_{j \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j a_{ji}}{\mu x_i - \sum_{j \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j a_{ji}} < \eta < 1 \tag{9.35}$$

As mentioned above, this is not enough to obtain that  $I_{\mu\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x})} = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$  because some  $a_{ji}$  may be nought. However, by construction,  $i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}$  implies that  $i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x})}$  and therefore  $I_{\mu\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x})} \supseteq I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}$ . On the other hand,  $I_{\mu\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x})} = I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}$  if, and only if,  $a_{ji} = 0$ , each  $i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}$  and each  $j \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}}$ . But then matrix  $\mathbf{A}$  would be decomposable. This being impossible, we obtain that  $I_{\mu\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x})} \supset I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}$ . This is enough to say that the procedure can be iterated for a number of times lower than the (finite) number of commodities (also because if  $\mathbf{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ , then  $\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x})$  is proportional to  $\mathbf{x}$ ). Hence we can define:

$$\mathbf{h}_1(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{g}(\lambda(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{x}) \tag{9.36}$$

$$\mathbf{h}_j(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{g}(\lambda(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{h}_{j-1}(\mathbf{x})) \quad j = 2, \dots, n-1 \tag{9.37}$$

$$\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{h}_{n-1}(\mathbf{x}) \tag{9.38}$$

{120}------------------------------------------------

There is one further aspect considered by Besicovitch. In a remark he argued that ‘we may keep one of our industries intact’ in order to avoid all multipliers becoming zero. With no loss of generality, assume that the industry in question is industry 1. Therefore function  $\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x})$  must be redefined as

$$g_i(\mu, \mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} x_i & \text{if } i \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \text{ and } 1 \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \\ \eta x_i & \text{if } i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \text{ and } 1 \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \\ \frac{1}{\eta} x_i & \text{if } i \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \text{ and } 1 \notin \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \\ x_i & \text{if } i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \text{ and } 1 \notin \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \end{cases} \quad (9.38)$$

Further, this function has the property that if  $\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ , then  $\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$ . As seen in the second section of this chapter, Sraffa followed a different, but equivalent, strategy to avoid all multipliers becoming zero. He kept the amount of labor fixed. If we follow this strategy, then function  $\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x})$  must be redefined as

$$g_i(\mu, \mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \theta x_i & \text{if } i \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \\ \theta \eta x_i & \text{if } i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}} \end{cases} \quad (9.39)$$

where

$$\theta = \frac{\beta}{\sum_{j \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j l_j + \eta \sum_{j \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j l_j} \quad (9.40)$$

Also this function has the property that if  $\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{\mu\mathbf{x}} = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ , then  $\mathbf{g}(\mu, \mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$ .

Also in Besicovitch’s proof there is a family of potential algorithms involved. In order to have a proper algorithm we must have a way to define how  $\eta$  is chosen. For example, if we chose  $\eta$  in the middle of the range in which it can vary, we would have

$$\eta = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \max_{i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} \frac{\sum_{j \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j a_{ji}}{\mu x_i - \sum_{j \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j a_{ji}} \quad (9.41)$$

and in general any possible choice could be defined as a choice of  $0 < \alpha < 1$  in the expression

$$\eta = \alpha + (1 - \alpha) \max_{i \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} \frac{\sum_{j \in \hat{I}_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j a_{ji}}{\mu x_i - \sum_{j \in I_{\mu\mathbf{x}}} x_j a_{ji}} \quad (9.42)$$

{121}------------------------------------------------

For each sequence  $\{a_i\}$ ,  $0 < a_i < 1$ , we have a different algorithm; but whatever sequence  $\{a_i\}$  is chosen, it is easily proved that the conditions stated by Salvadori (2008) hold and therefore all the potential algorithms considered by Besicovitch converge to the desired result. In fact, for any given sequence  $\{a_i\}$  function  $\phi(\mathbf{x})$  is continuous and can start from any point in  $S$ .

#### **Sraffa and Besicovitch**

Sraffa did not use the function  $\phi(\mathbf{x})$  used by Besicovitch. He recognized that what is important is ‘adjusting the proportions of the industries of the system in such a way that of each basic commodity a larger quantity is produced than is strictly necessary for replacement’ and that at each step the desired result is closer, but he did not consider the fact that the ‘imaginary experiment’ may work through an infinite number of steps without approaching the Standard commodity.

Why did Sraffa not use the proof available to him and provided by Besicovitch in September 1944? A simple answer could be that Sraffa thought that the exposition of the proof could be simplified and that he failed to carry out the simplification required. This is a possible interpretation. However, there are other cases in which Sraffa made no use of an available proof by Besicovitch. For instance, when in the 1950s Sraffa was faced with the need to define basics and non-basics in joint production, he conceived a definition in terms of a tax on the production of single commodities (a tithe). A tax on the production of a basic commodity affects all prices and the wage rate (for a given rate of profit), whereas a tax on the production of a non-basic commodity affects only prices of some non-basic commodities (if the numeraire is fixed only in terms of basic commodities). He was convinced to use the linear dependence definition we find in the book (§ 58) by Besicovitch (the whole story is told by Kurz and Salvadori, 2004). The tax argument appears in the book (§ 65), but it is a consequence, not the definition. Interestingly, Besicovitch proved three months after Sraffa had accepted the definition in terms of linear dependence that Sraffa’s original idea was correct and that actually the definition could be given in terms of the tax. However, the proof is extremely demanding in terms of mathematical calculations (see Kurz and Salvadori, 2004). Sraffa made no mention of this proof by Besicovitch in his book.

Both the proof of the existence of the Standard commodity and the distinction between basic and non-basic commodities recall the concluding remarks in Sraffa’s Preface to his book:

It will be only too obvious that I have not always followed the expert advice that was given to me – particularly with regard to the notation adopted, which I have insisted on retaining (although admittedly open to objection in some respects) as being easy to follow for the non-mathematical reader.

Despite his interest in the existence of a proof, Sraffa was keen to provide one only if it was ‘easy to follow for the non-mathematical reader’. He thought that

{122}------------------------------------------------

the non-mathematical reader would understand his argument in section 37. If the mathematical reader were to find it incomplete, then such a reader would also be able to find a complete proof, which Sraffa knew existed.

### Conclusion

In this chapter I have explored the relationship between the proof of the existence of the Standard commodity contained in section 37 of Sraffa's (1960) book and the proof supplied to Sraffa by Besicovitch on 21 September 1944, and investigated the completeness and consistency of such a proof. I also postulated some reasons which led Sraffa to omit this proof in his book in favour of an incomplete argument.

### Appendix A. An example

Let

$$\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & h \\ k & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \mathbf{l} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2} \\[6pt] \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix} \quad \beta = 1 \quad 0 < h < k < 1 \tag{9.A.1}$$

It is easily calculated that the eigenvalue of maximum modulus of matrix  $\mathbf{A}$  is  $\sqrt{hk}$  and that the left eigenvector associated with this eigenvalue normalized by the condition (9. A. 1) is

$$\left[ \frac{2(k - \sqrt{hk})}{k - h} \quad \frac{2(\sqrt{hk} - h)}{k - h} \right] \tag{9.A.2}$$

It is easily recognized that

$$\mathbf{R} = \left\{ \mathbf{q} \in \Re^2 \,\middle|\, \frac{2k}{1 + k} \le q_1 \le \frac{2}{1 + h}, \; q_2 = 2 - q_1 \right\} \tag{9.A.3}$$

Finally, let us consider the function

$$\phi(\mathbf{q}) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 - 2\varepsilon \end{bmatrix} + \varepsilon \mathbf{q} \tag{9.A.4}$$

with

$$0 < \varepsilon < \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{h}{k}} \tag{9.A.5}$$

{123}------------------------------------------------

From inequalities (9.A.5) we obtain the inequality

$$\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon} < \frac{2(k-\sqrt{hk})}{k-h} \tag{9.A.6}$$

from which we obtain<sup>3</sup> that  $\lambda(\mathbf{q})\phi(\mathbf{q}) - \mathbf{A}^T\phi(\mathbf{q}) > \mathbf{0}$  for each  $\mathbf{q} \in S_1$ , whereas this property does not hold for  $\mathbf{q} \in S_2$ , where

$$S_1 = \left\{ \mathbf{q} \in S \,\middle|\, q_1 < \frac{1}{1-\varepsilon} \right\} \tag{9.A.7}$$

$$S_2 = \left\{ \mathbf{q} \in S \,\middle|\, \frac{1}{1-\varepsilon} \le q_1 < \frac{2(k-\sqrt{hk})}{k-h} \right\} \tag{9.A.8}$$

Further, it is easily verified that  $\mathbf{q} \in S_1 \Rightarrow \phi(\mathbf{q}) \in S_1$ . Therefore each element of any sequence defined by the conditions

$$\mathbf{q}_0 \in S_1, \quad \mathbf{q}_{t+1} = \begin{cases} \mathbf{q}_t & \text{if } \lambda(\mathbf{q}_t)\mathbf{q}_t - \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{q}_t = \mathbf{0} \\ \phi(\mathbf{q}_t) & \text{if } \lambda(\mathbf{q}_t)\mathbf{q}_t - \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{q}_t \neq \mathbf{0} \end{cases} \tag{9.A.9}$$

satisfies the conditions stated by Sraffa, but

$$\lim_{i \to \infty} \lambda(\mathbf{q}_i) = (1-2\varepsilon)k > \sqrt{hk} \tag{9.A.10}$$

$$\lim_{i \to \infty} \mathbf{q}_i = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{1-\varepsilon} \\[6pt] \frac{1-2\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon} \end{bmatrix} \neq \begin{bmatrix} \frac{2(k-\sqrt{hk})}{k-h} \\[6pt] \frac{2(\sqrt{hk}-h)}{k-h} \end{bmatrix} \tag{9.A.11}$$

The last limit is the unique fixed point of function (9.A.4).
