## 10 Sraffa and long-period general equilibrium<sup>1</sup>

*Duncan Foley*

#### Partial equilibrium: Marshall

The nineteenth-century conception of economic equilibrium was a *long-period equilibrium* in which the profit rates on all capital goods were equalized through competition. (While Walras seems to have thought of long-period equilibrium as a realized state of the economy, Smith, Ricardo, and Marx seem to have regarded it more as a benchmark or center of gravity around which actual prices and profit rates would gravitate.) But in certain key respects the marginalist principle of pricing by scarcity and marginal cost of producing goods contradicts this long-standing methodological precept. From a marginalist point of view the returns to capital goods are just rents (more often in the case of capital called *quasi-rents*), like the return to land, and there is no reason to think at any point in time that the composition of the capital stock is such that the quasi-rents on each type of capital good will represent the same rate of return on its reproduction cost. Walras encountered this logical problem and grappled with it but was unable to come to a completely satisfactory solution.

Alfred Marshall, who shaped economics as a course of study for Cambridge students in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, reasoned in terms of *partial* rather than *general* equilibrium analysis. Since Marshall's analysis is still a familiar part of standard undergraduate economic theory, we will simply summarize its main features here, emphasizing those aspects that play a key role in twentieth-century developments.

Marshall focuses his attention on an *industry* in which a large number of relatively small competing firms produce a relatively uniform output, under conditions of free entry and exit. Marshall distinguishes two conceptions of equilibrium in an industry: a *short-run* equilibrium in which the capital stocks and productive capacities of existing firms are taken as given; and a *long-run* equilibrium in which firms can adjust the size of their productive capacities, even to the point of exiting the industry altogether, and potential competitors can enter. In the short run the firms face a market-determined price none of them individually can influence, and adjust their output so that their *marginal* cost of production is equal to the market price (a consequence of their assumed goal of profit maximization). The industry supply curve in output-price space is the horizontal summation of all the individual firm marginal cost curves (above average variable

{129}------------------------------------------------

cost). The short-run equilibrium of the market occurs where this short run supply curve intersects the market demand curve, and equates the marginal cost of output (which is the same in equilibrium for all the firms) to the demand price, which is the marginal rate of substitution between the industry's output and the *numéraire* good.

But at short-run equilibrium market price may settle above or below the *average* cost of the firms (including the “normal” profit rate as a cost of capital). If the short-run market price settles above average cost, the firms in the industry will be enjoying *economic* or *pure* profit, returns in excess of the normal profit rate in the economy, and conversely economic losses if the short-run market price settles below average cost. In the former case the economic profits will attract new entrants to the industry, shifting the industry short-run supply curve to the right and forcing down the short-run equilibrium price, and in the latter case the economic losses will lead to the exit of firms from the industry, shifting the industry short-run supply curve to the left and raising the short-run equilibrium price. The industry can reach long-run equilibrium only when the number of firms and their individual capacities have adjusted so that the short-run equilibrium price is equal to their minimum *average* cost, and economic profits in the industry are zero (or, what is the same thing, that their profit rate is equal to the normal profit rate of the whole economy). The industry long-run supply curve is thus the locus of minimum average cost points. At long-run equilibrium the industry is also in short-run equilibrium, because the marginal cost curve intersects the average cost curve at minimum average cost.

Since individual firms will always adjust their capacity to the minimum average cost point, the forces that might make the industry long-run supply curve slope upward or downward must, in Marshall's reasoning, be *external* to the firm, that is, forces that lead the cost curves of individual firms to *shift* upward or downward as *industry* output changes, even if they do not change their own output. According to Marshall, these externalities could be *pecuniary*, in the case that they reflected scarcity of fixed resources like land, and were communicated to the individual firms by changes in market-determined rents, or *technological*, in the case where they reflected costs imposed (or advantages conferred) by rising industry output that were not priced as rents in any market.

What is striking about this analysis is that the long-run equilibrium is determined by considerations, namely the equalization of industry profit rates to the normal profit rate for the whole economy, so that economic profits are zero, which are logically independent of the marginal conditions for short-run profit maximization. (In fact, in the case of technological externalities, the equilibrium will fail to equate price to social marginal cost.)

### **Sraffa and long-period equilibrium**

Piero Sraffa first came to widespread notice among English-speaking economists when he published two articles on the compatibility of Marshallian equilibrium analysis with the assumption of non-constant returns to scale in firm technologies

{130}------------------------------------------------

(Sraffa, 1925, 1926). Sraffa concluded that the assumption of decreasing returns to scale was incompatible with a realistic application of Marshall's ideas because profit-maximizing firms would always seek to shrink their scale to lower costs, and firm production would disappear altogether. He also rejected the hypothesis of increasing returns to scale at the firm level, on the ground that profit-maximizing firms would seek to expand to lower costs, and eventually their number would shrink to the point where the Marshallian hypothesis of competition was no longer reasonable.

At this point Sraffa appears, naturally enough, to have begun thinking about the *general equilibrium* implications of Marshallian long-run equilibrium (see Kurz, 2000, ch. 1) in the light of his knowledge of the theories of profit rate-equalizing prices developed by the Classical political economists and Marx. The "normal" rate of profit that anchors Marshall's partial equilibrium analysis would appear in a general equilibrium setting in which several industries co-existed as the Classical political economists' "natural" rate of profit, or Marx's "average" rate of profit, so that one natural generalization of Marshall's conception of long-run equilibrium in a single industry is the Classical conception of long-period equilibrium in which profit rates and wages were equalized across sectors. (The importance of Marshall in the development of Sraffa's thought is controversial, at least. It may be that Sraffa abandoned the Marshallian line of thought entirely in favor of a return to Classical conceptions. On the other hand, it is hard to imagine how a general equilibrium version of Marshall's long-run equilibrium would differ much from Sraffa's construction.)

In the late 1920s and early 1930s Sraffa developed a powerful and insightful analysis of this problem. He delayed in publishing these results, however, until several decades later (Sraffa, 1960). By that time other approaches to general equilibrium theory generalizing Marshallian short-run equilibrium, based on equalization of marginal cost and price, had been developed to a considerable degree.

#### **The circulating capital model**

Because we will come across this notion again and again, let us spend a moment here to formalize it. In order to represent an economy with  $n$  commodities we will regard bundles (or lists) of the commodities as elements of the mathematical space  $R^n$  of *vectors* whose components are  $n$  real numbers,  $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ . We will always regard vectors as *column* vectors, and write the transpose of a vector  $x$  as  $x^T$ . We write  $x \gg 0$  to mean that *every* component of  $x$  is strictly greater than zero,  $x \ge 0$  to mean that every component of  $x$  is greater than or equal to zero and at least one component is strictly greater than zero (so that  $x \neq 0$ ), and  $x \geqq 0$  to mean that every component of  $x$  is greater than or equal to zero. The *inverse* of a matrix  $A$ , if it exists, is written  $A^{-1}$ .

A common and fundamental model of production is the *circulating capital* model, in which the inputs to each productive *activity* or *process* are used up in the *productive period*. (We will see later that this model can be interpreted to represent

{131}------------------------------------------------

much more general temporal patterns of production.) An activity, or process (words which we will use interchangeably to describe production) consists of a vector  $b \in R^n$  of *outputs* of produced commodities which appear at the end of the production period, a vector  $a \in R^n$  of input commodities which are required at the beginning of the production period, and a scalar  $l$ , representing the amount of labor required to operate the activity. The whole collection of, say,  $m$ , processes available to an economy, called its *technology*, can be summarized by  $n \times m$  matrices  $B$  and  $A$ , and a vector  $l^T = (l_1, \dots, l_m) \in R^m$ . Each available process is represented by a column of  $B$ , the corresponding column of  $A$ , and the corresponding component of  $l^T$ .

We can represent the (*money*) prices of the commodities by a vector  $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n) \in R^n$  and the (money) wage by a scalar  $w$ . If  $x \in R^n$  is a bundle of commodities, then according to the rules of matrix multiplication,  $p^T x = p_1 x_1 + \dots + p_n x_n$  is the *value* of the bundle  $x$  at the prices  $p$ . We can also write  $p^T x$  as the *dot product*  $p \cdot x$ .

In the simplest version of this model we assume that there is just one process that produces each commodity, so that  $m = n$ , and each process produces just one unit of each commodity, so that  $B = I$ , the  $n \times n$   $n$ -dimensional identity matrix. If we operate the  $j$ th process at intensity  $x_j$ , the *gross output* of the system will be  $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ . To achieve these levels of operation will require the commodity inputs  $Ax$  and a labor input of  $l^T x$ . The *net product* is then  $y = x - Ax = (I - A)x$ , since it requires  $Ax$  to replace the inputs used up. If prices are  $p$  and the wage is  $w$ , the value of the gross output is  $p^T x$  and the value of the net output is  $p^T y = p^T (I - A)x$ , the total wages are  $w l^T x$ , and the total profits  $p_y^T - w l^T x$ .

The direct inputs required to produce the net output  $y$  are  $Ay$ , and the inputs required to produce those direct inputs are  $A^2 y$ , so that the total inputs required to produce  $y$  are  $(A + A^2 + A^3 + \dots)y$ . Thus we see that the gross output of a system producing the net output  $y$  will be  $(I + A + A^2 + \dots)y$ . If the matrix  $A$  is *viable*, meaning that it is possible to produce a positive net product of every commodity with it, or in mathematical terms, that there exists a vector  $x \geq 0$  such that  $(I - A)x \gg 0$ , then  $(I + A + A^2 + A^3 + \dots) = (I - A)^{-1}$ . In this way we see Smith's point that  $x = (I - A)^{-1}y$ , or  $y = (I - A)x$ , as we saw by considering just one round of production.

#### **Sraffa's conception**

Sraffa adopts the circulating capital model as his fundamental tool of analysis. The assumptions that the number of processes in use is equal to the number of commodities and that profit rates are equalized leads to a set of  $n$  equations to determine the  $n$  prices of commodities and the profit rate. Sraffa then has to work out whether or not and under what conditions these equations give rise to economically meaningful price systems.

To defend the generality of the results he derives in this framework, he makes two preliminary observations which have far-reaching implications.

{132}------------------------------------------------

#### **Joint production and depreciation**

First, Sraffa argues that the circulating capital framework can, with an appropriate interpretation of the commodity space, reflect very general patterns of capital depreciation. The key to this insight is to allow for *joint production*. Sraffa’s idea is to distinguish capital goods of different ages and conditions by making them independent components of the commodity space. Thus we would have not just ‘drill presses’ as a commodity input to production, but ‘new drill presses,’ ‘one-period old drill presses,’ ‘two-period old drill presses,’ and so forth. Thus there might be a process of production that uses labor and new drill presses to produce as joint products, some product and one-period-old drill presses. The new drill press, in accordance with the requirements of the circulating capital model, is completely ‘used up’ in the process of production, but reappears as the joint produce ‘output,’ a one-period-old drill press. Depending on the exact coefficients representing the efficiency of new drill presses, one-period-old drill presses and so forth, this set-up can represent arbitrary time patterns of use-value depreciation of capital goods. But in order to embrace arbitrary patterns of use-value depreciation in the model, it must explicitly allow for joint production.

In the case of joint production one might worry that the number of processes in use would be smaller than the number of commodities, because one process can produce more than one commodity. But Sraffa argues that in the general (or as modern mathematical economics would put it, generic) case, in order to meet a given social demand for output it will be necessary to operate the same number of processes as commodities. A single process producing two or more outputs jointly cannot in general produce them in arbitrarily given *proportions*.

While this analytical device is very powerful and allows for a substantial clarification and simplification of capital theory (but at a considerable cost in terms of the generality of certain analytical results as we shall see), and was also adopted by John von Neumann as a solution to the problem of time-patterns of production, it is not entirely satisfactory. The difficulty is that in this context the ‘production period’ itself is arbitrary. This would not be a serious problem if the substance of the economic results did not depend on the exact calendar period taken as the production period. We could, for example, take a very short period, such as a day or even an hour, and, at least theoretically, work everything out on that basis. But this approach runs into the difficulty that the commodity space itself explodes as the conventional time period becomes shorter and shorter (we need, for example, one-hour-old drill presses, two-hour-old drill presses, and so on), so that there is no natural limit to the analysis as the time period becomes extremely small. (This is related to the fact that the concept of ‘gross’ or ‘total’ output in the circulating capital model is not really well-defined for arbitrarily small periods of production.) Another way to put this difficulty is that in a continuous-time model of production there would be an infinite continuum of capital goods of each type, and the specification of the joint-product technology would be mathematically very difficult, if not impossible.

{133}------------------------------------------------

#### Land and scarce resources

Second, Sraffa argues that the existence of land and other scarce resources does not vitiate the power of the circulating capital model analysis. Sraffa agrees that at any level of social production there may be an “intensive” or “extensive” margin in the use of scarce resources. (The extensive margin refers to the case where the scarce resources are graded in quality, so that the technology that actually determines costs depends on the lowest quality resource actually being used. The intensive margin refers to the case where the resource, say, land, is of uniform quality but limited in quantity, so that an expansion of production requires the operation of more land-intensive processes.) But given the level of production, if there are several qualities of a scarce resource being utilized, there will also be corresponding rents, so that one can, as Ricardo and Marx did, determine prices looking at production with the marginal resource quality, assuming that the rent on the marginal resource is zero. In the case of limited land of uniform quality, the intensive margin will generally require the operation of *two* different processes of production, more and less land-intensive, to produce a given social output. The simultaneous operation of these two processes will supply the necessary condition to calculate the rent on the scarce resource.

In fact, as Sraffa saw it, the problem of land and joint production raised exactly the same analytical issues and could be solved in exactly the same way.

#### No joint production and no choice of technique

Sraffa begins by considering the simplest case, where there is one and only one process to produce each commodity, and each process produces only one commodity. Sraffa, for reasons which we will understand better in a moment, chooses to analyse the case where wages are paid at the end of the period. (This might be justified if the workers’ subsistence wage were paid at the beginning of period, and were already included as commodity inputs in the  $A$  matrix, and the compensation agreement included a bonus at the end of the period.) Under those assumptions  $B = I$ , and the long-period equilibrium (money) prices, money wage, and profit rate must satisfy:

$$p^T = (1+r)p^T A + w l^T \tag{10.1}$$

This matrix equation represents  $n$  equations (one for each commodity), in  $n + 2$  variables, the  $n$  prices, the wage, and the profit rate. One degree of freedom here represents the arbitrary normalization of money prices. We can take an arbitrary numéraire  $d \in R^{n \ge 0}$  and add the normalizing condition

$$p^T d = 1 \tag{10.2}$$

(for example  $d = (1, 0, \dots, 0)$  to make the first commodity the numéraire) or take  $w = 1$ , taking the wage as the numéraire.

{134}------------------------------------------------

This adds one more equation, but the system is still underdetermined, having one degree of freedom. Sraffa argues that this degree of freedom represents the essentially social *distributional* relations of the economy.

The logic of this analysis is somewhat complicated by the possibility, which has not been ruled out so far, that the economy might “come apart” into several self-sufficient subsystems, each of which uses as inputs only its own outputs. Sraffa defines a commodity as *basic* if it is required directly or indirectly for the production of *every* commodity. There is also the formal possibility that the vector  $l = 0$ , so that labor is not required at all. Sraffa assumes that there is at least one basic commodity in the system, and that labor is required in the production of at least one basic commodity, so that labor is also required directly or indirectly in the production of every commodity.

In fact, the analysis of this system is most straightforward if we assume that the system is *viable*, so that there exists  $x \geq 0$  with  $(I - A)x > 0$ , and that *every* commodity is basic. In this case the matrix  $A$  is *indecomposable*, that is, it is impossible to rearrange the rows and columns in such a way that a self-sufficient subsystem which does not require inputs of other commodities exists.

For a given  $w$  (which we might take to be equal to unity), and  $r$ , the solution to equation (10.1) is:

$$p^T(r) = wl^T(I - (1 + r)A)^{-1}$$

When  $r = 0$ , since we have assumed  $A$  is viable, we know that  $(I - A)^{-1} = I + A + A^2 + \dots$ , and if  $A \geq 0$  is a semipositive matrix, every component of this series is a semi-positive matrix, so that  $(I - A)^{-1}$  is a semi-positive matrix, which implies that  $p^T(0) = w(I - A)^{-1T} \geq 0$  since  $l^T \geq 0$ . Thus for  $r = 0$  we have an economically meaningful price system (which is actually proportional to the embodied labor coefficients). Now if  $r$  is not too large, we would expect  $(I - (1 + r)A)^{-1} \geq 0$  as well, and we would have a price system  $p(r) = w(I - (1 + r)A)^{-1T} \geq 0$ . This is indeed the case. There is a maximal profit rate  $R > 0$  such that if  $0 < r < R$ , the corresponding  $p(r) \geq 0$ . Furthermore it is not too hard to guess that as we raise  $r$ , holding  $w$  constant, none of the components of  $p(r)$  can become smaller. (Essentially the economic intuition behind this is that if we raise the profit rate the price in each sector has to increase, which will push up costs in all the sectors.) But then we see that the real wage measured in *any* numéraire must fall as  $r$  increases, since the prices of all commodities will be increasing. As  $r$  approaches the maximal profit rate  $R$ , the prices rise without bound, effectively becoming infinite, and driving the real wage to 0. At the maximal profit rate  $R$ , however, there is a solution to equation (10.1) with  $w = 0$ . From a mathematical point of view  $1 + R = 1/\lambda^*$  where  $\lambda^*$  is the largest *eigenvalue* of the matrix  $A$  and  $p(R)$ , the price system corresponding to  $w = 0$ , is the left-hand eigenvector of  $A$  corresponding to  $\lambda^*$ , so that  $\lambda^*p^T(R) = p^T(R)A$ . Mathematicians know these facts as the *Perron-Frobenius Theorems for nonnegative, indecomposable, square matrices*.

{135}------------------------------------------------

A crucial conclusion that emerges from this analysis of long-period general equilibrium positions is that there is an antagonistic trade-off between the level of real wages and profit rates. Since this was one of the most important insights Ricardo and Marx gleaned from the labor theory of value, Sraffa's analytical proof in a multi-commodity system of production is a validation of the general Classical approach to the problem of distribution.

It remains, however, to understand how many of these insights can be generalized to the important cases where there is a choice of technique, so that there is more than one way to produce each commodity, where there is joint production, so that the same process can produce more than one commodity, and where there are scarce non-reproducible resources.

#### **No joint production with choice of technique**

Suppose now that the number of processes is larger than the number of commodities, but continue to assume that there is at least one process that produces each commodity and that each process produces only one commodity (no joint production).

Again, holding the money wage constant (or setting it equal to 1), and taking the profit rate  $r$  as given, consider a particular  $n \times n$  matrix  $A$  that has one process to produce each commodity. Such a collection of processes is called a *technique*. Then we can (if  $r$  is not too large) find the corresponding price system  $p(r, A)$ . Using this price system and profit rate, we could calculate the price we would have to charge to produce the  $j$ -th commodity with some *other* process, say  $(a'_j, l'_j)$ , which would be  $p'_j = (1 + r)p^T(r, A)a'_j + wl'_j$ . (This is a natural economic idea, since it is exactly the calculation entrepreneurs would make in the course of considering whether to shift from process  $(a_j, l_j)$  to  $(a'_j, l'_j)$  in producing commodity  $j$ .) If  $p'_j > p_j(r)$ , entrepreneurs would reject the new process on the grounds that it would be too costly to implement. If, on the other hand,  $p'_j < p_j(r)$ , entrepreneurs would adopt the new process, and competition would force the price of commodity  $j$  downward. Not only that, but because commodity  $j$  is basic, and thus enters as an input directly or indirectly into the production of every other commodity, the prices of *all* the commodities would fall, and the real wage in any numéraire would rise. Entrepreneurs would in fact continue to test every available process in this way, until the technique adopted could not be improved, that is until there was no alternative process whose introduction would lower the prices of all the commodities for a given profit rate.

As the profit rate (or the real wage) changes, the minimum-cost technique might change, too. The real wage-profit rate relation for the economy is in fact the lower envelope of the real wage-profit rate relations for all its possible techniques. There will be particular real wage-profit rate points where two processes can coexist, because they will have the same price for the commodity given the prices of all the other commodities. These configurations are called *switchpoints*. Except by a fluke, only one new process can enter the cost-minimizing technique at each switchpoint.

{136}------------------------------------------------

In economies without scarce land resources or joint production, the insights of the simple model carry over transparently when there is a choice of technique. There is still a trade-off between the real wage and the profit rate, and still one degree of freedom in the equations determining prices, which can be used to specify distribution in the economy, either by choosing the real wage or the profit rate.

This model gives rise to a decisive criticism of the neoclassical hope that there might be some general relation between the *value of capital* and the profit rate across equilibrium positions that would validate the neoclassical production function, which purports to relate the value of net output to the value of capital and labor as inputs to production, and to identify the profit rate (or interest rate) with the marginal product of capital from this production function. Two phenomena are easy to demonstrate in this model that are inconsistent with the neoclassical conception of capital.

First, it is possible to have *reverse capital deepening*. This phenomenon occurs when the value of capital per worker at equilibrium prices rises as the profit rate rises. Since the profit rate in the neoclassical conception is supposed to be a measure of the scarcity of capital, the neoclassical theory predicts an inverse relation between the quantity of capital (supposedly measured by the value of the capital stock per worker) and the profit rate. Reverse capital deepening is inconsistent with this prediction.

Second, it is possible to have *reswitching of techniques*. Reswitching occurs when a particular technique (a collection of processes, one for each commodity) is cost minimizing at a low profit rate and again at a higher profit rate, with some other technique chosen for intermediate profit rates. If the general idea of “capital” can be identified with a particular technique of production (as, for example, Austrian economists have sometimes argued), then a higher profit rate should correspond to a less capital-intensive technique. But if the *same* technique is adopted at low and higher profit rates, it is impossible to sustain any coherent ordering of capital-intensity of technique with the profit rate.

These points are the main outcome of the “Cambridge capital controversy” of the 1960s and 1970s. Despite general acceptance of these analytical results, neoclassical economists continue to use production functions linking labor and the value of capital to the value of output as a foundation for growth models.

#### Joint production and land

If an economy confronts a limited resource such as land, the cost minimizing technique cannot be determined without reference to net output. A profit-seeking capitalist economy will exploit the cheapest methods of production to produce low levels of net output, which will use either the best land or the most land-intensive techniques of production, and only cultivate less-fertile land or adopt more land-intensive techniques if it needs to produce a larger net output. Sraffa clearly acknowledges the dependence of the technique in use on the size and composition of net output in his discussion of this problem. While neoclassical economics

{137}------------------------------------------------

subsumes the determination of output into the general equilibrium problem of determining output and input prices in a simultaneous system, Sraffa argues that the determination of net output has no systematic functional relation to output and input prices (for example, through household demand), and must be taken as one of the elemental givens of the system in analyzing the determination of equilibrium prices. Thus Sraffa is led to the idea of seeking the cost-minimizing technique that can produce a given level of net output for each level of the wage or profit rate.

In this conception of equilibrium there are additional variables, rents, which must be determined. To keep matters as simple as possible, suppose that land is uniform in quality, but limited in quantity, so that there is one additional variable, the uniform rent on land, to be determined. Sraffa argues that in this situation there will also generically be an additional equation, because in order to produce the given vector of net output, it will be necessary to operate *two* processes for the production of one of the commodities. Since both processes must achieve the average rate of profit, this adds the necessary additional condition to determine rent. Sraffa argues that in order to use up all the land there will generically be one commodity for which two processes, effectively one more and one less land intensive, will be operated.

Sraffa argues that the problem of joint production is analytically analogous to that of scarce resources. In the joint production case the system also threatens to be underdetermined because the number of processes operated might fall short of the number of commodities to be priced. But, as in the case of land, Sraffa argues that in order to meet a generic net output demand, it will be necessary with joint production to operate the same number of processes as there are commodities. (In some situations some of the commodities may actually have a zero price, and can be eliminated from the count.)

#### **The general model**

We can see these results Sraffa reached through verbal reasoning in a formal model. Given the profit rate  $r$ , it simplifies matters to charge the profit rate in physical terms on inputs (see Duménil and Lévy, 1982; Foley, 1985).  $(B - (1 + r)A)x$  is the *r-net product* of the system for the profit rate  $r$ . There is one scarce resource (land), the input coefficients of which are represented by the vector  $u^T$  (analogously to  $l^T$  for labor inputs). Suppose that, given a money wage  $w$ , we try to allocate resources so as to minimize the wage bill, while meeting the constraint of producing a given  $r$ -net product  $z$ , and using no more than the available land, normalized to unity. This gives rise to the following mathematical programming problem (actually a linear programming problem):

$$\begin{aligned}
& \max_{x \geq 0} - wl^T x \\
\text{subject to } & -(B - (1 + r)A)x \leqq -z \\
& u^T x \leq 1
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.3}$$

{138}------------------------------------------------

This programming problem (which I have written as a maximization problem and changed the signs of the constraints to fit the pattern of the Lagrangian analysis) has the Lagrangian:

$$\begin{aligned} L(p, v, x) &= -wl^T x - p^T (-(B - (1 + r)A)x + z) - v(\mu^T x - 1) \\ &= -(p^T z - v - (p^T (B - (1 + r)A) - v\mu^T - wl^T)x) \end{aligned} \quad (10.4)$$

Here  $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$  is the vector of Lagrange multipliers or shadow prices associated with the requirements to produce the given  $r$ -net product, and  $v$  is the shadow price (shadow rent) associated with the land constraint.

The negative of this Lagrangian, as I have suggested by re-grouping it in the second line, also arises from the *dual* problem:

$$\begin{aligned} &\max_{p, v \geq 0} p^T z - v \\ &\text{subject to } p^T (B - (1 + r)A) - v\mu^T - wl^T \leqq 0 \end{aligned} \quad (10.5)$$

In this interpretation, the prices and rent are the variables to be solved for, subject to the constraint that no process earns more than the given profit rate  $r$ . In the Lagrangian looked at from the point of view of the dual problem, the vector  $x$  of operating levels for the processes are the Lagrange multipliers associated with the profitability constraint. We are now maximizing with respect to  $p$ ,  $v$  and minimizing with respect to  $x$ , which requires the change of sign of the Lagrangian.

It is not hard to see that in general the solution to problem (10.3) will involve operating  $n + 1$  processes to meet the constraints. It might happen by a fluke that it was just possible to meet the constraints operating fewer processes, but then a small perturbation of the  $r$ -net product vector  $z$  would require the activation of the extra processes. It is also not hard to see from the fact that a saddle-point of the Lagrangian simultaneously represents the solution to both the primal and dual problems that any process operated at a positive level will just meet the profitability constraint, and any process that falls short of the profitability constraint will not be operated. Since the prices and rent satisfy the dual constraint, they are a meaningful solution to Sraffa's equations for prices.

It is possible to show that the prices that solve these mathematical programming problems cannot fall as the profit rate increases, and that there is a maximal profit rate for which the primal problem is feasible (see Foley, 1985).

Thus we see that Sraffa's method can be generalized to apply to joint production and scarce resources. In this case it is necessary to know the net product (well,  $r$ -net product – I leave as an exercise the exploration of the relation between the  $r$ -net product constraint and the corresponding net product constraint) and resources available to the economy as well as the technology in order to determine the equilibrium prices or prices of production. In the simple production model without scarce resources, the prices of production are independent of the net output.

{139}------------------------------------------------

(When  $r = 0$  the prices of commodities determined by this method are embodied labor coefficients, which are sometimes called “labor values”. This derivation shows that it is possible to find non-negative embodied labor coefficients in the case of joint production and with scarce resources, as long as one is prepared to incorporate information about the net product and the resource constraints in the analysis.)

#### **Some other questions about Sraffa**

#### *Constant returns to scale*

A good deal of ink has been spilled over the question of whether or not Sraffa requires the assumption of constant returns to scale on the processes of production to reach his main results. The reconstruction of Sraffa’s argument I have attempted here suggests that he does not, since it emphasizes in the general case the importance of specifying the scale of the economy through the ( $r$ -)net output vector and the availability of scarce resources. Although we have written the technology in matrix form, suggesting that one can multiply it by any vector of operations levels, it is clear that the basic analysis could go through even without this simplifying analytical assumption.

What seems to be really at issue here is the difference between prices that cover *average costs* of production including the normal profit rate (as Marshall’s long-run partial equilibrium would have it) and prices that equal *marginal costs* at equilibrium, as Marshall’s short-run partial equilibrium and much of the Walrasian general equilibrium literature assumes. The point is that under the assumption of constant returns to scale average costs are equal to marginal costs. So with the assumption of constant returns to scale it is possible for a marginalist to interpret Sraffa’s prices of production as something like marginal cost prices. While at first glance this formulation might seem to be a promising avenue for the reconciliation of the Classical and neoclassical points of view, it has turned out in fact to be a dead end more productive of debates at cross-purposes than clarification of the issues.

#### *Competition and industries*

Sraffa is not very explicit about the theory of competition or economic dynamics that might underlie his profit rate-equalizing prices. Some of his followers have claimed that this amounts to a methodological innovation, a new principle for understanding prices from the point of view of reproduction without any assumptions about competition.

On the whole, this latter argument seems implausible. Sraffa worked from Marx and the Classical political economists, whose theory of competition, even if it was not worked out in explicit mathematical form, was clear enough: profit-seeking entrepreneurs enter or exit particular industries in search of higher profits. It is hard to see what in Sraffa’s analysis is inconsistent with this Classical notion of competition (which is also echoed, perhaps in an imperfect and somewhat confused

{140}------------------------------------------------

form by Marshall's long-run partial equilibrium analysis). If we suppose that Sraffa sought to express the analytical heart of this Classical vision, it puts his work closer to the mainstream of economic analysis and emphasizes its continuity with other similar attempts.

But this interpretation does leave Sraffa open to the question of how the sectorization of the economy (including the determination of the commodity space) is accomplished in the first place. Is this just a convenient statistical device (like the classification of industries into 1-, 2-, and 3-digit categories in the US census of manufactures)? Or does the sectorization of the economy reflect some more fundamental principle? This is not an idle theoretical question, because the identification of firms with sectors has become increasingly difficult with the development of contemporary capitalism.

#### ***What to do with Sraffian analysis?***

If one accepts, as these notes suggest is reasonable, the basic analytical correctness of Sraffa's contribution, what does one learn from it, and where does one take it in terms of a research program?

A perusal of Kurz and Salvadori (1995) shows two of the most vigorous developments in the Sraffian tradition. One is an acute critique of the history of economic thought at a high level. Related to this strand is the continuing wrangle of the Sraffians with the few surviving neoclassicals over the concept of capital, and the attempt of Sraffians to create a second front in this war in the form of a critique of Walrasian general equilibrium theory in its Arrow-Debreu form. A second is a progressive mathematical research program aimed at generalizing and exploring details of the Sraffian production model.

Unfortunately neither of these lines of work, impressive as they are intellectually in themselves, has had the impact on questions of policy or applied economics generally their intellectual depth and broad implications would justify. As mainstream economics gradually abandons its aspirations to a general philosophical understanding of the economy and emphasizes empirical studies intended to bolster one or another policy measure, the way is open for the Sraffian tradition to assert itself as a distinctive political economy.
