{142}------------------------------------------------

## 11 Surplus approach to value and distribution and structural economic dynamics

### Interpretation and uses of Sraffa's analysis

*Enrico Bellino and Ariel Luis Wirkierman*

### Introduction

The re-statement of Classical economic analysis put forward by Sraffa (1951) gave rise to intense discussions in the following decades. The sharp break with the Marginal method *and* theory would find its foundational statement in *Production of Commodities by Means of Commodities* (Sraffa 1960). The theory of value and distribution had to be re-examined through the Classical lens Sraffa proposed, recalling, to a certain extent, what had happened with the theory of output more than two decades before, with the appearance of Keynes (1936).

The implications of Sraffa's analysis were far-reaching. The determination of relative prices of production was carried out without any reference to the theory of demand and supply equilibrium, distribution of income was not an endogenous result of the counter-balancing forces acting on relative scarcity of 'factors'. The very notion of 'factors' of production was called into question, in particular, the quantity of capital, which could not be conceived as a value magnitude independent of distribution. And closely associated to this, the term 'cost of production' had to be abandoned as the circular process made apparent the interdependent character of *value*, finding its ultimate *objective cause* in the notion of *physical real costs*. In this context, the notion of *value* itself is *motivated* by the need to give an aggregate measure of the physical composite commodity that constitutes the *surplus product* of the system.

There are different streams along which Sraffa's analysis has been developed and extended from 1960 onwards. One of them places Sraffa's analysis within the method of long-period positions (present in the Classical economists and early Marginalists) and builds upon it a rigorous and general statement of the **Surplus Approach to Value and Distribution – SAVD** from now on – (see, e.g. Garegnani 1987).

Another stream extends the field studied by Sraffa, by taking into account the evolution of physical quantities and relative values, as triggered by the continuous operation of technical progress, so characteristic of modern industrial systems. A framework for the analysis of the evolving economic structure consistent with Sraffa's contribution is found in the approach of **Structural Economic Dynamics – SED** from now on<sup>1</sup> – (see, e.g. Pasinetti 1981, Pasinetti and Scazzieri 1987).

{143}------------------------------------------------

In view of these considerations, the aims of this chapter are, in the first place, to state some of the main arguments of Sraffa (1960) by taking a specific methodological route (next section). Second, to present and discuss the interpretation and uses of Sraffa's (1960) system that can be attributed to each of the aforementioned approaches (sections three and four). In the third place, to establish points of contact between the two approaches as regards the separate determination of relative values and physical quantities produced (fifth section). A final remark concludes.

#### ***Production of Commodities as a point of departure***

In Sraffa's analysis, the output levels and methods of production are taken as given without assuming constant returns. The problem is to determine a system of relative values of a *circular process* of production and consumption without any recourse to the forces of supply and demand equilibrium. This is first carried out for a viable economic system in conditions of subsistence (Sraffa 1960, Ch. I).

When the notion of *physical surplus* is introduced (Sraffa 1960, Ch. II), its very presence *motivates* the need to measure the relative values of commodities. In fact,

For Quesnay [. . .] the cost is [. . .] an element of the productive process, which must be exactly measured in order to compare it with the product and thus determine whether product contains *a surplus over and above cost*.

(ibid. [D2/4, M1.7]: 25–6, our italics) (Garegnani 2005, p. 480)

Therefore, this physical surplus, being a composite commodity different in kind from the produced means of production, faces the Classical authors with a question of 'measurement'. The question is how to find the commodity values *consistent with* a circular process, providing a set of weights to measure this surplus as an aggregate magnitude. For an answer, the true nature of costs needs to be clarified.

However, if we were to identify costs with production *expenses*, at some point we would necessarily involve *circular* reasoning. Sraffa, then, traces the evolution of the notion of *cost*:

the trend has been from meaning by cost the means necessary to enable production to be made, to meaning the incentive required to induce somebody to overcome the sacrifice involved in production'

(D3.12.4: A5.6; underlining in the original) (Garegnani 2005, p. 475)

It is the first meaning which Sraffa considers to be the Classical notion of cost.

Hence, the physical requirements of produced means of production and the composite commodity that provides for the subsistence of labour *define* physical real costs. These costs are physical quantities of commodities in given proportions, according to the methods of production being employed.

A further step is taken. When the *wage* is considered as part of the surplus, and not as a necessary consumption in the same ground as produced means of production, the distribution of the *net product* between social classes has to be determined and the 'quantity of labour employed in each industry has now to be

{144}------------------------------------------------

represented explicitly, taking the place of the corresponding quantities of subsistence' (Sraffa 1960, pp. 10–11).

To see this, let us now represent the production equations in Sraffa (1960, p. 11) – the so-called Sraffa's 'third equations' – in usual matrix form:<sup>2</sup>

$$\mathbf{p}^T \hat{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{A} \hat{\mathbf{q}} (1 + \pi) + \mathbf{a}_n^T \hat{\mathbf{q}} w \quad (11.1)$$

$$\mathbf{p}^T (\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{A} \mathbf{q}) = 1 \quad (11.2)$$

The *net product* of the system ( $\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{A} \mathbf{q}$ ) is taken as *numéraire*. Moreover, Sraffa considers as 'known quantities' the produced means of production ( $\mathbf{A} \hat{\mathbf{q}}$ ), the total labour requirements ( $\mathbf{a}_n^T \hat{\mathbf{q}}$ ) and the *gross* quantities produced ( $\mathbf{q}$ ). Hence, we can express technical methods as physical unit input requirements per unit of *gross* output ( $\mathbf{A}$ ,  $\mathbf{a}_n^T$ ), acknowledging that the whole set of data does not change when relative values are being determined.<sup>3</sup>

Notice also from the equations that 'the system can move with one degree of freedom' (Sraffa 1960, p. 11), because the number of unknowns exceeds the number of equations by one. Then, if any of the distributive variables is fixed exogenously with respect to system (11.1)–(11.2), the other can only be computed *simultaneously* with prices.

Finally, we also notice that physical real costs constitute parameters in the equations and, as regards the physical quantities of the net product, 'It is impossible for the aggregate quantity of any commodity represented in this expression [(11.2)] to be negative owing to the condition of self-replacement assumed' (Sraffa 1960, p. 11).

Hence, given the properties just mentioned, we arrive at the conclusion that, once any of the distributive variables ( $\pi$ ,  $w$ ) is fixed,

essentially, the physical conditions of production of the commodities and the need to allow production to be repeated are *sufficient* to determine relative prices quite independently of what are generally understood as 'demand and supply forces'.

(Garegnani 2005, p. 469, our italics)

This can be seen by solving the system represented by (11.1)–(11.2):

$$w = \frac{1}{\mathbf{a}_n^T (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}(1 + \pi))^{-1} (\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{A} \mathbf{q})} \quad (11.3)$$

$$\mathbf{p}^T = \mathbf{a}_n^T (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}(1 + \pi))^{-1} w \quad (11.4)$$

where  $w$  is 'the wage per unit of labour, which like prices will be expressed in terms of the chosen standard' (Sraffa 1960, p. 11).

One further step may still be taken. We have determined  $w$  simultaneously with  $\mathbf{p}^T$ , given  $\pi$ . One of the crucial points of Sraffa's analysis (1960) is that the

{145}------------------------------------------------

distribution of income can be determined *before* prices are fixed, if either  $\pi$  or  $w$  are known. To unambiguously relate  $w$  and  $\pi$ , before computing relative values, Sraffa introduces the Standard commodity. In order to do so, he solves the following *q-system* (see Sraffa 1960, p. 24):

$$\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{g}(1+R) = \hat{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{g} \quad (11.5)$$

$$\mathbf{a}_n^T \hat{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{g} = 1 \quad (11.6)$$

The logic of the exercise is to effect a *virtual* re-proportioning of *gross* quantities through a set of multipliers represented by vector  $\mathbf{g}$  (with  $\mathbf{g} > \mathbf{0}$ , if there are only basic commodities in the system):

The multipliers must be such that the resulting quantities of the various commodities will bear the same proportions to one another on the right-hand sides of the equations [(11.5)] (as products) as they do on the aggregate of the left-hand sides (as means of production).

(Sraffa 1960, pp. 23–4)

But as (11.5) is an homogeneous system, (11.6) normalizes the size of the whole system by making the virtual re-proportioning of physical quantities employ the labour available in the *actual* system. If  $\mathbf{q}$  is known, then, by defining  $\mathbf{x} := \hat{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{q} \equiv \hat{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{g}$ , we can solve the following eigenproblem:

$$\frac{1}{R}\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \quad (11.7)$$

where, according to Perron-Frobenius theorems (see Pasinetti 1977, Ch.V),  $\mathbf{x}^*$  is the column eigenvector corresponding to the maximum eigenvalue associated to matrix  $\mathbf{G} := (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}$ ,  $\lambda^*(\mathbf{G}) = 1/R$ . And  $R$  is the *Standard-ratio* of the system (see Sraffa 1960, p. 21). It is straightforward then to compute  $\mathbf{g}^* = \hat{\mathbf{q}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}^*$ .

When  $w$  and  $\mathbf{p}^T$  are measured in terms of the *Standard net product* (see Sraffa 1960, Ch. IV), so that  $\mathbf{p}^T(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})\mathbf{x}^* = 1$ , we obtain:

$$\pi = R(1 - w) \quad (11.8)$$

What is interesting is that this relation holds for the actual system, as long as we adopt the *Standard net product as numéraire*. Then, equations (11.1) and (11.8), for a given  $\pi$ , are *sufficient* to determine  $w$  before relative values  $\mathbf{p}^T$  are *computed*:

$$w = \frac{R - \pi}{R} \quad (11.9)$$

$$\mathbf{p}^T = \mathbf{a}_n^T (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}(1 + \pi))^{-1} \frac{R - \pi}{R} \quad (11.10)$$

{146}------------------------------------------------

This result can be interpreted as the crucial manifestation of Sraffa's *purpose* for the theory of value:

according to the Sraffian approach, the essential task of the theory of value consists of identifying the conditions which, when satisfied, assure the regular working of the economic system. If (and only if) these conditions are fully specified, we can proceed to the rather trivial computation of the corresponding necessary prices. In the third equations, the distributional setting, i.e. the precise knowledge of *both*  $r$  and  $w$ , is part of the conditions.

(Gilibert 2006, pp. 47–8)

While the technical requirements for reproduction, the biological needs associated to a subsistence wage, and the institutional uniform profit rate are clearly part of this set of conditions sought by Sraffa, the distribution of income between wages and profits due to a surplus wage has to find an objective solution before the 'rather trivial computation' of prices can be performed. The formal statement of this objective condition is given by (11.8). And its formulation is possible thanks to the *analytical device* of the Standard commodity.

It is now possible to go through possible interpretation and uses of Sraffa's (1960) equations of production found in the SAVD and the approach of SED, respectively.

#### **Normal long-period production prices and the notion of a *core* of surplus theories**

The SAVD restores the categories and logic prevalent in the reasoning of the Classical economists. The organizing principle of the SAVD is the notion of *social surplus* ( $S$ ). It is basically a residual obtained when all *necessary consumption* ( $NC$ ) is deduced from the *social product* ( $SP$ ), i.e.  $S = SP - NC$ .

This equation involves a causal relation which abstracts from many complications arising when it has to be actually computed. In fact, these three concepts –  $S$ ,  $SP$  and  $NC$  – can be considered as 'highly abstract notions' whose determination is mediated by problems of measurement (because of the physical heterogeneity of commodities) and interdependence (because the social product is generated through a circular process of production and consumption).

For the SAVD, Sraffa's 'representative system of production' presents a 'price-equations-method of determining profits' (Garegnani 1987, p. 568). Profits constitute the social surplus ( $S$ ), obtained as a residual once all capital advanced as means of production and wages (i.e. necessary consumption,  $NC$ ) has been deduced from *gross* production (i.e. social product,  $SP$ ).

However, the underlying logic of the theory does not render itself immediately transparent with the price-equations-method. In fact, 'the nature of profits as a residual can be clarified by Sraffa [...] only by showing how prices just sufficient to repay wages and replace the means of production become contradictory when a surplus product comes into existence' (Garegnani 1984, p. 311n).

{147}------------------------------------------------

Formally, to represent Sraffa's (1960) system the SAVD considers the following production equations:

$$\mathbf{p}^T \hat{\mathbf{q}} = (\mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{A} \hat{\mathbf{q}} + w \mathbf{a}_n^T \hat{\mathbf{q}})(1 + \pi) \quad (11.11)$$

$$w = \mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{d} \quad (11.12)$$

where (11.11) assimilates equations (11.1), with the only difference being that wages are treated as capital advanced, and the *wage* rate is *given* in terms of a composite commodity. In this way, 'the assumption of a uniform real wages ensures that, in all industries, variable capital consists of the same composite "wage commodity" and that we may apply to it the single price obtainable from the prices of its constituent commodities' (Garegnani 1987, p. 568).

For the SAVD the following circumstances are assumed as known prior to the determination of profits (social surplus) (see Garegnani 1987, p. 560): (i) the composite commodity that constitutes the real wage ( $\mathbf{d}$ ), (ii) the composite commodity of *gross* produced quantities ( $\mathbf{q}$ ), and (iii) the methods of production ( $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{a}_n^T$ ).

On making these assumptions the SAVD is following Classical economists like Quesnay, Smith and Ricardo (Garegnani 1987, p. 561). Of course, 'the circumstances taken as "given" in the Classical approach are subject to a considerable degree of mutual dependence' (Ravagnani 2002, p. 378). In fact, these 'three sets of circumstances were data *when determining the nonwage distributive variables and the relative prices*, and not data for the theory as a whole' (Garegnani 2002, p. 243). This clarifies their attribute of 'intermediate data' (see Garegnani 2007, p. 186).

The relations represented by equations (11.11)–(11.12), the set of 'intermediate data' and the results derived from them by means of 'short chains of deductive reasoning' (Garegnani 1987, pp. 561–2), constitute the *core* of surplus theories. The crucial problem in the analytical core is to determine profits (i.e. the social surplus  $S$ ).

In this chapter, two fundamental relations of the core will be *deduced*: the *simultaneous* determination of relative values and profits (the value of the social surplus), and the constraint that binds the distribution of income between wages and profits.

To determine relative prices and profits, it is possible to define a socio-technical matrix of necessary consumption,  $\mathbf{A}^+ := \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{d}\mathbf{a}_n^T$ , composed of produced means of production required by each industry  $\mathbf{A}$ , as well as the commodities required by the labour input  $\mathbf{d}\mathbf{a}_n^T$ , receiving the *real* wage (11.12).<sup>4</sup> Now, to determine the *uniform* rate of profits  $\pi$ , *together with* relative values  $\mathbf{p}^T$  we solve the following eigenproblem:

$$\frac{1}{1 + \pi} \mathbf{p}^T = \mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{A}^+ \quad (11.13)$$

{148}------------------------------------------------

where, according to Perron-Frobenius theorems (see Pasinetti 1977, Ch.V),  $\mathbf{p}^{T*}$  is the row eigenvector corresponding to the maximum eigenvalue associated to the socio-technical matrix,  $\lambda^*(\mathbf{A}^+)$ , so that:  $\pi^* = 1/\lambda^*(\mathbf{A}^+) - 1$ .

Once this problem is solved, and an appropriate *numéraire* (e.g. labour) is chosen (so that  $w = \mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{d} = 1$ ), we obtain the social surplus (profits) by deducing the value of necessary consumption (*NC*) from the value of the social product (*SP*), i.e. we compute the endogenous magnitudes of the system:

$$SP = \mathbf{p}^{T*} \mathbf{q} \quad (11.14)$$

$$NC = \mathbf{p}^{T*} \mathbf{A}^+ \mathbf{q} \quad (11.15)$$

$$S = SP - NC = \mathbf{p}^{T*} (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}^+) \mathbf{q} = (1/\lambda^*(\mathbf{A}^+) - 1) \mathbf{p}^{T*} \mathbf{A}^+ \mathbf{q} \quad (11.16)$$

It is interesting to note the *dual* character of the rate of profits put forward by the SAVD. On the one hand, ‘the rate of profit can be directly envisaged as a relative value, namely the value of the Surplus product (a composite commodity) in terms of the Necessary consumption (a second composite commodity)’ (Garegnani 1984, p. 302n). However, as we see when we compute it,  $\pi^*$  is a technological variable determined by the socio-technical matrix of necessary consumption.

Let us now turn to the second relation to be deduced from (11.11)–(11.12).

It can be noticed that, for a given technique  $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{a}_n^T)$ , an increase in the components of the physical real wage  $\mathbf{d}$  entails a decrease in  $\pi$ , as  $\lambda^*(\mathbf{A}^+)$  is a continuous increasing function of the elements of  $\mathbf{A}^+$  (see Pasinetti 1977, p. 272, Theorem 3). However, if some components of  $\mathbf{d}$  increase while others decrease, we need to evaluate the overall effect on the wage rate. To deal with this problem we can consider wages entirely as a part of the surplus and express the prices of commodities and the wage rate in terms of the Standard commodity. In this case (as wages are capital advanced at the beginning of the production period), it can be shown (see Pasinetti 1977, pp. 131–2) that the resulting constraint linking wages and profits – *before* prices are determined – is given by:

$$\pi = \frac{R(1-w)}{R+w} \quad (11.17)$$

which is an inverse hyperbolic relation between  $w$  and  $\pi$ . It should be noticed that, notwithstanding its non-linear character, (11.17) is independent of relative prices, so that the *rate* of profits can be determined *before* prices are computed.

It thus seems clear: ‘The “core” might in fact be described as constituting the “theory of value” such as we find in the surplus theories’ (Garegnani 1984, p. 297n). But we have not so far asked ourselves, what is the *purpose* of the theory of value as intended by the SAVD? The answer to this question begins by noting the crucial role of the *assumption* of a *uniform* rate of profits in the analysis.

{149}------------------------------------------------

In the SAVD the uniform  $\pi$  in (11.11) represents the outcome of the competitive process in a *capitalist* system. Prices in Sraffa's equations are: 'the exchange ratios that would tend to prevail, in conditions of free competition, when the produced quantities of the different commodities conform to the respective 'effectual demands'. This, in turn, implies that the whole theoretical position is to be regarded as a *normal* position, aimed at defining a centre of gravitation for the prices and quantities of the actual economy' (Ravagnani 2002, p. 371).

Furthermore, it is asserted that 'he [Sraffa] is sufficiently clear that what comes out of the solution of the equations are prices that we *expect to be realized* in the markets as "normal" or "production" prices' (Garegnani 2005, p. 474, our italics). This is the way according to which the correspondence between observed and theoretical magnitudes is preserved.

Therefore, the interpretation given by the SAVD of Sraffa's (1960) production equations entails a very definite *correspondence to reality* of the theoretical magnitudes computed. Not only the relation between market prices and production prices is implicitly assumed to be of a certain type (that governed by a process of gravitation), but also the *time* dimension of the equations acquires a definite character: 'Sraffa's system of production cannot be properly said to be set in a 'particular year' (the *actual* magnitudes corresponding to it, would, if anything, be a moving average calculated over *several* years' (Garegnani 1988, p. 256). In fact, 'no distinction is made between the price of a commodity entering the production cycle as an input and the price of the same commodity considered as an output at the end of the process' (Ravagnani 2002, p. 371).

In this way, even a very definite interpretation of the production coefficients  $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{a}_n^T)$  of (11.11) is advanced: 'the tendency to adopt cheaper methods will bring the economy to a definite technique that giving the highest wage for the given rate of profit' (Garegnani 1984, p. 293n). Hence, the solution for  $\mathbf{p}^T$  has been computed using the *dominant* technique of the spectrum available during the time frame corresponding to the long-period position considered.

To conclude, it may be stated that the ultimate purpose of the SAVD is the description of the working of a capitalist system and, in particular, that of explaining profits as the *surplus* of this system, that is, a revenue existing due to the fact that wages do not absorb the entire net product.

#### **Natural prices as necessary requirements of a set of growing subsystems**

#### ***Interpreting Sraffa's method***

Alongside the perspective on Sraffa's (1960) production equations presented above, it is possible to discover within Sraffa's analysis the seeds of a deeper and, perhaps, more abstract level of inquiry, which is at the basis of the approach of SED.

To see this, let us turn again to the assumption of a uniform rate of profits.

In Sraffa's (1960) system, 'we add the rate of profits (which *must* be uniform for all industries) as an unknown' (Sraffa 1960, p. 6, our italics). However, the justification for this 'must' is not explicitly sought in the competitive process of

{150}------------------------------------------------

the system. In fact, when Sraffa asks himself how to justify or explain the rate of surplus, i.e. the equal percentage added to initial stock of means of production of each industry, among the possible answers, Garegnani (2005) states:

Sraffa's answer is not, as one might perhaps naturally expect, that it is a condition directly imposed by free competition on the markets. Rather, it is sought in the necessity of ensuring that capital is not removed from branches of the economy which would otherwise finish up with a lower rate of profit and would prevent the system from reproducing itself on an unchanged scale. (Garegnani 2005, p. 475)

What is, then, behind a uniform  $\pi$ ? If we do not wish to 'prevent the system from reproducing', then  $\pi$  must be uniform. Hence, it is an intrinsic need to comply with the reproduction requirements of the circular process.

The assumption can, of course, be interpreted as an institutional feature founded on the Classical view of the process of capitalist competition. But if this process is assumed to involve a particular correspondence to reality, e.g. the notion of gravitation, the operation of the adjustment of the system must be either specified or assumed. And while this would need the explicit statement of forces at work, Sraffa (1960) makes no *explicit* reference to any adjustment mechanism as regards his assumption of a uniform  $\pi$ .

The underlying issue is whether we can distinguish between the uniformity assumption, even recognising its institutional nature, and the gravitation process that is associated to it. A possible logical separation would indicate a novel methodological route for the *purpose* of the theory of value (see Gilibert 2006).

Sraffa himself states that 'we are all the time concerned *merely with the implications of the assumption* of a uniform price for all units of a commodity and a uniform rate of profits on all the means of production' (Sraffa 1960, p. 91, App. B, our italics).

In this vein, Sraffa's price equations could also be interpreted as a logical consequence of the necessary conditions imposed by the problem formulated: 'the original Sraffian approach to the theory of value: **Find a set of conditions that will make these prices appear to be necessary**' (Gilibert 2006, p. 47, boldface in the original).

Therefore, the unknowns of the production equations (11.1) could stand for those exchange ratios that, if realized, allow each *industry* to recover the purchasing power necessary to repeat the production process on an, at least, unchanged scale, and distribute the surplus generated according to the distributive rule given by (11.8).

In effect, we can see the whole of Sraffa's (1960) Part I as a very rigorous statement of a set of conditions that make the exchange ratios computed appear as 'necessary prices'. For example, 'the proposal to split the wage into two parts, the first defined in physical terms and paid in advance, the second defined in value and paid afterwards, can only conform to analytical needs' (Gilibert 1989, p. 188). And the role of the Standard commodity, as presented in this chapter at the end of

{151}------------------------------------------------

the second section, is precisely that of stating a rigorous condition for the determination of distribution, from which prices would *logically* follow.

It is possible to relate this interpretation of the production equations to their role in the approach of SED. For this approach, Sraffa's (1960) analysis is located at the stage of 'pure theory':

The problems of economic theory that emerge at this stage are either in terms of *necessary* relations, if certain goals are to be achieved (e.g. full employment, price stability, etc.), or in terms of *logically consistent* relations, or in terms of *normative rules*, or in terms of those problems which are generated by the basic forces at work in a dynamic context.

(Pasinetti 2002, p. 337, our italics)

However, under this interpretation, the correspondence to reality of the prices computed from the production equations would not necessarily comply with their role as strong attractors in a gravitation process.

But we may go even further. What would be the consequences of *changing* the set of conditions on which the necessary prices obtained by Sraffa are computed? It would amount to turning upside down the way of reasoning. What the SAVD has done is to give a particular (very relevant and coherent) interpretation to the solution of the 'system of production', under the set of conditions *given* by Sraffa. In contrast, it may be thought that – within the approach of SED – the role of Sraffa's (1960) production equations has been to provide a novel *purpose* for the theory of value (as proposed by Gilibert (2006)) and the '*foundations* of a theory of income distribution' (Pasinetti 1988b, p. 135), where the set of necessary conditions giving rise to *natural prices* has been modified, with respect to that originally put forward by Sraffa (1960).

Let us now explore the notion of natural prices in the approach of SED. In order to arrive to its formulation, the *unavoidable* necessary step is to present the *analytical device* of a growing subsystem.

#### ***Growing subsystems***

With the introduction of a *surplus*, the need arises for an 'analytical device that allows us to separate in an unambiguous way what pertains to the surplus from what pertains to the circular process' (Pasinetti 1986, p. 7).

The *method* of subsystems (Sraffa 1960, App. A) fulfills this task. It allows us to perform a *virtual* re-partitioning of produced quantities ( $\mathbf{q}$ ), labour ( $\mathbf{a}_n^T \mathbf{q}$ ) and produced means of production ( $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}$ ) originally allocated within each *industry* 'into as many parts as there are commodities in its net product, in such a way that each part forms a smaller *self-replacing* system the net product of which consists of only one kind of commodity' (Sraffa 1960, App. A, p. 89, our italics).

But when the system is no longer in a self-replacing state, 'the exact meaning of "reproduction" is no longer straightforward' (Ravagnani 2001, p. 357). Circularity may not necessarily be *exact* repetition of the production process.

{152}------------------------------------------------

In particular, when the quantities produced exceed those required to replace means of production used up and the surplus is not entirely devoted to final consumption, it is valid to study the relation between the *net product* and the expansion of *productive capacity* of the system. This, however, entails going ‘beyond the assumption of taking physical quantities as given’ (Pasinetti 1988b, p. 138).

The approach of SED proposes to go exactly in *this* direction.

To begin with, we may differentiate – within the net product – between final consumption commodities (which are still part of the *physical surplus* of the system) and produced means of production that *re-enter* the circular process to expand the system’s productive capacity, i.e. *net investment*.

It is clear that this distinction entails a change in the notion of net product, which now includes only those quantities produced over and above the self-replacement *and* expansion of the means of production. Hence, it is with respect to the vector of consumption commodities that we can ‘partition the economic system into as many such newly defined subsystems as there are *consumption goods*’ (Pasinetti 1988a, p. 126, our italics).

In this context we may ask: what are the logical implications of *assuming* that investment demand corresponding to the expansion of productive capacity is *determined* by the growth needs of each subsystem?

To answer this question we can proceed analogously to the way Sraffa did, but as regards the system of physical quantities instead of the system of relative values, i.e. define the set of equations that make the physical quantities produced appear as necessary if certain conditions must be met. In this case, the previous condition establishes that net investment shall be completely induced by the growth of *effective demand* for each final consumption commodity.

Formally, we take Sraffa’s (1960) *q-system* (equations (11.5) and (11.6)) as a point of departure, but, instead of taking  $\mathbf{q}$  as given and effect a *virtual* re-proportioning to get a uniform physical surplus factor ( $R$ ), we consider the re-proportioning vector as given (and equal to the unitary vector  $\mathbf{u}$ ), and *determine* total quantities produced  $\mathbf{q}$ , if *net investment* must exactly meet the requirements of additional means of production, dictated by the expansion of effective demand for consumption goods.

Then, our system of physical quantities producing  $m$  final goods during time period  $t$  is formulated as:

$$\mathbf{A}(t)\mathbf{q}(t) + \sum_{i=1}^m (g + r_i)\mathbf{A}(t)\mathbf{q}^{(i)}(t) + \mathbf{c}(t) = \mathbf{q}(t) \quad (11.18)$$

$$\mathbf{a}_n^T(t)\mathbf{q}(t) = L(t) \quad (11.19)$$

where

$$(1 + (g + r_i))\mathbf{A}(t)\mathbf{q}^{(i)}(t) + \mathbf{c}^{(i)}(t) = \mathbf{q}^{(i)}(t) \quad (11.20)$$

$$\mathbf{c}(t) = \sum_{i=1}^m \mathbf{c}^{(i)}(t) \quad (11.21)$$

{153}------------------------------------------------

$$\mathbf{c}^{(i)}(t) = \mathbf{e}_i c_i(t) \quad (11.22)$$

$$\frac{d \ln c_i(t)}{dt} = g + r_i \quad (11.23)$$

for  $i = 1, \dots, m$ .

We see that  $\mathbf{c}(t)$  stands for the consumption goods vector during period  $t$ , each of its components  $c_i(t)$  expanding at a given compound *steady*<sup>5</sup> growth rate  $g + r_i$  (i.e. population growth and *per-capita* proportional change in demand for commodity  $i$ ); and  $\mathbf{q}^{(i)}(t)$  stands for the total quantities produced within subsystem  $i$ .

Equations (11.20) show that for each element of the consumption vector  $c_i(t)$  a whole circular process of self-replacement and expansion of means of production and a surplus of consumption good  $i$  can be established, conforming a relatively autonomous part within the whole system, *once* the set of growth rates  $(g + r_i)$  and the technique in use  $(\mathbf{A}(t), \mathbf{a}_n^T(t))$  for time period  $t$  are *given*.

Hence, by solving for  $\mathbf{q}^{(i)}$  in (11.20), we can define each *growing* subsystem (or *hyper*-subsystem) by a vector of physical quantities  $(\mathbf{q}^{(i)})$ , an absolute level of employment  $(L_i(t))$  and a set of produced means of production  $(\mathbf{s}^{(i)})$ , required to produce vector  $\mathbf{c}^{(i)}(t)$  and its expansion at rate  $(g + r_i)$  (see Pasinetti 1988a, p. 127):

$$\mathbf{q}^{(i)}(t) = (\mathbf{I} - (1 + (g + r_i))\mathbf{A}(t))^{-1} \mathbf{c}^{(i)}(t) \quad (11.24)$$

$$L_i(t) = \ell^{T(i)}(t) \mathbf{c}^{(i)}(t) = \ell_i^{(i)}(t) c_i(t) \quad (11.25)$$

$$\mathbf{s}^{(i)}(t) = \mathbf{A}(t) \mathbf{q}^{(i)}(t) = \mathbf{M}^{(i)}(t) \mathbf{c}^{(i)}(t) = \mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t) c_i(t) \quad (11.26)$$

where

$$\ell^{T(i)}(t) := \mathbf{a}_n^T(t) (\mathbf{I} - (1 + (g + r_i))\mathbf{A}(t))^{-1} \quad (11.27)$$

$$\mathbf{M}^{(i)}(t) := \mathbf{A}(t) (\mathbf{I} - (1 + (g + r_i))\mathbf{A}(t))^{-1} \quad (11.28)$$

for  $i = 1, \dots, m$ .

Two points must be clear. First, it can be checked from (11.18) and (11.24) that, because of linearity  $\sum_{i=1}^m \mathbf{q}^{(i)}(t) = \mathbf{q}(t)$ , so that the sum of all hyper-subsystems conforms to the original system.

In second place, the meaning of the  $i$ -th component of vector  $\ell^{T(i)}(t) - \ell_i^{(i)}(t)$  – and the  $i$ -th column of matrix  $\mathbf{M}^{(i)}(t) - \mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t)$  – are crucial within the approach of SED.

On the one hand,  $\ell_i^{(i)}(t)$  stands for the vertically hyper-integrated labour coefficient required to produce a unit of consumption good  $i$  in hyper-subsystem  $i$ . This means that it represents the labour embodied in the direct, indirect and hyper-indirect (i.e. additions to productive capacity) requirements of means of production to obtain a unit of final commodity  $i$ .

{154}------------------------------------------------

On the other hand, the composite commodity  $\mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t)$  is a unit of vertically hyper-integrated productive capacity, and stands for the direct, indirect and hyper-indirect means of production required to produce a unit of final consumption commodity  $i$  in hyper-subsystem  $i$ .

Conceptually, we may understand the possibilities of working in terms of hyper-subsystems by contrasting them with a disaggregated formulation in terms of industries. Let us identify the following elements in a system of physical quantities:

$$[\mathbf{c}(t), \mathbf{s}(t), \mathbf{L}(t), \mathbf{q}(t) - (\mathbf{s}(t) + \mathbf{c}(t))] \quad (11.29)$$

i.e. consumption, produced means of production, employment and net investment, respectively.

It can be noticed that as times goes by, changes in the methods of production  $(\mathbf{A}(t), \mathbf{a}_n^T(t))$  – because of *technical progress* – would upset both the commodity composition and relationships between  $\mathbf{s}(t) = \mathbf{A}(t)\mathbf{q}(t)$  and  $L(t) = \mathbf{a}_n^T(t)\mathbf{q}(t)$  (e.g. the degree of mechanisation), as well as between  $\mathbf{s}(t)$  and  $\mathbf{q}(t)$  (e.g. the capital intensity). However, if we consider the same magnitudes at the level of each hyper-subsystem:

$$[c_i(t), \mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t)c_i(t), \ell_i^{(i)}(t)c_i(t), (g + r_i)\mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t)c_i(t)] \quad (11.30)$$

and express them in terms of each unit of the consumption commodity with respect to which they are defined, we get:

$$[1, \mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t), \ell_i^{(i)}(t), (g + r_i)\mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t)] \quad (11.31)$$

We can see the importance of vertically hyper-integrated labour  $(\ell_i^{(i)}(t))$  and productive capacity  $(\mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t))$ . This very particular composite commodity –  $\mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t)$  – is the *unit of measurement* adopted all throughout the approach of SED to measure produced means of production. And it is a physical unit of measurement of capital goods that summarizes all the requirements to self-replace and expand a circular process corresponding to commodity  $i$ . The convenience of this unit of measurement is that:

a physical unit of productive capacity, by being defined with reference to the commodity that is produced, continues to make sense, as a physical unit, whatever complications technical change may cause to its composition in terms of ordinary commodities.

(Pasinetti 1973, p. 24)

Therefore, even though technical progress is upsetting the commodity composition of productive capacities, we can establish the following relationship

{155}------------------------------------------------

between the number of units of this composite commodity  $\mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t)$  and the *number* of units of consumption good for which it is being produced:

$$\#(\mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t)) = \alpha_i \times \#(c_i(t)), \quad \alpha_i > 0 \quad (11.32)$$

for  $i = 1, \dots, m$ , where  $\#(x)$  indicates the absolute number of instances of  $x$ .

In the case where net investment is completely induced by the growth of *effective demand* for each final commodity, we would have  $\alpha_i = 1$ , for  $i = 1, \dots, m$ . Of course, one could also perform an analysis where  $\alpha_i \neq 1$ , and so establish to what extent the accumulation of units of productive capacity corresponds (or is in excess or shortage) to the requirements of growth of consumption.

But then, if we analyse the case where  $\alpha_i = 1$ , by adopting as a unit of measurement for capital goods in subsystem  $i$  its corresponding unit of vertically hyper-integrated productive capacity for final commodity  $i$ , the previous re-presentation (11.31) can be accordingly modified (see Pasinetti 1988a, pp. 133–4):

$$[1, 1, \ell_i^{(i)}(t), (g + r_i)] \quad i = 1, \dots, m \quad (11.33)$$

In this way, consumption, productive capacity, employment and net investment can be described by means of a set of vertically hyper-integrated sectors. And even if technical progress exerts a change in the methods of production, affecting labour productivity together with the commodity composition of productive capacities, relations expressed by condition (11.32) and vector (11.33) remain unaffected as time goes by. The shifts that in a disaggregated inter-industry scheme would affect the coefficients themselves, in the approach of SED involve only a variation of the *same* coefficient:  $\ell_i^{(i)}(t)$ , i.e. vertically hyper-integrated labour (see Pasinetti 1981, p. 116).

#### ***The value side of a growing subsystem***

We are now in a position to formulate the notion of *natural* prices in the approach of SED.

In order to do so, let us first clearly state the assumptions:

**A1:** ‘there will be a particular natural rate of profits for each hyper-subsystem’ (Pasinetti 1988a, p. 129).

**A2:** there is a uniform price for each commodity *within* each hyper-subsystem (see Pasinetti 1988a, p. 129).

**A3:** there is a uniform surplus wage rate for the whole system.

From **A2** it follows that there is ‘a specific set of *natural prices* for each particular hyper-subsystem’ (Pasinetti 1988a, p. 129). Formally, the equations of production can now be stated as:

$$\mathbf{p}^{T(i)}(t)\hat{\mathbf{q}}^{(i)}(t) = \mathbf{p}^{T(i)}(t)\mathbf{A}(t)\hat{\mathbf{q}}^{(i)}(t)(1 + \pi_i) + \mathbf{a}_n^T(t)\hat{\mathbf{q}}^{(i)}(t)w \quad (11.34)$$

for  $i = 1, \dots, m$ .

{156}------------------------------------------------

As  $(\mathbf{A}(t), \mathbf{a}_n^T(t))$  are defined with respect to a specific  $\mathbf{q}^{(i)}(t)$ , we can solve for prices, taking physical quantities as given. Hence, the price for each commodity in hyper-subsystem  $i$  is given by:

$$\mathbf{p}^{T(i)}(t) = \mathbf{a}_n^T(t)(\mathbf{I} - (1 + \pi_i)\mathbf{A}(t))^{-1}w \quad (11.35)$$

for  $i = 1, \dots, m$ .

Accordingly, recalling the importance of the notion of vertically integrated productive capacity (discussed in the preceding section) we can define the price of units of productive capacity in each hyper-subsystem:

$$\mathbf{p}_k^{T(i)}(t) = \mathbf{p}^{T(i)}(t) \mathbf{M}^{(i)}(t) \quad (11.36)$$

for  $i = 1, \dots, m$ .

It can be seen that each element of vector  $\mathbf{p}_k^{T(i)}(t)$  is a linear combination of the prices of commodities within each hyper-subsystem, where the weights are each of the columns of matrix  $\mathbf{M}^{(i)}(t)$ . In particular, for the unit of productive capacity defined with respect to commodity  $i$  in hyper-subsystem  $i$ , we have:  $\mathbf{p}_k^{T(i)}(t)\mathbf{e}_i = p_{k_i}^{(i)}(t) = \mathbf{p}^{T(i)}(t)\mathbf{m}_i^{(i)}(t)$ .

This allows us to characterise the value side of each hyper-subsystem. By proceeding in a way analogous to the previous section, we define the following components in terms of a disaggregated system of relative prices:

$$[\mathbf{p}^T(t), \mathbf{p}_k^T(t), w, \pi] \quad (11.37)$$

i.e. prices of commodities, prices of direct productive capacities ( $\mathbf{p}_k^T(t) = \mathbf{p}^T(t)\mathbf{A}(t)$ ), wage rate and profit rate, respectively. If we now consider the same magnitudes at the level of each growing subsystem, we have:

$$[p_i^{(i)}(t), p_{k_i}^{(i)}(t), w, \pi_i] \quad i = 1, \dots, m \quad (11.38)$$

It can be immediately seen the correspondence between each element of (11.38) and (11.33). In this way, we have a complete description of each subsystem. But a very interesting element arises. The last component of each vector indicates a correspondence between the rate of growth and the rate of profit of each subsystem. In the general case, these need not be equal to each other. But what would be the logical implications of assuming them to coincide?

We have a set of  $m$  profit rates  $\pi_i$  and a uniform  $w$ , that have not yet been determined. Sraffa's analysis consisted in establishing a linear negative relation between a uniform  $\pi$  and  $w$ , emphasizing that the particular distributive configuration of society could not be determined 'mechanically'.

In contrast, within the approach of SED, the last step to arrive at *natural prices* involves stating the following assumption:

**A4:** the natural rate of profit  $\pi_i$  equals the growth rate of effective demand for consumption commodity  $i$ ,  $(g + r_i)$ .

{157}------------------------------------------------

Once we assume **A4**, we close the price system connecting it to the rate of expansion of physical quantities in each hyper-subsystem. But this has a remarkable implication. Replacing  $\pi_i = g + r_i$  into (11.35), recalling definition (11.27), and expressing prices in labour-commanded terms (i.e. setting labour as the *numéraire*), we finally obtain *natural* prices:

$$\mathbf{p}^{T(i)}(t) = \ell^{T(i)}(t) \quad (11.39)$$

for  $i = 1, \dots, m$ .

In each hyper-subsystem,

The value of the physical quantity of each consumption good that is produced turns out to be *equal to* the physical quantity of labour which has directly, indirectly and [ . . . ] hyper-indirectly been required by its production.

(Pasinetti 1988a, p. 129, our italics)

Thus, natural prices are completely determined by the physical requirements of reproduction and growth of each hyper-subsystem, measured in terms of labour. Income distribution has again been determined *before* prices are computed, however, the implication of a different necessary condition – assumption **A4** – has been studied. An interesting similarity of *purpose* could be inferred from equations (11.39) and the attribute *natural* as advanced by Sraffa in a document called ‘*Natural value*’:

When A. Smith etc. said ‘natural’ he did not in the least mean the ‘normal’ or the ‘average’ nor the ‘long run’ value. He meant that physical, truly natural relation between commodities, that is determined by the equations, and that is not disturbed by the process of securing a greater share in the product. ‘Exchange value’ was the result of natural value disturbed permanently by the scramble for the surplus.

(D3/12/11; E2.73; underlining in the original) (Garegnani 2005, p. 474)

In this case, the ‘scramble for the surplus’ is solved before prices are computed by establishing a particular configuration of profit rates that satisfies ‘that physical, truly natural relation between commodities’: the self-replacement and expansion of each sub-system.

Moreover, by setting  $\pi_i = g + r_i$ , the value of profits equals the corresponding value of demand for net investment in each hyper-subsystem. Then,

Total profits emerge as a kind of prior claim to share in the final national income, while total wages – by being (conceptually) determined after profits have been determined already – emerge as a kind of residual, [ . . . ] a ‘surplus’ that remains over and above what has been charged for profits.

(Pasinetti 1981, p. 144)

{158}------------------------------------------------

Once again, the argument has been turned upside down. In the approach of SED, under the configuration of natural prices, profits have a determining role and the total amount of wages (equal to total consumption) constitutes the ‘surplus’ of the system. How did this change come about? First, the notion of physical surplus has been modified by considering net investment a part of necessary consumption within the circular process and, therefore, making the net product consist only of commodities produced for final consumption. In the second place, by adopting the *natural* configuration of profit rates, profits provide exactly the purchasing power that finance investment in each hyper-subsystem. As a consequence, wages absorb the whole *net product* of the system:

And when the wage absorbs the whole net product, the commodity is equal in value to the labour that directly or indirectly [or hyper-indirectly, we must add] has been required to produce it.

(Sraffa 1960, App. A, p. 89)

As a general conclusion,

the reduction of all capital goods to physical quantities of labour is complete. There remains no longer any profit residual, thanks to the concept of a ‘natural’ rate of profit; and there remains no longer any commodity residual either, thanks to our technical-progress approach to capital accumulation.

(Pasinetti 1981, p. 199)

This last observation deserves some further reflection.

#### **A reflection on growth, profits and the labour theory of value**

In the approach of SED, the rates of expansion of the net product of each subsystem ( $g + r_{i}$ ) constitute the *natural* rates of profit. These are computed on the *value* of vertically hyper-integrated productive capacity. In this way, prices balance the differing productivities of hyper-integrated labour of each growing subsystem in the presence of unbalanced requirements of additional productive capacity, given that each of these hyper-subsystems has a different capital intensity. As a result, *natural* prices reflect an equality between labour embodied and labour commanded at the level of each final commodity.

The fact of interpreting Sraffa’s price equations as *necessary* prices that conform to a set of conditions allows for a treatment of the system of physical quantities in the same spirit. Within the approach of SED (Pasinetti 1988a), it is clear that net investment of an *actual* economy will not correspond to the sum of the required additional productive capacity of each subsystem (as a consequence,  $\alpha_{i}$  in (11.32) will be different from one).

However, in the same way as Sraffa obtains a set of prices that conform to a set of necessary conditions, the relative values *and* physical quantities obtained in Pasinetti’s (1988a) equations reflect just another set of necessary conditions,

{159}------------------------------------------------

highlighting the specific subsystem nature of both investment and profits in an unbalanced growth economic system.

On the side of physical quantities, the reproducibility requirements come to the fore when subsystems are growing, because the continuous effect of technical progress on productivity and real income trigger changes in the techniques in use and the commodity composition of net output.

On the side of relative values, while Sraffa was concerned with the logical implications of the assumption of a *uniform* rate of profits for a *viable* system, *natural* prices in Pasinetti (1988a) reflect the logical implications of the requirement of *uniform* value of net product per unit of labour in each growing subsystem. It is in this sense that ‘a growing economic system logically implies a *natural* rate of profit [for each hyper-subsystem]’ (Pasinetti 1981, p. 130). And, as a remarkable implication, the uniform wage rate  $w$  is reflecting a ‘basic principle of equal rewards for equal amounts of homogeneous labour’ (Pasinetti 1981, p. 132).

With the notion of physical real costs, *value* was obtained as a necessary result of interdependence. But it was just a ‘word’ devoid of content as a category ascribed to any *individual* commodity. In effect, for the SAVD, the labour theory of value had the analytical role of ‘expressing independently of distribution the aggregate on which a theory founded on the notion of social surplus naturally operates’ (Garegnani 2005, p. 485). So it is clear that the notion of physical real cost has a *logical* precedence over labour values:

‘Physical real cost’, where it becomes clear that the expression is intended to refer to the subsistence required by the labour necessary for the direct and indirect production of the commodity in question, and not to labour itself along Ricardian or Marxian lines.

(Garegnani 2005, p. 464)

In contrast, for the approach of SED, the redefinition of labour embodied to include hyper-indirect labour requirements has given rise to a particular notion of *natural* price (as obtained in (11.39)). And this notion of natural price entails a dual character.

On the one hand, it recognizes the interdependent nature of value as the means of production required for self-replacement and expansion constitute physical real costs. These heterogeneous commodities enter the price equations as data to find necessary exchange ratios.

On the other hand, however, to each input (and output) in the system ‘an index can be associated summarising all operations which have been performed on it’ (Pasinetti 1981, p. 134). This index summarizes the very concept of *value*. As such, it needs an *abstract* but homogeneous unit of measurement, which will be given by the hyper-integrated labour embodied in each commodity. The content of this index will change *only with* changes in labour requirements. Because, within the natural configuration of profit rates, a *given* change in distribution through profits can only occur due to a change in the growth requirements of productive capacity, which employ a certain amount of additional labour.

{160}------------------------------------------------

#### The separate determination of relative values and physical quantities

Behind the separate determination of physical quantities and relative prices there is a deeper aspect concerning method in Classical economic analysis: the idea that the normal or natural determination of a variable is the outcome of asymmetric relations of cause and effect, and that the direction of causality plays a prominent role (Pasinetti 1965, pp. 244–5). In contrast, within the Marginal method, endogenous variables are always simultaneously determined because they are linked by symmetric relations, so that there is total interdependence among them. Then,

all variables are regarded as mutually determined and mutually determinative. In this case we may say that the problem is approached as an *equilibrium problem*. The analysis is undertaken according to the *equilibrium principle*. In contradistinction to this approach is the scholastic way of thinking based on the chain-of-cause notion.

(Frisch 1992, p. 397, italics in the original)

The *equilibrium principle* is best reflected in the theory of demand and supply. In particular, within Marginal economic theory, ‘a demand schedule can only affect the price of the corresponding product to the extent to which it affects distribution’ (Garegnani 1983, p. 310). This is so because the functional relationship between commodity prices and final demand crucially depends on relative factor prices adjusting to the proportion of their employment as inputs (rising unit costs) when demand for final output changes.

When this demand and supply equilibrium theory of distribution is abandoned (as done both in the SAVD and in the approach of SED), even in presence of variable returns, the determination of outputs entails them to be treated as independent variables *when* determining relative prices (Garegnani 1983, 1987).

As a consequence, within the SAVD, the asymmetric character of the relations is stressed, as well as the role of historical factors in the ‘spheres of distribution, accumulation and technical change’ (Garegnani 1987, p. 563). And even within the set of ‘intermediate data’, the key starting point in the analysis is that of a ‘*separate* determination of the real wage and social product’ (Garegnani 1987, pp. 561–2).

As for the determination of *gross* physical quantities produced, ‘the *volume* of the social product depends on: (i) the stage reached by accumulation [. . .]; (ii) the technical conditions of production which regulate the physical product per labourer [. . .]. [The] *commodity composition* of the social product, on the other hand, was studied mainly from the angle of the needs of reproduction’ (Garegnani 1987, p. 561).

{161}------------------------------------------------

It is interesting to note that in the approach of SED, as we have seen above, the ‘needs of reproduction’ of each subsystem *i* play a crucial role in the determination of the commodity composition of total output  $\mathbf{q}(t)$ . In fact, net investment in each subsystem is induced by the growth needs of productive capacity, according to the variations of effective demand for final consumption commodities.

As regards the SAVD, it must be clear that data and unknowns within the core (as specified above) have relationships of mutual dependence. However, short chains of deductive reasoning suitable of being expressed in exact mathematical form are only those that determine the unknowns once the data were first separately determined.

In fact, the Classical economists would not accept ‘the possibility of expressing the dependence of outputs upon changes in distribution by means of functional relations [. . .] of sufficient generality and with persistence over time’ (see Garegnani 1984, p. 298).

This is not to say that the structure of relative prices (and thus of distribution) does not influence the composition of consumption demand. However,

The multiplicity of these influences and their variability according to circumstances was in fact understood to make it impossible to reconduct them to *necessary* quantitative relations like those studied in the ‘core’ [. . .].  
(Garegnani 1984, p. 297)

Of course, with a changing price structure real per-capita income would change, and this would trigger non-proportional change in the structure of demand for final consumption commodities (Pasinetti 1981, Ch. IV). However, there is neither a marginal substitution between goods determining an equilibrium demand *schedule*, nor the establishment of a functional relationship giving closed form to the income-effect arising from the ever changing price structure.

In this respect, the approach of SED limits itself to acknowledge the empirical fact that the change in real income will have a non-proportional effect on the commodity composition of effective demand for consumption goods. Nonetheless, the *evolution* of the structure of consumption demand is taken as given, recognizing as well the historical factors influencing this evolution.

In effect, in the SAVD relative commodity outputs depend on the level of general purchasing power (the net output in terms of a composite commodity), the distribution of income ( $w, \pi$ ) and the technical conditions of production ( $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{a}_n^T$ ) (see Garegnani 1987, p. 564). If these elements determine  $\mathbf{q}$  and are given when determining  $\mathbf{p}^T$ , then we can consider  $\mathbf{q}$  as given when determining  $\mathbf{p}^T$ . This, of course, recalls the *relative* autonomy of the price and physical quantity systems in Sraffa’s analysis (Pasinetti 1977, pp. 111–12). However, if the *aggregate level* of *real* income has to be known to determine the particular *composition* of demand, then the price vector  $\mathbf{p}^T$  weighting the composite commodity taken as standard of value has to be known before physical quantities demanded can be determined.

{162}------------------------------------------------

In fact, in the approach of SED, when we assume the *natural* configuration of the rates of profit:

The whole process may be viewed as a succession of asymmetrical relations, which evince a definite causation chain. The first exogenous factor of our scheme, technology, which is at the origin of the whole process, directly determines the structure of natural (relative) prices, independently of anything else. *But technology also determines the height of potential per capita income.* At this point, when the price structure has been (conceptually) determined already, the consumers' decisions and the population size (the other two exogenous factors in our scheme) come in to determine physical quantities to be produced.

(Pasinetti 1981, p. 142, our italics)

This *asymmetric* chain of causation reminds us of the two distinct stages of analysis present in the SAVD:

In the first, the effect of the change in real wage was examined while taking the outputs as given. In the second stage, the possible effect on *outputs* of the initial change was analysed in accordance with the circumstances of the case under consideration, jointly with its possible secondary effects on prices and distribution, in the case of non constant returns to scale.

(Garegnani 1984, p. 299)

In both chains of reasoning, it must be clear that 'it does not seem possible to postulate functional relations of known properties [...] by which to determine the individual incomes *and* the quantity demanded associated with different prices of the product' (Garegnani 1987, p. 565, our italics).

Moreover, in both approaches, the conceptual solution of the natural or normal price system (respectively) precedes that of the physical quantity system. It is clear, though, that  $\mathbf{p}^T$  depends on  $\mathbf{q}$  through the methods of production employed.

In order to deal with this issue, within the SAVD, if there is a change in a *direct* determinant of prices – i.e. technique ( $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{a}_n^T$ ) or any of the distributive variables – we first solve the new system of prices by keeping the old quantities. Then, as the effect of the new vector of prices on effective demand leads to variations in physical quantities, possibly affecting the methods of production, we study the further feedback effect on prices. This procedure is an iterative process that is carried on until 'output changes are not sufficient to prompt further significant modifications in production methods' (Ravagnani 2007, p. 10).

In contradistinction, within the approach of SED, the complex process which leads to the new technique and to the new commodity composition of consumption demand, as a result of a change in a direct determinant of  $\mathbf{p}^T(t)$ , is

{163}------------------------------------------------

not explained through feedback mechanisms between quantities and prices. Its existence is, of course, recognized (within an institutional set-up). But its explanation is beyond the scope of the analysis. In fact, in each period  $t$ , the technique in use ( $\mathbf{A}(t)$ ,  $\mathbf{a}_n^T(t)$ ) and the vector of final consumption demand  $\mathbf{c}(t)$  are taken as given.

#### A final remark

This chapter has presented some essential elements of two relevant approaches derived from Sraffa's analysis, emphasizing their peculiarities and uncovering points of contact.

The first approach considered has been the SAVD, which provides a rigorous and general description of the working of capitalist systems rooted in the view of the Classical economists. Under this view profits appear as the surplus of the system, that is, a revenue originated by the institutional set-up of society, which prevents wages from absorbing the entire net social product.

The second approach considered has been that of SED, which provides an analytical framework of necessary relations within the evolving structure of modern industrial systems. A possible interpretation and use of Sraffa's equations has been proposed in connection to the role that 'pure theory' has in this approach. In particular, the solution to the price equations has emerged as the logical implication of a set of conditions necessary for the reproduction and growth of each hyper-subsystem. If these conditions become desirable within an industrial system, then the approach opens up the possibility for an original normative analysis, where the efficiency properties of the system can be established without any reference to the notion of individual rationality.

Historically, the two approaches analysed have been developed along parallel paths. Nevertheless, they share significant features, the most evident of which is the separate determination of relative prices and physical quantities. The present attempt to consider differences and examine similarities has been conceived with a view to opening up a fruitful dialogue.

- 2 All throughout our analysis we will work with single-product industries, circulating capital, no natural resources and an annual cycle of production. This has been done in order to bring to the fore the conceptual discussions at stake. As for notation, boldface lowercase letters stand for vectors, boldface uppercase letters stand for matrices, all vectors are column vectors, unless explicitly transposed, and vectors with a hat are diagonal matrices whose main diagonal contains the elements of the corresponding vector.

{164}------------------------------------------------

- 3 We will determine relative values for given methods of production  $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{a}_n^T)$ , corresponding to a vector of *gross* physical quantities  $(\mathbf{q})$  (see Eatwell 1977, p. 63, n.10).
- 4 It is interesting to note that under this configuration, the consumption out of wages is part of the *circular process*, and it is entirely determined by the requirements of a given composite commodity  $\mathbf{d}$ .
