# **Part IV**

## **Linear models of production**

{195}------------------------------------------------

### 14 Extensive rent and multiple equilibria<sup>1</sup>

*Christian Bidard*

### Extensive cultivation models

When the demand for agricultural goods increases, the extension of cultivation on lands of the same grade sets no significant economic problem: the same marginal methods are used and no changes in prices, wages or rents occur. A limit is reached when the corresponding land becomes scarce. Then the prices of the agricultural products rise and cultivation is extended to a new land or, alternatively, more intensive methods are substituted for the present ones on the same land. To isolate extensive cultivation proper, we assume a unique method of cultivation on each type of land (because of that one-to-one correspondence, it is indifferent to refer to a land or an agricultural method). Sraffa (1960) argued that the order of cultivation is not a natural phenomenon and may change with the exogenous distribution variable. Let the rate of profit be given. Post-Sraffian studies have shown that the extension of cultivation follows a simple rule: the lands are cultivated in the order of the decreasing real wages they yield for a zero rent. Since that order is well defined, there exists a unique equilibrium for each demand basket, flukes apart. The equilibrium is characterized on the physical side by a unique set of cultivated lands and, on the value side, by a unique associated set of prices, wages and rents.

The standard theory of extensive cultivation summarized above admits two significant restrictions (e.g., see Kurz and Salvadori, 1995, Chapter 10, section 1.1): (i) the industrial methods are given, and (ii) the agricultural product is unique. Our first objective is to understand the exact role played by these hypotheses. For simplicity, we shall mainly consider bisector models, with one agricultural good (corn) and either one industrial good (iron) or a second agricultural good (rice). Models of the second type are more complex but those of the first type suffice to understand the origin of the difficulties linked to the abandonment of either assumption (i) or (ii). One of them is the possible occurrence of multiple equilibria. We shall also show that, besides the equilibria identified by Ricardo and Sraffa, other equilibria of a different type (‘external’ equilibria) may exist. The main result of the study makes a bridge between the multiplicity puzzle and the existence of an external equilibrium of a certain type.

{196}------------------------------------------------

#### A generic equality

Consider for a while a multisector model with  $n$  agricultural or industrial commodities. The model is of the extensive type when a unique method of cultivation is available on each type of land. The final demand vector  $d$  admits  $n$  degrees of freedom. Flukes apart, slight changes in demand are met by slight changes in the activity levels of the operated techniques, be they marginal agricultural methods or industrial methods. Let  $n'$  be the total number of marginal lands and operated industrial methods. The physical adaptation of the net product to demand requires that  $n'$  be at least equal to  $n$ . Conversely, since a price equation with a zero rent is associated with each marginal method and each operated industrial method,  $n'$  does not exceed  $n$  in order to avoid an over-determination of prices. Therefore, the equality

$$\begin{aligned} &\text{number of marginal lands + operated industrial methods} \\ &\qquad = \text{number of goods} \end{aligned} \tag{14.1}$$

holds generically for long-term equilibria.

#### Possibility of multiple Ricardian equilibria

We consider more specifically bisector models ( $n = 2$ ) with an agricultural sector producing corn, complemented either by an industrial sector producing iron or a second agricultural sector producing rice. Several types of lands exist, but each type of land admits a unique method of cultivation (in particular, the corn lands differ from the rice lands, if any). A significant difference between the two families of models is that, in a long-term equilibrium, rice can be produced by several methods simultaneously (with, however, a unique marginal rice method). The second family of models is therefore more complex. In both cases, our recourse to formalization is minimum: only the sign of the potential rent matters (if it is positive, the corresponding land is totally cultivated; if it is negative, that land is not cultivated at all; it is zero on the marginal lands) and the standard properties of single-product systems without lands suffice to conclude.

In this chapter, the rate of profit is given, positive and small enough to ensure the existence of an equilibrium (Salvadori, 1986). The demand basket is also given (even if it is not always specified and is sometimes considered as a parameter). In a Ricardian equilibrium, and flukes apart, there is one marginal corn land and either one operated iron method (first family) or one marginal rice method (second family). To start with, we consider a corn–iron model and state a few simple properties which derive from the examination of the value side.

##### *Property 1*

The marginal corn land and the operated iron method define the vector of prices, wage and rents and the set of fully cultivated lands.

{197}------------------------------------------------

###### *Proof*

Up to a factor, the price vector is defined by the industrial methods and the marginal conditions of production in agriculture, as underlined by Ricardo. The potential rent on any land is calculated as the gap between the value of its product and the production cost, normal profits included. Its sign determines whether that land is totally cultivated (the land is ‘intra-marginal’) or not cultivated at all (it is ‘ultra-marginal’).

##### ***Property 2***

Given the operated iron method, the order of cultivation of the corn lands coincides with the decreasing real wages they pay for a zero rent.

###### *Proof*

Let the iron method be specified. By Property 1, a marginal corn land *i* associated with it defines a price-and-wage vector. Another land *j* is ultra-marginal (and, therefore, is cultivated after land *i* when demand increases) if method *j* is more costly than method *i*. The theory of choice of methods elaborated by Sraffa for industrial methods applies: the real wage associated with the use of method *i* is higher than that associated with method *j*. Hence the rule on the order of cultivation.

##### ***Property 3***

The order of cultivation of lands may change with the operated iron method.

###### *Proof*

This statement is rather intuitive for the readers of Sraffa’s book.

Symmetrically to Property 3, the cost-minimizing iron method may change with the marginal corn land. One feels that the existence of different rankings explains the multiplicity of equilibria for a given vector of demand. But what matters for multiplicity? Is it the influence of the iron method on the order of cultivation of the corn lands (first interpretation), or is it that of the marginal corn land on the cheapest iron method (second interpretation)? If the cost-minimizing iron method is independent of the marginal land, the iron sector can be reduced to a unique effective method and, then, the order of cultivation is unique. Therefore, multiplicity stems from the fact that the cheapest iron method varies with the marginal land (second interpretation).

This result allows us to identify the simplest family of models for which multiplicity can occur: they are bisector corn–iron models. The phenomenon is illustrated by an example chosen in order to meet minimum requirements: there are two corn lands 1 and 1′, two iron methods 2 and 2′, and the reader can check

{198}------------------------------------------------

that the corn method 1 is cheaper than method 1' whatever the iron method. By contrast, the relative cheapness of the iron methods 2 and 2' depends on the marginal corn land.

#### ***Example 1***

The rate of profit is  $r = 10\%$ . There are two lands 1 and 1' (land 1 area = 4,928 acres, land 1' area > 144 acres). Each acre produces one net quarter of corn (this inessential feature facilitates calculations). There are two iron methods 2 and 2'. The demand vector is  $d = (1,412\text{ qr. corn}, 1,486\text{ t. iron})$ .

##### *First solution*

Method 1: 1800 qr. corn + 450 t. iron + 150 labour + 4800 acres land<sub>1</sub> → 6600 qr. corn

Method 2: 3388 qr. corn + 3388 t. iron + 532.4 labour → 5324 t. iron

This solution is sustained by the price vector  $p_{12} = (p_{\text{corn}} = 1, p_{\text{iron}} = 6, w = 11)$ . Methods 1' and 2' described below pay extra-costs at these prices and are not operated.

##### *Second solution*

Method 1: 1848 qr. corn + 462 t. iron + 154 labour + 4928 acres land<sub>1</sub> → 6776 qr. corn

Method 1': 16 qr. corn + 4 t. iron + 24 labour + 144 acres land<sub>1'</sub> → 160 qr. corn

Method 2': 3660 qr. corn + 732 t. iron + 671 labour → 2684 t. iron

In that solution, land 1' is marginal and land 1 is totally cultivated (note that method 1 is the same as in the first solution but is now operated at maximum activity level). This solution is sustained by the price vector  $p_{1'2'} = (1, 4, w = 5.2)$ . At these prices, land 1 yields a positive rent while method 2 pays extra-costs and is not operated.

Example 1 can be immediately transformed into another relative to the second family of models we consider, with two agricultural goods: it suffices to proceed to a nominal change of ‘iron’ into ‘rice’, to introduce data relative to the areas of rice lands per quarter produced, and to choose the available areas of lands in order that, in each of both equilibria, no rice land is fully cultivated so that the rents on these lands are zero.

As an aside of that study, it turns out that the symmetry in the conditions defining the standard framework used for the study of extensive rent (the industrial methods are given and the agricultural product is unique) is slightly misleading: what really matters is that the methods of production are given in all sectors but one. The observation that several solutions may coexist in the presence of several agricultural products was made by D’Agata (1983) and other authors, and later by Erreygers (1990; Erreygers’s example fits strictly with the extensive cultivation

{199}------------------------------------------------

framework). The reasoning and the example above show that the presence of several agricultural goods is inessential for the result.

#### **The notion of an external equilibrium**

The equilibria studied in the previous section involve one marginal corn method and either one industrial method or one marginal rice method: these are ‘normal’ or ‘Ricardian’ equilibria. For  $n = 2$  goods, the equality (14.1) is then read as  $1 + 1 = 2$ . But one may notice that, for  $n = 2$ , equality (14.1) allows for another combination, with no marginal land and the coexistence of two iron methods ( $0 + 2 = 2$ ).<sup>2</sup> Let us explain when and why this type of equilibrium occurs:

#### *Example 2*

The rate of profit is  $r = 20\%$ . The unique corn method 3 and the two iron methods 4 and 4′ are described below. The corn land is homogenous and its total area is 102 acres.

Method 3: 100 qr. corn + 30 t. iron + 26 labour + 100 acres land  $\rightarrow$  200 qr. corn

Method 4: 40 qr. corn + 20 t. iron + 66 labour  $\rightarrow$  100 t. iron

Method 4′: 20 qr. corn + 40 t. iron + 66 labour  $\rightarrow$  100 t. iron

Let us study the behaviour of a solution when demand increases. For a low level of demand, the rent is zero and the prices  $p_{34} = (1, 1.5, w = 1)$  are determined by the unique corn method and the iron method 4, which is then cheaper than method 4′. The equilibrium is of the Ricardian type. With increasing demand, there comes a moment when land is fully cultivated. It is, however, possible to overcome this physical limit thanks to a partial substitution of the industrial method 4′ for 4. The economic conditions required for that substitution are:

- On the value side, the prices are then determined by the joint use of both iron methods. For this to happen, the corresponding price-and-wage vector  $p_{44'}$  must be positive and land must yield a positive rent at these prices, otherwise corn would not be produced. These conditions are met in Example 2, the prices being  $p_{44'} = (33, 33, w = 14)$ .
- On the quantity side, the partial substitution of the new iron method 4′ for 4 must lead to an increase in production. As a matter of fact, method 4 can be seen as a way to transform an investment of 40 qr. corn into 80 t. iron (in terms of net product), whereas method 4′ is more efficient in this regard as it transforms 20 qr. corn into 60 t. iron. Given the scarcity of land, that property allows for an increase in the production of both corn and iron.

In such a long-term equilibrium, the prices and the rent(s) on land(s) are determined by the iron sector. Following Saucier (1981), who first recognized its existence, we call it an ‘external extensive rent equilibrium’, or ‘external equilibrium’ for

{200}------------------------------------------------

short. The phenomenon has similarities with another: in his study of intensive cultivation, Sraffa argued that ‘two methods of cultivation [are] used consistently side by side on similar lands determining a uniform rent per acre’ (*Production*, section 87), but Saucier (1981) showed that the coexistence of methods may well occur in industry instead of agriculture and dubbed this phenomenon ‘external intensive rent’. While external intensive rent is acknowledged in the specialized literature (e.g. Kurz and Salvadori, 1995), external extensive rent has been less successful: apparently, the only systematic study on the topic is that of Erreygers (1991, 1995).

When it is imbedded in a corn–rice model, external rent gives rise to curious swings in cultivation. Let us substitute rice for iron in the above example and introduce vast rice lands 4 and 4′. An observer who follows the evolution of cultivation when demand increases will notice that rice is initially cultivated on land 4. When the corn land 3 is totally cultivated, the cultivation of rice regresses on land 4 and is progressively transferred to the other rice land 4′: the cause of the transfer is also external to the rice industry since land 4 is not fully cultivated when the phenomenon occurs.

Let us return to a corn–iron model. Even if Example 2 exhibits a case of external equilibrium, each feasible level of demand is met in a unique way. But let us modify the example and replace method 4′ by another 4″ such that the above-mentioned value conditions for external rent are still met, but the physical conditions are reversed: we suppose now that method 4″ is *less* efficient than 4 for the transformation of corn into iron. These conditions, which define the case of ‘regressive external rent’, generate a multiplicity of equilibria: a first equilibrium of the Ricardian type is obtained by cultivating land partly and using the then cheaper method 4 to produce iron; a second equilibrium of the external type results from ‘overflowing’: land is totally cultivated, but the surplus of corn is partly spoilt because it is transformed into iron partly by means of method 4 and partly by means of the less efficient method 4″. A numerical example with one corn land 3 and two iron methods 4 and 4″ is:

#### ***Example 3***

The rate of profit = 20%. Methods 3 and 4 are those of Example 2, and method 4″ is defined below. The land area is 102 acres. The demand vector is  $d = (60\text{ qr. corn}, 50\text{ t. iron})$ .

##### *First solution (Ricardian equilibrium)*

Method 3: 100 qr. corn + 30 t. iron + 26 labour + 100 acres land → 200 qr. corn

Method 4: 40 qr. corn + 20 t. iron + 66 labour → 100 t. iron

The prices are  $p_{34} = (1, 1.5, w = 1)$ . At these prices, method 4″ defined below is more costly than method 4.

{201}------------------------------------------------

##### *Second solution (regressive external equilibrium)*

Method 3: 102 qr. corn + 30.6 t. iron + 26.52 labour + 102 acres land → 204 qr. corn

Method 4: 6.3 qr. corn + 3.15 t. iron + 10.395 labour → 15.75 t. iron

Method 4'': 35.7 qr. corn + 68 labour → 68 t. iron

Positive prices  $p_{44''}$  are determined by the two iron methods. At these prices, the corn land yields a positive rent and is fully cultivated. The rate of transform of corn into iron for method 4'' (35.7 qr. corn → 68 t. iron) is smaller than for method 4 (1 qr. corn → 2 t. iron).

#### **Algebraic characterization of external rent**

In this more technical section, we provide an algebraic characterization of external rent in a bisector corn–iron model, with one method of cultivation for corn and two industrial methods for iron. It is therefore a generalization of examples 2 (external progressive equilibrium) and 3 (external regressive equilibrium).

Let  $(a_i, b_i, l_i)$  be the corn, iron and labour coefficients of method  $i$  ( $i = 1, 2, 2'$ ) per unit of gross product. Consider the matrix

$$M = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - (1 + r)a_1 & -(1 + r)b_1 & -l_1 \\ -(1 + r)a_{2'} & 1 - (1 + r)b_{2'} & -l_{2'} \\ -(1 + r)a_2 & 1 - (1 + r)b_2 & -l_2 \end{bmatrix} \tag{14.2}$$

Let the iron method 2 be cheaper than 2' when rent is zero. In the absence of rent, Bidard's criterion (2004, pp. 81–2) for industrial systems applies and asserts that the determinant of  $M$  is positive. Consider an external equilibrium, corresponding to the full cultivation of land and the joint use of both iron methods which define a positive price vector  $p_{22'}$ . The product of the first row of  $M$  by  $p_{22'}$  is equal to the positive rent per acre; those of the second and third rows are zero. Alternatively, the vector  $p_{22'}$  can be viewed as the product of  $M^{-1}$  by a vector with a first positive component and two zero components. Therefore  $p_{22'}$  is positive if and only if the entries of the first column of  $M^{-1}$  are positive. Up to the positive determinant of  $M$ , these entries are the cofactors of the first row of  $M$ . The positivity of these cofactors is written

$$\frac{l_2}{l_{2'}} < \frac{1 - (1 + r)b_2}{1 - (1 + r)b_{2'}} < \frac{a_2}{a_{2'}} \tag{14.3}$$

These inequalities allow for external rent. External regressive rent requires an additional physical condition, viz. that method 2' is less efficient than 2 in the transformation of corn into iron. The condition is written as an inequality:

$$\frac{a_2}{a_{2'}} < \frac{1 - b_2}{1 - b_{2'}} \tag{14.4}$$

{202}------------------------------------------------

Conditions (14.3) and (14.4) together imply  $b'_2 < b_2$ . Then all ratios intervening in these conditions are smaller than one. A progressive equilibrium is obtained when condition (14.3) holds and inequality (14.4) is reversed.

#### The origin of multiplicity

In a corn–iron model, a long-term equilibrium is of the Ricardian type if the prices are determined by a marginal land and an iron method, of the external type if there are determined by two iron methods. Example 1 has shown the possible coexistence of two Ricardian equilibria. The section above on the notion of an external equilibirum has explained that regression is a source of multiplicity, with one normal and one external equilibrium. The present section establishes a hidden connection between these two results and identifies regression as the *unique* source of multiplicity. To illustrate the property, we return to Example 1, for which two Ricardian equilibria have been found. Further investigations show the existence of a third equilibrium which is of the regressive external type.

#### *Example 4*

The data are those of Example 1. Besides the two Ricardian equilibria identified above, another external equilibrium for which the price vector is defined by the two iron methods 2 and 2′ is:

Method 1: 1848 qr. corn + 462 t. iron + 154 labour + 4928 acres land<sub>1</sub> → 6776 qr.  
corn

Method 2: 1911 qr. corn + 1911 t. iron + 300.3 labour → 3003 t. iron

Method 2′: 1605 qr. corn + 321 t. iron + 294.25 labour → 1177 t. iron

The prices are  $p_{22'} = (1, 5, 8)$ . At these prices, land 1 yields a positive rent and is fully cultivated, whereas cultivation on land 1′ would be too costly. Method 2 is operated for a low level of demand and the newly introduced method 2′ has a lower rate of transform of corn into iron (8/15 t. iron per quarter of corn invested for method 2′, instead of 8/14 for method 2). That third equilibrium is therefore external and regressive.

We intend to show that this property is general: the coexistence of two Ricardian solutions implies that of a third solution with regressive external rent. The lesson is that multiplicity, even when it takes the form of two Ricardian equilibria, reveals the presence of a regressive external rent; beyond the appearances, regressive external rent is not *a* source of multiplicity, as shown in the earlier section 4, but the *unique* source of multiplicity. Unfortunately, the proof of that result is rather involved. For the sake of convenience, the proof is relegated to an appendix where it will lie forever.

Let us rather consider a last numerical example to illustrate a consequence of that result. A noteworthy characteristic of Example 5 is that the description of the economy is incomplete, as the data relative to the production of corn are lacking.

{203}------------------------------------------------

#### ***Example 5***

Consider a corn–iron model with extensive cultivation and a certain number of lands. The rate of profit is 10 per cent and the three iron methods are:

Method 2: 0.4 corn + 0.3 iron + 1 labour → 1 t. iron

Method 2′: 0.2 corn + 0.5 iron + 1 labour → 1 t. iron

Method 2″: 0.1 corn + 0.75 iron + 1 labour → 1 t. iron

We look at the possible existence of multiple Ricardian equilibria. Since multiplicity implies the existence of a regressive external rent, let us identify the corresponding equilibrium. With two iron methods operated simultaneously, the only three candidates are made of the combinations (2, 2″), (2′, 2″) or (2, 2′). The first combination is excluded because method 2′ pays over-profits at its associated prices, and the second because the wage would then be negative: only the combination (2, 2′) can sustain an external equilibrium, with land 1 yielding a positive rent at prices  $p_{22'} = (1, 1, 0.23)$ . Here enters a new argument: consider an arbitrary corn method  $C$  which pays over-profits at prices  $p_{22'}$ ; then the relative cost of methods 2 and 2′ when method  $C$  is operated is independent of the exact characterization of  $C$ . If one makes the calculation for the method  $C$ : 1 labour → 1 corn, it turns out that method 2 is cheaper and is operated first. An external rent appears when method 2′ is introduced. But since the rate of transform of corn into iron for method 2′ (0.2 qr. corn gives 0.5 t. iron) improves on that of method 2 (0.4 corn gives 0.7 t. iron), that external rent is progressive. The overall conclusion is that no regressive external equilibrium exists, therefore the Ricardian equilibrium is unique. Remarkably enough, that result follows from the examination of the iron methods only.

#### **Conclusion**

This study has first identified the simplest extensive cultivation model for which multiple equilibria can occur: it is a bisector model with one agricultural product (corn) and one industrial product (iron) with two methods of production in the industrial sector. Two types of long-term equilibria are distinguished: those of the Ricardian type involve a marginal land and one iron method; those of the external type are characterized by the coexistence of two iron methods which determine the prices independently of the agricultural methods. An external equilibrium is progressive if, when a marginal land becomes fully cultivated, the newly introduced iron method allows for a higher rate of transform of corn into iron. Then the partial substitution of that method for the old allows it to meet an increasing demand. A regressive external equilibrium, characterized by the introduction of a less efficient iron method, may exist as well. Regression is a source of multiplicity. The main result of our analysis is that the coexistence of two Ricardian equilibria implies that of a third regressive external equilibrium, and therefore regression is the unique source of multiplicity. A parallel can be drawn with the theory of intensive rent proper: in that case, multiplicity also

{204}------------------------------------------------

comes from the insertion of a new method which turns out to be inefficient (Bidard, 2010). The similarity suggests a research programme on more general land models.

### Appendix

#### Multiplicity requires regressive external rent

Let there be an extensive cultivation model with an arbitrary number of corn methods and (for simplicity) two iron methods 2 and 2', a given positive rate of profit  $r$  and a given demand vector  $d$ , and assume two Ricardian equilibria. The first equilibrium calls for the marginal land 1 and the iron method 2: these methods define the prices, the wage and the potential rents on the other lands and determine which lands are totally cultivated and which are left fallow. The same for the second equilibrium with the marginal land 1' and the iron method 2'. We intend to show the existence of a third equilibrium of the regressive external type. The proof is in three main steps: we first study the value side and show that positive prices are associated with the joint use of the iron methods 2 and 2' (property P4 below), thus giving rise to external rent. Then the study of the quantity side shows that the external combination (2, 2') is regressive (property P8). Finally, we show that this combination can produce the required basket, therefore that (2, 2') is an external regressive equilibrium which coexists with the two Ricardian equilibria (property P9).

For a given rate of profit, let (1, 2) and (1', 2') define two Ricardian equilibria, where 1 and 1' are the respective marginal lands. The iron methods differ, otherwise the iron sector might be reduced to one method and the solution would be unique. Similarly, the marginal lands differ otherwise the associated cheaper iron method would be the same. The notation

$$P1: (1, 2) \succ (1, 2')$$

means that the iron method 2' is more costly at the positive equilibrium prices  $p_{12}$ . This is equivalent to the fact that method 2 yields over-profits at prices  $p_{12}$ . Symmetrically, the second equilibrium implies that:

$$P2: (1', 2') \succ (1', 2).$$

If neither land 1 pays a positive rent at prices  $p_{1'2'}$ , nor land 1' at prices  $p_{12}$ , an industrial system made of the methods (1, 1', 2, 2') (by 'industrial system', we mean that the land inputs are ignored because they are free) would admit both equilibria (1, 2) and (1', 2'). This being excluded for industrial systems, we assume without loss of generality that land 1 yields a positive rent (or positive over-profits) at prices  $p_{1'2'}$ :

$$P3: (1, 2') \succ (1', 2').$$

{205}------------------------------------------------

Let labour be chosen as numéraire. Since the set  $(1, 2')$  of methods yields more than the ruling rate of profit at the positive prices  $p_{1'2'}$ , the prices  $p_{12'}$  are positive. By (P1) method 2 yields over-profits at prices  $p_{12'}$ , and by (P2) it pays extra-costs at prices  $p_{1'2'}$ . Therefore, method 2 yields the ruling rate of profit for some adequately chosen convex combination  $\lambda p_{12'} + (1 - \lambda) p_{1'2'}$ . Since method  $2'$  yields the ruling rate for any combination of  $p_{12'}$  and  $p_{1'2'}$ , the positive vector then obtained is the price vector  $p_{22'}$ . Hence:

P4: The prices  $p_{22'}$  are positive and such that  $p_{12} < p_{12'} < p_{22'} < p_{1'2'}$ ; at prices  $p_{22'}$  land 1 yields a positive rent whereas land  $1'$  pays extra-costs.

There exists a virtual corn method  $C$  such that  $p_{22'} = p_{C2}$ . Let  $L_{ij}$  denote the set of corn lands or methods which yield a positive rent at prices  $p_{ij}$  and consider any corn method  $t \in L_{12}$ . Given the iron method 2, we have  $p_{C2} > p_{12} > p_{t2}$ , therefore method  $t$  yields over-profits at prices  $p_{22'} = p_{C2}$ . This shows that  $t \in L_{22'}$ .

P5: The partially cultivated land 1 and the fully cultivated lands  $L_{12}$  at the  $(1, 2)$  equilibrium are fully cultivated at prices  $p_{22'}$ :  $L_{12} \subset L_{22'}$ .

A similar argument shows that:

P6: The fully cultivated lands  $L_{22'}$  at prices  $p_{22'}$  are also fully cultivated at the  $(1', 2')$  equilibrium:  $L_{22'} \subset L_{1'2'}$ .

Let  $c_1$ ,  $c_{1'}$  or  $c_t$  be the respective net baskets obtained when land 1,  $1'$  or  $t$  is totally cultivated, and  $c_2$ ,  $c_{2'}$  the net baskets per unit activity level for the iron methods (all these baskets have a positive and a negative component). When a pair of methods like  $(1, 2)$  or  $(t, 2; t \in L_{12})$  yields the positive rate of profit  $r$  or more at the positive prices  $p_{12}$ , the Hawkins–Simon theorem asserts that the determinant obtained by combining the corresponding net baskets vector is positive, therefore  $\det(c_1, c_2) > 0$  and  $\det(c_t, c_2) > 0$  for  $t \in L_{12}$ . More generally:

P7:  $\det(c_1, c_2) > 0$ ,  $\det(c_{1'}, c_{2'}) > 0$ ,  $\det(c_1, c_{2'}) > 0$ ,  $\det(c_t, c_{2'}) > 0$  for  $t \in L_{1'2'}$ , and  $\det(c_t, c_{2'}) > 0$  for  $t \in L_{22'}$ .

At the  $(1, 2)$  equilibrium, the overall net product  $d$  of the economy is obtained by cultivating a part  $\theta_1$  of land 1, the whole lands  $L_{12}$  and by operating the industrial method 2 at a certain activity level  $\alpha_2 > 0$ :

$$d = \theta_1 c_1 + \sum_{t \in L_{12}} c_t + \alpha_2 c_2 \tag{14.A.1}$$

At the  $(1', 2')$  equilibrium, the same basket is obtained by cultivating a part  $\theta_{1'}$  of land  $1'$ , the whole lands  $L_{1'2'}$ , and by operating the industrial method  $2'$  at level  $\alpha_{2'} > 0$ :

{206}------------------------------------------------

$$d = \theta_{1'} c_{1'} + \sum_{t \in L_{1'2'}} c_t + \alpha_{2'} c_{2'} \tag{14.A.2}$$

By (P5) and (P6), we have  $1 \in L_{1'2'}$  and  $L_{12} \subset L_{1'2'}$ . Subtracting equality (14.A.2) from (14.A.1) leads to

$$\alpha_2 c_2 - \alpha_{2'} c_{2'} = \theta_1 c_1 + (1 - \theta_{1'}) c_{1'} + \sum_{t \in L_{1'2'} - L_{12} - \{1\}} c_t$$

Properties (P7) show that the determinants obtained by combining any vector on the right-hand side of this equality with vector  $c_2$ , is positive, therefore:

$$\text{P8: } \det(c_2, c_{2'}) > 0.$$

This last relation, which is equivalent to inequality (14.4), shows that the rate of transform of corn into iron is greater for method 2, therefore the two Ricardian solutions are linked by a regression: at the (1, 2) equilibrium, land 1 is partly cultivated, lands  $L_{12}$  are fully cultivated and the iron method 2 is used to transform corn into iron; at the (1', 2') equilibrium, lands 1, all lands  $L_{12}$  and possibly some others are fully cultivated, and corn is transformed into iron by means of the less efficient method 2'.

There remains to show that the combination (2, 2') can satisfy demand. Consider the algebraic vector decomposition on vectors  $c_2$  and  $c_{2'}$ :

$$d - \sum_{t \in L_{22'}} c_t = \beta_2 c_2 + \beta_{2'} c_{2'} \tag{14.A.3}$$

Method 1 belongs to  $L_{22'} - L_{12}$  by (P5). Subtracting equality (14.A.3) from (14.A.1) gives

$$(1 - \theta_1) c_1 + \sum_{t \in L_{22'} - L_{12} - \{1\}} c_t + (\beta_2 - \alpha_2) c_2 = -\beta_{2'} c_{2'}$$

The determinant made of the left-hand side vector and vector  $c_2$  is positive according to property (P7), and it has the sign of  $\beta_{2'}$  according to property (P8), therefore  $\beta_{2'}$  is positive. Similarly, by subtracting equality (14.A.3) from (14.A.2),  $\beta_2$  is positive. Equality (14.A.3) describes how the basket  $d$  is produced by means of the methods operated at prices  $p_{22'}$ . The overall conclusion is:

P9: In the presence of two Ricardian long-term equilibria, the joint use of both iron methods sustains a third equilibrium of the regressive external type.

The result can be generalized to more than two methods in the iron industry.

### 15 Why are there negative input– output coefficients?

## The ‘commodity technology assumption’ revisited

*Christian Lager*

I came to know Heinz D. Kurz in spring 1988 when he became full professor in Graz, where I was working on my PhD. Because of the formal similarity to my own field of research, which was at that time input–output analysis, but also because of his sound arguments, Heinz needed little effort to convince me that the classical approach to economics provides a rigorous theoretical frame for input–output analysis. I dedicate this piece which may help to close the gap between applied input–output analysis and Sraffian economic literature to the *Festschrift* in honour of my literate teacher and close friend Heinz.

Joint production was and is – in actual fact – an important issue (Kurz, 1986; Steedman, 1984 or Kurz and Salvadori, 1995, chapters 8 and 9). Most statistical offices frequently publish input–output statistics which are based on make and use tables. There exist also some theoretical models of growth and distribution, in particular models built on the works of John von Neumann and Piero Sraffa, which are based on input and output tables and therefore are able to account for joint production. Nevertheless, joint production is widely neglected. One will hardly find a textbook that does not treat joint production as an unimportant complication rather than an interesting issue. The basic concepts of IO-analysis are also limited to single production. Input output coefficients are defined as inputs of commodity *i* per unit of output of a single product *j*. In the case of joint production inputs refer to bundles of outputs and can by no means be allocated to a single product. But this is exactly the aim of so-called technology assumptions and other methods.

There are two basic technology assumptions – the commodity technology model (CTM) and the industry technology model – several mixed or hybrid assumptions, and other methods. Kop Jansen and ten Raa (1990) and ten Raa and Rueda-Cantuche (2003) postulate some desirable and reasonable properties and test how well some methods to construct commodity by commodity coefficients perform. It appears that only the CTM exhibits all the desired properties.

In this chapter it is argued (on pure theoretical grounds), that ‘technology assumptions’ define joint production away and are, therefore, not suitable for that case. If there are some activities which produce jointly more than one homogeneous product it is – in general – not possible to derive IO-coefficients which refer to an output of one unit of a homogeneous product. The validity of the concepts of

{209}------------------------------------------------

IO-coefficients and of a Leontief-Inverse is limited to single production systems and cannot easily be carried over to general joint production.

The characteristics of joint production are studied and the very reason of negative intensities and negative quantities is detected. It is demonstrated that a joint production system may not always adjust completely to given final demand and, therefore, excess production is possible. Following the track of von Neumann and applying the rule of free goods (free disposal) the solutions for quantities and for prices can be determined by a linear programme.

Finally, a class of joint production systems is defined which exhibits all the important characteristics of single production systems. Useful concepts developed by Neo-Ricardian scholars such as ‘adjustability’ or ‘all-productiveness’ are presented.

Let  $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B} \in R_+^{n\times n}$  be semi-positive square matrices of inputs and outputs of dimension commodity by activity. Assume ***constant returns to scale***, i.e. if  $(\mathbf{a}^k, \mathbf{b}^k)$  is a feasible process characterized by the  $k$ -th column of the input and of the output matrix, then, for all intensities  $x_k > 0$ ,  $(\mathbf{a}^k x_k, \mathbf{b}^k x_k)$  is also a feasible process. In other words, a proportional change in the inputs of an activity results into a proportional change in the outputs of that activity without changing the proportions of the outputs. Note, that constant returns to scale imply constant *product mix* coefficients. However, this assumption does not postulate commodity technology!

The CTM assumes a single production process for each commodity  $j$ , characterized by a vector  $\mathbf{c}^j$  whose elements are the quantities of inputs of commodity  $i$  required to produce one unit of product  $j$ . The inputs used by an activity  $k$  depend on the output structure of that activity. Hence each element  $a_{ik}$  of the input matrix  $\mathbf{A}$ , which refer to inputs of an activity  $k$ , reflects a weighted average of the underlying commodity by commodity coefficients  $c_{ij}$  where the weights are determined by the outputs of process  $k$ .

Hence the CTM is defined by

$$\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij} b_{jk} = a_{ik} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \mathbf{CB} = \mathbf{A}. \tag{15.1}$$

If  $\mathbf{B}$  is regular the coefficients of the unobservable single production processes can be determined by

$$\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{AB}^{-1} \tag{15.2}$$

The CTM assumes that there is – in principle – a single production system which is not directly observable. Observable are ‘industries’ which produce some quantities of more than one commodity by combining more than one single production process. Joint production is thus considered as a statistical problem caused by aggregation. This assumption may have some justification if aggregate industries are concerned, which produce one characteristic primary product and, in addition, one or more secondary products which themselves are characteristic

{210}------------------------------------------------

products of other industries. In this case, it is straightforward to calculate non-negative matrices via a systematic search of possible sources of inaccuracy in the basic make and use tables. If, on the other hand, joint production proper is concerned, the CTA misses the point, is unacceptable and, after all, is not needed.

Given input and output matrices,  $\mathbf{A}$  and  $\mathbf{B}$ , and a vector of required net products (final demand), denoted by  $\mathbf{d}$ . The problem is to find a vector of intensities  $\mathbf{x}$  which supports the bundle  $\mathbf{d}$  such that

$$(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{d} \tag{15.3}$$

The straightforward solution of (15.3) is

$$\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{d}. \tag{15.4}$$

Furthermore, we may calculate the vector of gross products by

$$\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{Bx} = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{d}. \tag{15.5}$$

Note that the inverse matrices in (15.4) and (15.5) may be written as

$$(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} = \mathbf{B}^{-1}(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{AB}^{-1})^{-1} \tag{15.6}$$

and

$$\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{AB}^{-1})^{-1} \tag{15.7}$$

Note that the latter inverse may be considered as a generalization of the Leontief-inverse.

It is clear that the results for these solutions are the same as one would obtain by using the CTM. However, no ‘technology assumptions’ are required nor any matrix of commodity by commodity input coefficients have been calculated. Furthermore, meaningful solutions may be obtained even if the output matrix is singular or if  $\mathbf{AB}^{-1}$  contains negative elements.

Though we have avoided the problem of a singular output matrix and negative commodity by commodity input coefficients, there still remains the possibility of negative intensities and negative quantities. The following examples may be useful to detect the very reason for this problem of negative results.

Assume that there are two processes by which two commodities (wool and mutton) are jointly produced by means of wool, mutton and some primary factors.

Let  $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 4 \\ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$  and  $\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$  be input and output matrices of dimension product by process. Neglecting the primary factors and considering a stationary economy,

{211}------------------------------------------------

we may characterize the two processes also by the ‘netput’ matrix  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A}) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ , where the first row refers to process 1 and the second row refers to process 2.

The set of producible net outputs is given by the set  $\forall \mathbf{x} \geq 0; (\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A}) \mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} x_1 + \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} x_2$  and is depicted in Figure 15.1

Two rays originate from the origin: 'Activity 1: (2, -2)x1' pointing into the second quadrant and 'Activity 2: (-1, 4)x2' pointing into the fourth quadrant. A shaded region, labeled 'Set of producible net outputs', covers the entire first quadrant and extends into the second and fourth quadrants, bounded by the two rays.](14bdf4b663f2e0005843cd1f692c761a_img.jpg)

Figure 15.1: A graph showing the set of producible net outputs in the Wool-Mutton plane. The vertical axis is labeled 'Wool' and the horizontal axis is labeled 'Mutton'. Two rays originate from the origin: 'Activity 1: (2, -2)x1' pointing into the second quadrant and 'Activity 2: (-1, 4)x2' pointing into the fourth quadrant. A shaded region, labeled 'Set of producible net outputs', covers the entire first quadrant and extends into the second and fourth quadrants, bounded by the two rays.

Figure 15.1

Note that any non negative net product bundle of wool and mutton can be produced because the feasible set of net bundles contains the whole positive orthant.<sup>2</sup>

This observation is crucial for the non negativity of the solutions:

- i For all non negative bundles of net products  $\mathbf{d}$  there exist a non negative vector of intensities  $\mathbf{x}$  such that  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{d}$ .
- ii The inverse  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 2/3 & 1/6 \\ 1/3 & 1/3 \end{pmatrix} > 0$ .
- iii The generalized Leontief-inverse  $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{AB}^{-1})^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 19/3 & 7/3 \\ 10/3 & 7/3 \end{pmatrix} > 0$ .
- iv Therefore, the bundle of gross outputs  $\mathbf{q} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{AB}^{-1})^{-1} \mathbf{d}$  is non negative for all  $\mathbf{d} \geq 0$ .

These nice features disappear, if we change the input matrix slightly such that instead of four units of wool just two units of wool are required for the second

{212}------------------------------------------------

process. While the output matrix remains unchanged, the input matrix is now given by  $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ . The new ‘netput’ matrix is  $\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$  and the cone of producible net outputs is depicted in Figure 15.2.

In contrast to example 1, that set does not contain the whole positive orthant. Hence some proportions of net outputs are not producible. If more than four times the quantities of mutton than quantities of wool are demanded, then there exist no positive intensities by which the two processes can produce the required bundle.

The inverses  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{1}{5} & \frac{1}{5} \end{pmatrix}$  exist but contain negative elements.

Hence solutions for any demanded bundle of net products can be calculated, but negative intensities for the first activity will result if the bundle of net products demanded is not an element of the producible set.

Figure 15.2

Assume, for instance, that 10 units of wool and 50 quantities of mutton are demanded. These proportions are not supported by the system. Even if only process 2, which specializes in the production of mutton, will be activated there is too much wool or not enough mutton. A solution for (15.4) can be obtained but will result in a *negative intensity* for process 1 such that some wool will be ‘absorbed’ and additional mutton will be ‘produced’ by that process. Hence the linear combination  $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} x_1 + \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} x_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix}$  has the solution  $x_1 = -1$  and  $x_2 = 12$ . Negative intensities are not acceptable. Hence the method proposed by (15.4) will work for the case that the demanded bundle is producible but cannot be applied in general.

{213}------------------------------------------------

Another route is suggested by von Neumann: allow for excess production, i.e. substitute equation (15.3) by the inequality  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})\mathbf{x} \geq \mathbf{d}$ , and, if necessary, invoke the rule of free goods (free disposal).

In example 2 this approach will result in  $x_1 = 0$  and  $x_2 = 12, 5$ . The demand for mutton is exactly met but wool is produced in excess and has to be disposed of by a (free) disposal process. For a more careful and general discussion of the von Neumann systems with free or costly disposal see Lager (2001).

In order to obtain some more rigorous and more general findings we may utilize the following definitions and concepts developed by scholars working in the Sraffian tradition.

#### ***Definition 1***

A system of production is **strictly viable** if it is possible to produce a positive net output.

$$\exists \mathbf{x} \geq 0, \quad (\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})\mathbf{x} > 0$$

Note that in this case it is possible to produce **any** net output or more than that. Hence it is possible to match any vector of finished products if there is free disposal.

#### ***Definition 2***

A product  $i$  is said to be **separately producible** if it is possible to produce a net output consisting of one unit of that product but nothing else, i.e.

$$\exists \mathbf{x}^i \geq 0, \quad (\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})\mathbf{x}^i = \mathbf{e}_i,$$

where  $\mathbf{e}_i$  is a vector whose  $i$ -th element is equal to 1 and all other elements are equal to zero.

#### ***Definition 3***

A system of production is **all-productive** if all products are separately producible.<sup>3</sup>

All-productive systems have the following nice properties:

- All-productive systems can produce **any** semi-positive net output, i.e.  $\forall \mathbf{d} \geq 0, \quad \exists \mathbf{x} \geq 0, \quad (\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{d}$ .
- If and only if the system is all-productive, then the inverse  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}$  is semi-positive. Note that that the vector  $\mathbf{x}^i$  in definition 2 is the  $i$ -th column of the inverse  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}$ . Therefore, an all-productive system has a semi-positive net-output inverse by definition and if  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} \geq 0$ , then all products are separately producible.

{214}------------------------------------------------

- If – but not only if – the system is all-productive, the generalized Leontief inverse is non-negative, i.e.  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} \geq 0 \Rightarrow \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{AB}^{-1})^{-1} \geq 0$ . The proof for the ‘if statement’ follows from the fact that the product of two semi-positive matrices is non-negative. The evidence for the ‘not only if’ statement is provided by the example in the appendix.
- All-productive systems have always (semi-)positive solutions for intensities.  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{x} \geq 0$ .
- All-productive systems have always (semi-)positive solutions for gross outputs.  $\mathbf{Bx} = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{q} \geq 0$ .
- All-productive systems have always (semi-)positive solutions for total capital requirements.  $\mathbf{Ax} = \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{k} \geq 0$ .
- All-productive systems have always (semi-)positive solutions for labour values.<sup>4</sup>  $\mathbf{l}'(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} = \mathbf{v} \geq 0$ .

We may also explore the relation between semi-positive commodity by commodity input coefficients and all-productive systems:

- If – but not only if – the commodity by commodity coefficients are semi-positive it follows that the generalized Leontief inverse is semi-positive, i.e.  $\mathbf{AB}^{-1} \geq 0 \Rightarrow \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{AB}^{-1})^{-1}$ . The proof for the ‘if’ statement follows from the fact that the generalized Leontief inverse is equal to the sum of a Neumann series of convergent semi-positive matrices, i.e.  $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{AB}^{-1})^{-1} = \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} (\mathbf{AB}^{-1})^t$ . The evidence for the ‘not only if’ statement is provided by the example in the appendix.
- It follows that semi-positive commodity by commodity coefficients guarantee semi-positive gross outputs, i.e.  $\mathbf{AB}^{-1} \geq 0 \Rightarrow \forall \mathbf{d} \geq 0; \quad \exists \mathbf{q} \geq 0 : \mathbf{q} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{AB}^{-1})^{-1} \mathbf{d}$ .
- But semi-positive commodity by commodity coefficients **do not** guarantee semi-positive intensity vectors.

### Summary and conclusion

In this chapter it is argued on pure theoretical grounds that a ‘technology assumption’ or any other method to estimate commodity by commodity (or industry by industry) input–output matrices neglects the very nature of joint production. In particular, the commodity technology model defines joint production away by assuming that there are only single production processes and observed joint production is a result of aggregation of single production processes to industries. A straightforward joint production model is proposed which avoids calculating commodity by commodity input–output matrices. The very reason for the still remaining problem of negative solutions is detected. The common feature of systems which may have negative solutions is that those systems do not support any bundle of net products. Finally a class of joint production systems is identified which rules negative solutions out and exhibits some other nice features of single production systems.

{215}------------------------------------------------

### **Appendix**

Let  $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$  and  $\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ .

The netput matrix  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A}) = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$  shows clearly, that not all net bundles in the positive orthant are producible, i.e. the system is not all productive.

Consequently,  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0,12 & -0,04 \\ 0,08 & 0,31 \end{pmatrix} \not\ge 0$ .

Nevertheless the generalized Leontief-inverse,  $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{AB}^{-1})^{-1} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1,27 & 0,58 \\ 0,65 & 1,12 \end{pmatrix} \ge 0$ , is positive.

Hence it is possible that there is a solution with negative intensities but gross outputs will be positive.

Though there is a positive generalized Leontief-inverse, the commodity by commodity input matrix calculated by the CTA contains negative coefficients:

$$\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{AB}^{-1} \approx \begin{pmatrix} -0,07 & 0,56 \\ 0,63 & -0,22 \end{pmatrix}.$$

### **Notes**

- 1 This route has been proposed by Steenge, 1990.
- 2 Note that also some negative amounts of wool or mutton are ‘producible’. That means that the system is also capable to dispose off some existing quantities of wool or mutton.
- 3 The concept of an all-productive system has been introduced by Schefold (1971, 1989). A similar concept, ‘the adjustment property’, has been presented by Bidard and Erreygers (1998).
- 4 Note that (semi-)positive prices of production require that the system is ‘*r*-all-productive’ and therefore  $(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A}(1 + r))^{-1} \ge 0$ .
