{217}------------------------------------------------

## 16 Convergence of a short-run equilibrium to a long-run equilibrium in an emission permit scheme

*Eiji B. Hosoda\**

### Introduction

Ronald Coase's great insight on environmental policies is that once property rights are established for environment, environmental problems can be controlled in a decentralized fashion. This idea has led to the trade of emission permits for pollutants or environmentally unfriendly substances that has become very common nowadays. In emission permit trading, unlike Coase's assumption of endogenous formation of a market, a market is designed by a government. As a result, the creation of a new market does not automatically lead to an efficient allocation, in particular because a government often fails to take into account the structural change of an economy that may occur in response to the creation of an emission permit market. If such a structural change is to occur, there is a large chance that the equilibrium targeted by a policy of tradable emission permits can never be achieved.

This chapter demonstrates that even if an equilibrium that satisfies a given emission target at every point of time is dynamically unstable, there is a practical and operational formula by which the government can determine an emission permit supply at each moment of time so as to achieve the target in the long run while guaranteeing the long-run stability of an equilibrium path. This study also obtains conditions under which an equilibrium path that satisfies a given emission target at every point of time is stable. In the case in which such a condition is not met, the emission permit supply formula is indispensable.

For the purpose of the above study, utilization of a multisectoral disaggregated model is essential. This is because an impact made by the creation of a tradeable emission permit market and activation of an abatement sector implies a structural change of industries, and only by means of a multisectoral disaggregated model can we analyse the influence of the introduction of tradable emission permits on stability conditions. It should be remembered that an analysis of effects of policy introduction or behavioural change on industrial structure has been conventionally considered as an important issue, as seen in Aoki (1977) and more recently Yano (1998). Another feature of our paper is that we adopt a linear descriptive model rather than a non-linear optimal model. In addition to convenience as a first approximation, the former model makes it possible to deduce an explicit solution path. Due to the very nature of the model, we can demonstrate a practical and operational formula of emission

{218}------------------------------------------------

permit supply by which the government can meet the target amount of emission while leading an economy to a steady-state equilibrium.

Certainly, there have been seminal analytical works on dynamic aspects of tradable emission permits. For instance, Rubin (1996) has analysed the workings of tradable emission permits, taking banking and borrowing into account, and shown that a dynamic equilibrium path attains the least-cost solution. Nagurney and Zhang (2001) have explored the working of an ambient permit scheme in a dynamic transportation model and deduced stability. Although their stance is similar to ours, there is a big difference between their model and ours; the former is based upon a tatonnement process but the latter is not. Grimaud (1999) has discussed the Aghion-Howitt type of endogenous growth model in a disaggregated version and successfully solved the implementation problems when there are some different types of distortions which are remedied by the introduction of emission permits. The disaggregation dealt with in the paper is, however, different from ours; the former implies existence of a number of intermediate goods, and the latter means that there are independent sectors of consumption goods and capital goods as well as an abatement sector.

It is worth mentioning that this paper may be situated in the new research line of market quality developed by Yano (2008). Since structural stability is an important element of market quality, and since it is demonstrated in this paper that a proper supply rule of emission permits as institutional infrastructure is indispensable to maintain stability, the present chapter may be considered as natural application of the theory of market quality to environmental policies.

Our procedure to show the main results is as follows. In the next section, we present the basic assumptions and fundamental model, and describe a short-run equilibrium and a steady-state equilibrium. In the third section, we will deduce stability conditions in a simple case where the target amount of emission permits is given and fixed at any moment of time. Although this supply formula of permits is not flexible, the stability conditions obtained are considered as a good reference point for the following section. In section 4, we will demonstrate a supply formula of emission permits by which the government can lead an economy to a steady state where the target amount of emission is met. It will also be mentioned that the fundamental conclusions are applicable to the case in which emission permits are valid eternally.

### **The model**

#### ***Basic assumptions***

Our model is described as follows: we assume that there are three representative actors in an economy, i.e., workers, capitalists and the government. Since we assume that workers do not save but only consume, we identify them as consumers.<sup>1</sup> In the same way, assuming that capitalists do not consume but only save to invest, we use firms and capitalists interchangeably.

The detailed assumptions on the three actors are as follows. Workers are employed and paid by capitalists. They also receive the sales proceeds of emission permits from the government, since the government is assumed to be an abstract

{219}------------------------------------------------

entity to control the amount of emission permits and does not spend. Their income, therefore, consists of the wages and the sales proceeds of emission permits, and they spend all their income on consumption.

Capitalists employ capital and workers, and organize production. They must also have a certain amount of emission permits, since production causes emission of pollutants, waste or whatever, which is regulated by the government. They earn profits, paying wages to workers and emission charges to the government. They save all their income for investment or capital accumulation.

The government's role in this paper is very abstract as we have mentioned. The government issues emission permits every year, sells them to capitalists, and pays the proceeds of the sales to workers. Thus, the fundamental role of the government is just to control the amount of emission permits. Actually, how and to whom the sales proceeds are paid back does not matter in the following discussion.

We assume, for a while, that emission permits are valid for a year, and must be renewed every year. The case where, once issued, emission permits remain valid for ever will be briefly discussed. The alternative assumption on duration of emission permits does not affect the essence of our argument.

As for the production side, we assume the following three-sector model. The first sector produces a capital good, and the second sector a consumption good. Both sectors input a capital good and labour, emitting pollutants or waste. The third sector is a process which abates emission of pollutants or waste. This process inputs a capital good and labour but does not emit pollutants or waste. We assume that the charge for the abatement service is the same as the price of a unit of emission permits in equilibrium, since the difference is supposed to be adjusted immediately. All the processes are subject to constant coefficient technology.

#### ***Notation and equations***

We adopt the following notation:

- $p_i(t)$  The price of the  $i$ -th commodity (a variable) at time  $t$ .
- $x_j(t)$  The activity level of the  $j$ -th process (a variable) at time  $t$ .
- $r(t)$  The rate of profit (a variable) at time  $t$ .
- $w(t)$  The wage rate (a variable) at time  $t$ .
- $p_k(t)$  The rental of capital at time  $t$ .
- $q(t)$  The price of a unit of emission permits (a variable) at time  $t$ .
- $n$  The growth rate of labour supply (a given parameter).
- $a_i$  The input of the capital good per output in the  $i$ -th process (a constant).
- $l_i$  The labour input per output in the  $i$ -th process (a constant).
- $\theta_i$  The capital-labour ratio of the  $i$ -th process, namely  $a_i/l_i$ .
- $b_i$  The emission rate per output in the  $i$ -th process (a constant).
- $K(t)$  Capital stock at time  $t$ .
- $B(t)$  The total amount of emission permits at time  $t$ .
- $L(t)$  Labour supply at time  $t$ .
- $b(t)$  Per capita amount of emission permits at time  $t$ , namely  $B(t)/L(t)$ .

{220}------------------------------------------------

If there is no room for misunderstanding, we sometimes abbreviate the time element  $t$  from mathematical expressions. Since we assume that the labour supply increases at the constant rate  $n$ , the labour supply at the  $t$ -th period is expressed as  $L(t) = L_0 e^{nt}$ , where  $L_0$  is the initial amount of the labour supply.

Now, the price system and the quantity system can be described as follows:

##### *Price system*

In a short-run equilibrium, each price equals unit cost of production, including purchase of emission permits. Thus,  $p_i = p_k a_i + w l_i + b_i$  must hold for  $i = 1, 2$ . Furthermore, the price of emission permits  $q$  equals the abatement cost by arbitrage, and so,  $q = p_k a_3 + w l_3$  holds. Considering that the rate of profit equals the capital rental divided by the price of capital good, we have  $r = p_k / p_1$  or  $p_k = r p_1$ . Then, the following must hold:

$$\begin{cases} p_1 = r p_1 a_1 + w l_1 + q b_1 \\ p_2 = r p_1 a_2 + w l_2 + q b_2 \\ q = r p_1 a_3 + w l_3 \end{cases} \quad (16.1)$$

where  $(p_1, p_2, w, p_k, q) \geq 0$ .

We adopt the consumption good as numerator, and set  $p_2 = 1$  in the following. The equations of (16.1) are the price-cost equations for the capital-good sector, the consumption-good sector and the abatement sector respectively. As we have mentioned, we assume that the price of emission permits equals the unit cost of abatement of the third sector by arbitrage. In other words, the difference between the emission right price and the abatement cost disappears immediately.

It must be noted that all the price variables are determined irrespective of demand once one of the variables, for instance the rate of profit  $r$ , is determined. Therefore, the short-run price formation is the same as the long-run one in the sense that prices are determined once the rate of profit,  $r$ , is determined by  $r = \text{the growth rate of capital stock}$ . This equality is obtained from the assumption on the behaviour of savings and consumption.

##### *Quantity system*

$$\begin{cases} x_1 = rK \\ x_2 = wL + Bq \\ K = a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 + a_3 x_3 \\ L = l_1 x_1 + l_2 x_2 + l_3 x_3 \\ B = b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 - x_3 \end{cases} \quad (16.2)$$

where  $(x_1, x_2, x_3) \geq 0$ .

The first and second equations of (16.2) mean the supply–demand equality for the capital good and the consumption good. Clearly, the third and fourth equations of (16.2) mean that both the capital stock and the labour are fully utilized. The

{221}------------------------------------------------

fifth equation of (16.2) implies that the emission constraint is binding.<sup>2</sup> In other words, supply of emission permits equals demand.

One remark is necessary here. In the supply–demand balance expressed above, i.e., (16.2), we assume that all supply–demand relationships are expressed as equalities instead of inequalities. This means that there is no excess supply for any good or emission permits. The no excess supply condition is particularly important for emission permits, since it affects the target amount of emission permits, as shown later.

Since  $x_1$  is nothing but capital accumulation, the first equation of (16.2) implies  $x_1/K = \dot{K}/K = r$ ; the growth rate of capital stock equals the rate of profit. Yet, it may not equal the growth rate of labour force, i.e.,  $\dot{K}/K = r \neq n = \dot{L}/L$ , in a short-run equilibrium.

#### ***Transformation of equations and a short-run equilibrium***

When the emission constraint is binding *and* the abatement sector is activated, we can transform equation (16.1), and the third and fifth equations of (16.2) to a convenient reduced form, namely, the following:

$$\begin{cases} p &= rpa_1^\dagger + wl_1^\dagger \\ 1 &= rpa_2^\dagger + wl_2^\dagger \end{cases} \tag{16.3}$$

$$\begin{cases} K + a_3B &= a_1^\dagger x_1 + a_2^\dagger x_2 \\ L + l_3B &= l_1^\dagger x_1 + l_2^\dagger x_2, \end{cases} \tag{16.4}$$

where  $p_1 = p$ ,  $p_2 = 1$ ,  $a_i^\dagger \equiv a_i + b_i a_3$  and  $l_i^\dagger \equiv l_i + b_i l_3$ . We call (16.3) and (16.4) the *augmented system*. This system may be interpreted as one where the abatement process is integrated in the capital-good sector and the consumption-good sector. That is, the abatement cost is taken into account in those sectors from the beginning.

Equations (16.3) and (16.4) can be expressed in matrix form as follows:

$$(p \; 1) = (rp, w) A^\dagger \tag{16.5}$$

$$\begin{pmatrix} K(t) & + & a_3B(t) \\ L(t) & + & l_3B(t) \end{pmatrix} = A^\dagger x(t), \tag{16.6}$$

where  $A^\dagger \equiv \begin{pmatrix} a_1^\dagger & a_2^\dagger \\ l_1^\dagger & l_2^\dagger \end{pmatrix}$  and  $x(t) \equiv \begin{pmatrix} x_1(t) \\ x_2(t) \end{pmatrix}$ .

Since the variables  $K$ ,  $B$  and  $L$  are given at any given moment, the vector  $x$  is determined by (16.6). Once  $x_1$  is determined, the rate of profit  $r$  is also determined from the formulation  $r = x_1/K$ , and so the price variables are determined either by (16.5).

{222}------------------------------------------------

Dividing the both sides of (16.6) by  $L(t) = L_0 e^{nt}$ , we have

$$\begin{pmatrix} k(t) & + & a_3 b(t) \\ 1 & + & l_3 b(t) \end{pmatrix} = A^\dagger y(t), \tag{16.7}$$

where  $y(t) \equiv x(t)/L(t)$ ,  $k(t) \equiv K(t)/L(t)$  and  $b(t) \equiv B(t)/L(t)$ . We will show in the next section the conditions on which there exists a short-run equilibrium such that  $y(t)$  (or  $x(t)$ ) is a positive vector, and it converges to a long-run equilibrium.

#### ***A steady state***

Before we proceed with the analysis of the dynamics, we look briefly at the steady state equilibrium. In a steady state, all the variables grow at the same rate, and so,  $n = \dot{L}/L = \dot{K}/K = r$  holds. Dividing all the variables by  $L(t) = L_0 e^{nt}$ , we obtain

$$\begin{cases} n & = & r \\ y_2 & = & w \quad + \quad bq \\ y_1 & = & n(a_1 y_1 + a_2 y_2 + a_3 y_3) \tag{16.8} \\ 1 & = & l_1 y_1 + l_2 y_2 + l_3 y_3 \\ b & = & b_1 y_1 + b_2 y_2 - y_3 \end{cases}$$

where  $(y_1, y_2, y_3) \geq 0$ , and  $y_i$  in (16.8) is expressed in terms of per capita value, i.e.,  $y_i(t) \equiv x_i(t)/L(t)$ . Hosoda (1994, 1996) has proved that the solution to (16.1) and (16.8) is unique and meaningful when the emission constraint is binding and the abatement sector is activated. Actually, there are two types of equilibrium solution as follows.<sup>3</sup>

##### *Type A*

A case where the emission constraint is binding, but the abatement process is not activated.

$$\begin{cases} y_1^* & = & \frac{na_2}{\Delta(n)} \\[6pt] y_2^* & = & \frac{1-na_1}{\Delta(n)} \\[6pt] y_3^* & = & 0 \\[6pt] p^* & = & \frac{l_1 + q(b_1 l_2 - b_2 l_1)}{\Delta(r^*)} \\[6pt] w^* & = & \frac{1-ra_1}{\Delta(r^*)} - q\frac{r(a_2 b_1 - a_1 b_2) + b_2}{\Delta(r^*)} \\[6pt] r^* & = & n = \frac{b l_2 - b_2}{a_2 b_1 - a_1 b_2 - b(l_1 a_2 - l_2 a_1)}, \end{cases}$$

where the function  $\Delta(z)$  is defined as  $\Delta(z) \equiv z(l_1 a_2 - l_2 a_1) + l_2$ .

{223}------------------------------------------------

##### *Type B*

A case where the emission constraint is binding and the abatement process is activated:

$$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} y_1^* = \frac{n\{a_2^\dagger(bl_3+1)-ba_3l_2^\dagger\}}{\Delta^\dagger(n)} \\ y_2^* = \frac{n\{-a_1^\dagger(bl_3+1)+ba_3l_1^\dagger\}+\{bl_3+1\}}{\Delta^\dagger(n)} \\ y_3^* = \frac{na_2(b_1-l_1b)+(1-na_1)(b_2-l_2b)}{\Delta^\dagger(n)} \\ p^* = \frac{l_1^\dagger}{\Delta^\dagger(r^*)} \\ w^* = \frac{1-r^*a_1^\dagger}{\Delta^\dagger(r^*)} \\ r^* = n \\ q^* = \frac{r^*(l_1a_3-l_3a_1)+l_3}{\Delta^\dagger(r^*)} \end{array} \right. \quad (16.9)$$

Here,  $\Delta^\dagger(n)$  is defined as  $\Delta^\dagger(n) = n(l_1^\dagger a_2^\dagger - l_2^\dagger a_1^\dagger) + l_2^\dagger$ .

Although there are two types of solution as mentioned above, let us consider the latter type mainly, that is, a solution of *Type B*. This is because a solution of *Type A* is obtained in a rare case where  $b$  (the amount of per capita emission permits) takes a special value. Furthermore, in a scheme of tradeable emission permits, the total amount of emission permits is often supposed to be restricted to a target value. This implies that  $b$  decreases continuously, and the abatement sector comes to activation anyway. Hence, we do not have to be bothered by a solution of *Type A*.

Our main concern is the case where the target of emission permits scheme is the control of the total amount of emission permits. A steady state of this economy is the state where per capita emission permits is zero, since  $\dot{b}/b = \dot{B}/B - \dot{L}/L = -n$  holds in a long-run.<sup>4</sup> Yet we will also refer to the case where the government tries to control *per capita* emission permits for a technical reason.<sup>5</sup> The problem is, then, whether, starting from an arbitrary short-run equilibrium, all the variables converge to those in the long-run equilibrium or not. Alternatively, we would like to know what conditions guarantee the convergence. We consider this problem in the next section.

#### **An assumption and classification**

Before proceeding with a stability analysis, let us add one assumption. We are interested in how introduction of trade of emission permits into an economy affects stability of equilibrium. In other words, the main issue of the present

{224}------------------------------------------------

chapter is to show whether a short-run equilibrium converges to a long-run equilibrium *when trade of emission permits is introduced, into an economy*. In other words, we would like to know whether the government has controllability to meet a target of a specific amount of emission permits.

Hence, our implicit assumption is that the original economy without any environmental restriction is stable, so that a short-run equilibrium converges to a long-run equilibrium. Otherwise, we have to consider a stabilization policy *irrespective of* an environmental restriction. Furthermore, it is natural to assume that there is a short-run equilibrium at any time period in the original economy.

According to Appendix A, a condition of existence of a short-run equilibrium and stability is explicitly expressed as follows:

$$\frac{a_1}{l_1} < k_0 < \frac{a_2}{l_2}.$$

That is, the capital–labour ratio of the capital–good sector is smaller than that of the consumption–good sector, and the initial capital stock *per person* is between the two ratios.

We have introduced trade of emission permits scheme into the original model, and this implies that an abatement sector (a costly disposal sector) must be taken into account when capital–labour ratios and capital stock per person are compared. Based on the assumption on capital–labour ratios, we can classify a technical situation concerning capital–labour ratios and the initial *per capita* capital stock into the following four cases:

$$\begin{array}{l} \text{Case (i)} \quad \frac{a_1}{l_1} < k_0 < \frac{a_2}{l_2} < \frac{a_3}{l_3} \\ \text{Case (ii)} \quad \frac{a_1}{l_1} < k_0 < \frac{a_3}{l_3} < \frac{a_2}{l_2} \\ \text{Case (iii)} \quad \frac{a_1}{l_1} < \frac{a_3}{l_3} < k_0 < \frac{a_2}{l_2} \\ \text{Case (iv)} \quad \frac{a_3}{l_3} < \frac{a_1}{l_1} < k_0 < \frac{a_2}{l_2}. \end{array}$$

We define a capital–labour ratio of the  $i$ -th sector as  $\theta_i$ , or equivalently  $\theta_i = a_i/l_i$ .

#### A stability condition: a simple case

##### Dynamics and deduction of stability conditions

In this section, we consider the circumstance in which the government controls the amount of newly issued emission permits,  $B$  or equivalently  $dB/dt = \dot{B}$ , following a very simple rule. We assume that the government issues emission permits at a constant growth rate for a while, allowing the case where the growth rate is zero or, in other words, the total amount of emission permits is constant. It must be

{225}------------------------------------------------

noted that zero growth rate of per capita emission permits can be treated as a special case of a constant growth rate.

For the system to be compatible with the steady state, the growth rate of emission permits must be equal to that of labour supply. Therefore,  $n = \dot{L}/L = \dot{B}/B$  must hold. This means  $L = L_0 e^{nt}$  and  $B = B_0 e^{nt}$ , where  $L_0$  and  $B_0$  are the initial amount of the labour supply and the total emission permits respectively. If the total emission permits is constant, clearly we have  $B = B_0$  which implies  $\dot{b}/b = -n$ . Thus, in the long-run,  $b \rightarrow 0$  holds. Consequently, we may put  $b = 0$  in the steady state solution.

Differentiating (16.6) with respect to  $t$ , we have

$$A^\dagger \dot{x} = \begin{pmatrix} \dot{K} \\ \dot{L} \end{pmatrix} + \dot{B} \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad (16.10)$$

where  $\dot{B} = 0$  in a constant-emission-permits scheme.

Taking  $x_1 = K$  into account, we can transform the above into

$$A^\dagger \dot{x} = \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ ne^{nt} L_0 \end{pmatrix} + \sigma ne^{nt} B_0 \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad (16.11)$$

where  $\sigma = 1$  implies a growing-emission-permits scheme (that is, a scheme where  $b = \text{constant}$ ), and  $\sigma = 0$  a constant-emission-permits scheme (that is, a scheme where  $B = \text{constant}$ ).

As before, let us define  $y_i(t) \equiv x_i(t)/e^{nt} L_0$  ( $i = 1, 2, 3$ ). Since  $\dot{x}_i(t) = e^{nt} \dot{y}_i L_0 + ne^{nt} \dot{y}_i L_0$ , we obtain

$$e^{nt} L_0 A^\dagger \dot{y} + ne^{nt} L_0 A^\dagger y = \begin{pmatrix} e^{nt} L_0 y_1 \\ ne^{nt} L_0 \end{pmatrix} + \sigma ne^{nt} L_0 b_0 \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix},$$

$$\text{where } y \equiv \begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{pmatrix}.$$

The above equation implies

$$A^\dagger \dot{y} + n A^\dagger y = \begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ n \end{pmatrix} + \sigma n b_0 \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix}$$

or

$$A^\dagger \dot{y} + n A^\dagger y = I_1 y + Q^\dagger, \quad (16.12)$$

where  $I_1$  and  $Q^\dagger$  are defined as follows:

$$I_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \text{ and } Q^\dagger = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma n b_0 a_3 \\ n + \sigma n b_0 l_3 \end{pmatrix}.$$

{226}------------------------------------------------

Assuming  $\det A^\dagger \neq 0$ , we have

$$\dot{y} = -(nI - A^{\dagger-1}I_1)y + A^{\dagger-1}Q^\dagger. \quad (16.13)$$

A general solution to (16.13) is a general solution to the homogeneous part of (16.13) plus a particular solution (an equilibrium solution) to (16.13).<sup>6</sup> A particular solution to (16.13) is expressed as

$$y^* = -(A^\dagger \Theta^\dagger)^{-1} Q^\dagger,$$

where  $\Theta^\dagger \equiv -(nI - A^{\dagger-1}I_1)$ . This solution is the same as the one given in the form of (16.9).

A general solution to the homogeneous part of (16.13) is expressed as

$$y = \alpha_1 v_1 e^{\lambda_1 t} + \alpha_2 v_2 e^{\lambda_2 t}, \quad (16.14)$$

where  $\lambda_i$  ( $i = 1, 2$ ) is a root of the characteristic equation

$$\det \{\lambda I - (A^{\dagger-1}I_1 - nI)\} = 0, \quad (16.15)$$

and  $v_i$  is an eigen vector corresponding to  $\lambda_i$  ( $i = 1, 2$ ). The pair  $(\alpha_1, \alpha_2)$  is determined by an initial condition. Calculating (16.15), we know that

$$\lambda_1 = -n + \frac{l_2^\dagger}{\det A^\dagger} \text{ and } \lambda_2 = -n,$$

where  $\det A^\dagger \equiv a_1^\dagger l_2^\dagger - a_2^\dagger l_1^\dagger$ . The general solution to (16.13) is expressed as

$$y(t) = \alpha_1 v_1 e^{\lambda_1 t} + \alpha_2 v_2 e^{\lambda_2 t} - (A^\dagger \Theta^\dagger)^{-1},$$

where  $\lambda_1 = -n + \frac{1}{\det A^\dagger} l_2^\dagger$ ,  $\lambda_2 = -n$ ,  $v_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{l_2^\dagger}{l_1^\dagger} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$  and  $v_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ .

A necessary and sufficient condition for  $y_i$  ( $i = 1, 2$ ) to be convergent is that both  $\lambda_1$  and  $\lambda_2$  are negative. Therefore, a stability condition is

$$n > \frac{l_2^\dagger}{\det A^\dagger}. \quad (16.16)$$

If  $a_1^\dagger l_2^\dagger < a_2^\dagger l_1^\dagger$  holds, (16.16) is satisfied since  $\det A^\dagger$  is negative in this case. Suppose otherwise. Then, (16.16) does not hold, since  $l_2^\dagger / \det A^\dagger = 1 / \{a_2^\dagger - (a_1^\dagger l_1^\dagger / l_2^\dagger)\} > 1/a_1^\dagger$  which is larger than feasible  $n$ .<sup>7</sup> So, we can have a stability condition as

$$\frac{a_1^\dagger}{l_1^\dagger} < \frac{a_2^\dagger}{l_2^\dagger}. \quad (16.17)$$

Thus, we can obtain the following proposition.

{227}------------------------------------------------

##### *Proposition 1*

*If and only if the consumption-good sector is more capital intensive than the capital-good sector in the augmented system, the dynamical system is stable and a short-run equilibrium converges to a long-run equilibrium.*

From this proposition, we can deduce the following sufficient condition for long-run convergence:

##### *Corollary 1*

*If  $\theta_1 < \theta_3 < \theta_2$  holds, a short-run equilibrium converges to a long-run equilibrium.*

*Proof.* Inequality (16.17) is equivalent to

$$\frac{\theta_1 - \theta_3}{1 + b_1 \left( \frac{l_3}{l_1} \right)} < \frac{\theta_2 - \theta_3}{1 + b_2 \left( \frac{l_3}{l_2} \right)}.$$

The above inequality is clearly satisfied, since the numerator of the left-hand side of the above inequality is negative while the one of the right-hand side is positive. ■

Although Proposition 1 and Corollary 1 guarantee that a short-run equilibrium converges to a long-run equilibrium under certain conditions, they do not necessarily mean that there is a meaningful solution for all  $t$ : some variables might take negative values. Yet, suppose that the initial *per capita* capital stock is greater than the capital-labour ratio of the capital-good sector and smaller than that of the consumption-good sector in the augmented system. Furthermore, suppose that the emission constraint coefficient  $B(t)$  is sufficiently small for  $t$ . Then, we can show that a short-run equilibrium is meaningful in the sense that supply-demand equality guarantees non-negative activities in all the sectors, i.e.,  $x_i(t) \geq 0$  ( $i = 1, 2, 3$ ) for any  $t$ .

To be more precise, we must define a feasible set in which non-negative  $y(t)$  moves, satisfying an equilibrium conditions. First we define a set  $Y$  as

$$Y \equiv \left\{ (y_1, y_2) \in \mathbb{R}_{++}^2 \mid 1 \leq l_1^\dagger y_1 + l_2^\dagger y_2 \right\}.$$

Since all the equilibrium paths  $(y_1(t), (y_2(t))$  starting from *any* initial condition, satisfy

$$1 + l_3 b(t) = l_1^\dagger y_1(t) + l_2^\dagger y_2(t), \quad (16.18)$$

it moves in a set  $Y$ . Notice

$$b(t) = \begin{cases} b_0 & : \text{A growing-emission-permits scheme} \\ b_0 e^{-nt} & : \text{A constant-emission-permits scheme.} \end{cases} \quad (16.19)$$

{228}------------------------------------------------

Define  $b_0^*$  as

$$b_0^* \equiv \min b_1 y_1 + b_2 y_2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad (y_1, y_2) \in Y.$$

Then, clearly the following holds:

$$0 < b_0^* e^{-mt} \leq b_0^* \leq b_1 y_1(t) + b_2 y_2(t),$$

where  $(y_1(t), y_2(t))$  is a solution path which corresponds to parameters  $b_0^*$ ,  $L_0$ , and  $K_0$ . Thus,

$$y_3(t) = b_1 y_1(t) + b_2 y_2(t) - b(t) \geq 0,$$

if  $(y_1(t), y_2(t))$  is positive.

Actually, we can strengthen Proposition 1 as follows:

##### *Proposition 2*

Suppose  $\frac{a_1^\dagger}{l_1^\dagger} < \frac{k_0 + a_3 b_0}{1 + l_3 b_0} < \frac{a_2^\dagger}{l_2^\dagger}$  and  $b_0 \leq b_0^*$  hold. Then, a short-run equilibrium vector  $(y_1(t), y_2(t), y_3(t))$  is non-negative with  $(y_1(t), y_2(t)) > 0$  for any non-negative  $t$  and converges to a long-run equilibrium.

*Proof.* See Appendix B. ■

In the above proposition, the condition

$$\frac{a_1^\dagger}{l_1^\dagger} < \frac{k_0 + a_3 b_0}{1 + a_3 b_0} < \frac{a_2^\dagger}{l_2^\dagger} \quad (16.20)$$

particularly plays a crucial role as shown in the appendix.

#### ***Short-run equilibrium and stability conditions***

It is very clear that the stability condition here is very similar to that in the traditional two-sector growth model (See Shinkai 1960, and Uzawa 1961). The conventional stability condition seems applicable to the economic model where trade of emission permits is introduced. It must, however, be remembered that *seemingly* the same capital-intensity condition must hold for the augmented system in our model.

Let us examine the condition of existence of a short-run equilibrium and stability a little further in this subsection. In the following discussion, as we have already mentioned, we assume that the original system without an environmental restriction has a short-run equilibrium and it converges to a long-run equilibrium,

{229}------------------------------------------------

since the purpose of the present chapter is whether introduction of emission-permits trading may destabilize an market or not. From Appendix A.1, we know the stability condition is  $a_1/l_1 < a_2/l_2$ . Furthermore, for an economy to have a meaningful short-run equilibrium,  $a_1/l_1 < k_0 < a_2/l_2$  must be satisfied. Then, using notation  $\theta_i \equiv a_i/l_i (i = 1, 2, 3)$ , we can order a capital-labour ratio of the third sector as follows:

$$\text{Case (i)} \quad \theta_1 < k_0 < \theta_2 < \theta_3$$

$$\text{Case (ii)} \quad \theta_1 < k_0 < \theta_3 < \theta_2$$

$$\text{Case (iii)} \quad \theta_1 < \theta_3 < k_0 < \theta_2$$

$$\text{Case (iv)} \quad \theta_3 < \theta_1 < k_0 < \theta_2$$

As for the cases (ii) and (iii), we have the following result:

##### Proposition 3

*Suppose either  $\theta_1 < k_0 < \theta_3 < \theta_2$  or  $\theta_1 < \theta_3 < k_0 < \theta_2$  holds. Then, there is a short-run equilibrium for all  $t$  and it converges to a long-run equilibrium if the following inequality is satisfied:*

$$\max_{i=1,2} \frac{1}{\theta_i - \theta_3} \left\{ (k_0 - \theta_i) \frac{1}{l_3} + (k_0 - \theta_3) \frac{b_i}{l_i} \right\} < b_0 \leq b_0^*. \quad (16.21)$$

*Proof.* See Appendix B. ■

The left-hand side of (16.21) imposes a restriction on the value of  $b_0$  from below. If the restriction is very strict, the range of  $b_0$  which the environmental authority can choose may be narrow.<sup>8</sup> Hence, we know that there is close relationship between the existence/stability condition and the feasible range of amount of emission permits.

#### A stabilization policy: a case where the target amount of emission permits is determined

#### Dynamics in a more plausible economy and a stabilization policy

In the preceding section, we have considered an economy where the government increases emission permits at a rate  $n$  or it keeps the total amount of emission permits constant. First, stability conditions were discussed (Proposition 1 and Corollary 1).

Next, we have shown what sort of condition is required to guarantee existence of a short-run equilibrium *and* to lead a short-run equilibrium to a long-run equilibrium (Proposition 2). Furthermore, we have also shown that a feasible range of the target amount of emission permits in the long run may possibly be narrowed if the government tries to stabilize an economy (Proposition 3).

{230}------------------------------------------------

Unless the technical conditions specified in Proposition 1 or Corollary 1 are satisfied, convergence of a short-run equilibrium to a long-run one cannot be guaranteed. This implies that an economy with an emission-permits scheme will not be maintained in the long-run. In other words, the introduction of emission-permits scheme *destabilizes* an economy. Particularly, when  $\theta_3 (= a_3/l_3)$  is quite large as in *Case (i)* or small as in *Case (iv)*, such an occasion is likely to appear.

For example, in the case of the CCS (Carbon Dioxide Capture and Storage) technology which abates  $\text{CO}_2$  emission, it seems very capital intensive, and thus  $\theta_3$  is possibly very large. Conversely, in the case of a recycling technology which reduces residuals disposed of in landfill, it may very labour intensive, and thus  $\theta_3$  is possibly very small. In both cases, a growing-emission-permits scheme or a constant-emission-permits scheme may destabilize an economy.

Furthermore, there may occur another problem: a short-run equilibrium may not exist when an emission-rights scheme is introduced into an economy, even if the convergence (stability) condition is satisfied. Stability without existence of a short-run equilibrium is absurd.<sup>9</sup> Altogether, one might suspect that environmental policies based upon Coase's great idea should come to nothing.

Then, it is natural to ask whether the government can make a short-run equilibrium exist and stabilize an economy, meeting the target amount of emission permits. Even if the target amount of emission permits in the long-run is determined, the amount of emission permits at each period may be allowed to diverge from the target amount in a dynamic process. If such freedom is given to the government, it is expected that the existence of a short-run equilibrium and its convergence to a long-run equilibrium will be more plausible.

Considering this, in this section we will deal with the case where a target amount of total emission permits is determined although the government can change the amount in the short-run. Thus, if a steady state is attained, the total amount of emission right is constant. What is required to the government is to lead an economy to a long-run equilibrium where the target amount of emission permits is constant.<sup>10</sup>

Obviously, the government may adjust the amount of emission permits in several ways. We suppose that the authority annually issues emission permits as follows:

$$\begin{aligned} B(t) = & \beta_1 \{x_1(t) - y_1^* e^{nt} L_0\} + \beta_2 \{x_2(t) \\ & - y_2^* e^{nt} L_0\} + (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0) L_0. \end{aligned} \quad (16.22)$$

We assume that parameters  $c_0$  and  $\beta_i$  satisfy  $\beta_i \leq b_i$ ,  $c_0 \geq 0$  and  $\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* \geq 0$ .

The rough idea of the adjustment rule (16.22) is as follows: the terms expressed in curly brackets mean the difference between the actual value of output and its steady-state value for both commodities. If there is no gap between two values for

{231}------------------------------------------------

both commodities, there is no need to change the supply of emission permits since the economy is already in a steady state. Only when it is not in a steady state is there a need to change the supply. But, can we set  $\beta_i$  properly so that an economy should be stabilized? This is the question we tackle.

At initial period  $t = 0$ , the total amount of emission permits is  $\beta_1 x_1(0) + \beta_2 x_2(0) + c_0 L_0$ . It is asked here whether an economy has a short-run equilibrium and can be stabilized starting from this amount of emission permits. The government can choose parameters  $\beta_1$ ,  $\beta_2$ , and  $c_0$  for the existence/stabilization purpose.

From (16.22), we can express a short-run equilibrium as

$$A^\dagger x(t) = \begin{pmatrix} K(t) \\ L(t) \end{pmatrix} + B(t) \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix}.$$

We will show a condition of a short-run equilibrium for non-negative  $t$  in Appendix C.1.

Differentiating (16.22), we have

$$\dot{B}(t) = \beta_1 \{\dot{x}_1(t) - ny_1^* e^{nt} L_0\} + \beta_2 \{\dot{x}_2(t) - ny_2^* e^{nt} L_0\}. \tag{16.23}$$

Substituting this  $\dot{B}(t)$  into (16.10), we can solve the differential equation in the same way as before. Namely, we have

$$A^\dagger \dot{x}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ ne^{nt} L_0 \end{pmatrix} + \{\beta_1 \dot{x}_1(t) + \beta_2 \dot{x}_2(t)\} \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix} - ne^{nt} L_0 (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^*) \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix},$$

which can be transformed into

$$\begin{aligned} A^\dagger \dot{y}(t) + nA^\dagger y(t) &= I_1 y(t) + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ n \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \beta_1 a_3 & \beta_2 a_3 \\ \beta_1 l_3 & \beta_2 l_3 \end{pmatrix} \dot{y}(t) \\ &\quad + n \begin{pmatrix} \beta_1 a_3 & \beta_2 a_3 \\ \beta_1 l_3 & \beta_2 l_3 \end{pmatrix} y(t) - n \begin{pmatrix} \beta_1 a_3 & \beta_2 a_3 \\ \beta_1 l_3 & \beta_2 l_3 \end{pmatrix} y^* \end{aligned}$$

Or equivalently, we have

$$\hat{A} \dot{y}(t) + n\hat{A} y(t) = I_1 y(t) + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ n \end{pmatrix} - n\Phi y^*, \tag{16.24}$$

where  $\Phi$  and  $\hat{A}$  are defined as

$$\Phi \equiv \begin{pmatrix} \beta_1 a_3 & \beta_2 a_3 \\ \beta_1 l_3 & \beta_2 l_3 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \hat{A} \equiv A^\dagger - \Phi.$$

{232}------------------------------------------------

It is easy to see that  $y^*$  is a particular solution to (16.24), where  $y^* = -(A^\dagger \Theta^\dagger)^{-1} Q^\dagger$  with  $\sigma = 0$ . In fact, substituting  $\dot{y}(t) = 0$  and  $y(t) = y^*$  into (16.24), we have

$$n\hat{A}y^* = I_1 y^* + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ n \end{pmatrix} - n\Phi y^* \Leftrightarrow nA^\dagger y^* = I_1 y^* + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ n \end{pmatrix},$$

which we have proved before:<sup>11</sup>

$$y^* = -(A^\dagger \Theta^\dagger)^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ n \end{pmatrix} = (nA^\dagger - I_1)^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ n \end{pmatrix}$$

We can solve (16.24) as before explicitly. Notice the solution path of  $(x_1(t), x_2(t))$  takes the form

$$\begin{cases} x_1(t) &= \left( -\alpha_1 \frac{\hat{l}_2}{\hat{l}_1} e^{\mu_1 t} + y_1^* \right) e^{nt} L_0 \\ \\ x_2(t) &= (\alpha_1 e^{\mu_1 t} + \alpha_2 e^{\mu_2 t} + y_2^*) e^{nt} L_0, \end{cases} \qquad (*)$$

where  $\mu_i (i = 1, 2)$  is a solution to the characteristic equation

$$\det \{\mu I - (\hat{A}^{-1} I_1 - nI)\} = 0.$$

As before, we know that

$$\mu_1 = -n + \frac{\hat{l}_2}{\det \hat{A}} \quad \text{and} \quad \mu_2 = -n,$$

where  $\hat{a}_i \equiv a_i + (b_i - \beta_i)a_3$  and  $\hat{l}_i \equiv l_i + (b_i - \beta_i)l_3$  and  $\hat{A} \equiv \begin{pmatrix} \hat{a}_1 & \hat{a}_2 \\ l_1 & l_2 \end{pmatrix}$ . Notice that the eigenvectors corresponding to  $\mu_i$  are

$$v_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{\hat{l}_2}{\hat{l}_1} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad v_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.$$

If  $\det \hat{A} < 0$  or equivalently  $\hat{a}_1 / \hat{l}_1 < \hat{a}_2 / \hat{l}_2$  holds, stability is guaranteed, and a short-run equilibrium, if exists, converges to a long-run equilibrium. Clearly  $\mu_1 < \mu_2 = -n < 0$  holds insofar as the stability condition is satisfied.

{233}------------------------------------------------

Moreover, we can show that

$$\frac{\hat{a}_1}{\hat{l}_1} < \frac{k_0 + a_3 c_0}{1 + l_3 c_0} < \frac{\hat{a}_2}{\hat{l}_2} \tag{16.25}$$

is a condition for existence of short-run equilibrium and stability. Namely, we have

##### *Proposition 4*

*If (16.25) holds and  $c_0$  is sufficiently small, a short-run equilibrium exists and converges to a long-run equilibrium.*

*Proof.* See Appendix C. ■

#### **A path to the steady state**

Since the government can change parameters such as  $\beta_i$  and  $c_0$ , following formulation (16.22), it may be able to stabilize an economy by choosing those parameters properly, even if the existence/stability condition is not satisfied in a constant-emission permits scheme.

Then, the target amount of emission permits is met in a long run. Let us first examine the range of the target amount of emission permits in this scheme.

We can show that, if the dynamic path is stable,

$$\begin{aligned} B^* &\equiv \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} B(t) = (\beta_2 \alpha_2 + \beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0) L_0 \\ &= L_0 \frac{l_2^\dagger}{\hat{l}_2} (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0). \end{aligned} \tag{16.26}$$

(See Appendix C.)

Choosing  $\beta_i$  and  $c_0$  properly, the government can change the target value  $B^*$ .

Let us explore how the government can choose  $B^*$ , keeping an existence/stability condition in mind. If the government choose  $c_0 > 0$  and  $\beta_i = 0$  for  $i = 1, 2$  with  $B^* = c_0$  without infringing the existence/stability condition, we do not have to depend upon the adjustment procedure expressed in (16.22). The constant amount of emission permits may, however, infringe the condition.

Notice that the existence/stability condition (16.25) is equivalent to

$$\frac{\theta_1 - \theta_3}{1 + (b_1 - \beta_1)(l_3/l_1)} < \frac{k_0 - \theta_3}{1 + l_3 c_0} < \frac{\theta_2 - \theta_3}{1 + (b_2 - \beta_2)(l_3/l_2)}. \tag{16.27}$$

From this, we know that we can always stabilize the economy by putting  $\beta_1 = b_1$ ,  $\beta_1 = b_2$  and  $c_0 = 0$ , since  $\theta_1 < k_0 < \theta_2$  holds by hypothesis. In this case, the total amount of emission permits in a long-run is calculated as

{234}------------------------------------------------

$$B^* = \left( 1 + \frac{b_2 l_3}{l_2} \right) (b_1 y_1^* + b_2 y_2^*) L_0.$$

Now, let us consider a range of the target amount of emission permits  $B^*$ , according to the cases given before respectively. In the following discussion, the reference point is  $\beta_i = b_i$  for  $i = 1, 2$  and  $c_0 = 0$ . Starting from this reference point, we can reduce  $\beta_1$  or  $\beta_2$  without violating the existence/stability condition as follows:

CASE (I)  $\theta_1 < k_0 < \theta_2 < \theta_3$ .

Then, all the numerators in (16.27) are negative. Hence, starting from  $\beta_i = b_i$  for  $i = 1, 2$  and  $c_0 = 0$ , we can reduce  $\beta_2$  keeping (16.27) holds. We can reduce  $\beta_2$  until  $\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* = 0$  holds. This means that we can reduce  $\beta_2$  until  $B^* = 0$ .

CASE (II)  $\theta_1 < k_0 < \theta_3 < \theta_2$ .

In this case, only the numerator of the right-hand side of (16.27) is positive, while the others are negative. Again, starting from  $\beta_i = b_i$  for  $i = 1, 2$  and  $c_0 = 0$ , we can reduce  $\beta_2$  until  $B^* = 0$ .

CASE (III)  $\theta_1 < \theta_3 < k_0 < \theta_2$ .

In this case, only the numerator of the left-hand side is negative, while the others are positive. Starting from  $\beta_i = b_i$  for  $i = 1, 2$  and  $c_0 = 0$ , we can reduce  $\beta_1$  until  $B^* = 0$ .

CASE (IV)  $\theta_3 < \theta_1 < k_0 < \theta_2$ .

In this case, all the numerators are positive. Thus, starting from  $\beta_i = b_i$  for  $i = 1, 2$  and  $c_0 = 0$ , we can reduce  $\beta_1$  until  $B^* = 0$  holds.

Thus, we can choose parameters  $\beta_1$  and  $\beta_2$  while setting  $c_0 = 0$ , and determine  $B^*$  in the range of

$$E \equiv \left[ 0, \left( 1 + \frac{b_2 l_3}{l_2} \right) (b_1 y_1^* + b_2 y_2^*) L_0 \right],$$

without violating the existence/stability condition.

When the government keeps  $\beta_i$  non-negative, clearly the initial amount of the emission permits  $\beta_1 x_1(0) + \beta_2 x_2(0)$  is also non-negative and thus, the amount of emission permits at any period is non-negative, too.<sup>12</sup>

Yet, if the government reduces the parameter  $\beta_i$  to a certain negative value as we assume here, we have to show that the initial amount of emission permits is non-negative, since negative amount of emission permits should be hard to be interpreted economically. Indeed, we can prove that it is non-negative under some conditions (See Lemma in Appendix C).

{235}------------------------------------------------

Thus, we have obtained the following result:

##### *Proposition 5*

*By choosing parameters properly, the government can take the target amount of emission permits from,  $E$ , and lead a short-run equilibrium to a long-run equilibrium if  $a_1^\dagger / l_1^\dagger \ge k_0$  ( $= K_0 / L_0$ ) holds in cases (i)–(ii) or if  $a_2^\dagger / l_2^\dagger \le k_0$  holds in cases (iii)–(iv).*

Let us deduce meaningful economic interpretation from the above proposition. In cases (i) and (ii),  $k_0 < a_2^\dagger / l_2^\dagger$  always holds. Hence, if  $a_1^\dagger / l_1^\dagger < k_0$  holds, this means that the stability condition is satisfied in a constant-emission-permits scheme, since  $a_1^\dagger / l_1^\dagger < k_0 < a_2^\dagger / l_2^\dagger$  holds. Thus, if the stability condition in a constant-emission-permits scheme is not satisfied,  $a_1^\dagger / l_1^\dagger \ge k_0$  must hold. Proposition 5 tells us that the existence/stability condition is satisfied if the government adopts the supply formula of emission permits (16.22) and chooses the target amount of emission permits from the range  $E$ , even if the stability condition is not satisfied in a constant-emission-permits scheme.

The circumstances are the same in cases (iii) and (iv). Suppose that the stability condition  $a_1^\dagger / l_1^\dagger < a_2^\dagger / l_2^\dagger$  is not satisfied in a constant-emission-permits scheme in these cases. This implies that  $a_2^\dagger / l_2^\dagger \le k_0$  ( $= K_0 / L_0$ ) holds. Even so, the government can lead a short-run equilibrium to a long-run equilibrium, following the formulation (16.22) if they choose the target amount of emission permits from  $E$ .

Next, let us consider the cases in which the existence of a short-run equilibrium condition is not satisfied although the stability condition is satisfied in a constant-emission-permits scheme. This means that either  $k_0^\dagger \le \theta_1^\dagger < \theta_2^\dagger$  or  $\theta_1^\dagger < \theta_2^\dagger \le k_0^\dagger$  holds, where  $k_0^\dagger \equiv \frac{k_0 + b_0 a_3}{1 + b_0 l_3}$ .

In cases (i) and (ii),  $k_0 < \theta_3$  holds and so  $k_0 < k_0^\dagger$  follows. Thus, unless the existence condition is satisfied, then  $k_0 < k_0^\dagger \le \theta_1^\dagger$  holds. On the other hands, in cases (iii) and (iv),  $k_0 > \theta_3$  holds and so  $k_0 > k_0^\dagger$  follows. Thus,  $\theta_2^\dagger \le k_0^\dagger < k_0$  holds. In any case, if the existence condition does not hold,  $k_0 < \theta_1^\dagger$  holds in cases (i)–(ii), and  $k_0 > \theta_2^\dagger$  in cases (iii)–(iv). According to Proposition 5, the government can make a short-run equilibrium exist and lead it to a long-run equilibrium insofar as they choose the target amount of emission permits from  $E$ .

Consequently, we have the following result:

##### *Corollary 2*

*Suppose  $\frac{a_1^\dagger}{l_1^\dagger} < \frac{k_0 + a_3 b_0}{1 + a_3 b_0} < \frac{a_2^\dagger}{l_2^\dagger}$  does not hold. Even so, the government can make a short-run equilibrium exist and lead it to a long-run equilibrium by adopting the formula of supply of emission right (16.22), insofar as the target amount of emission permits is in the range of  $E$ .* ■

{236}------------------------------------------------

Corollary 2 can be summarized as follows: let us consider that the government would like to control the amount of emission permits to, say,  $B^* \in E$ . Furthermore suppose that the condition of existence of a short-run equilibrium or the condition of stability is not satisfied in a constant-emission-permits scheme (or a growing-emission-permits scheme), or equivalently  $\frac{a_1^\dagger}{l_1^\dagger} < \frac{k_0 + a_3 b_0}{1 + a_3 b_0} < \frac{a_2^\dagger}{l_2^\dagger}$  does not hold.

Then, the government cannot manage an economy with a emission-right market in a short-run and/or in a long-run.

Even so, if the government does not stick to the constant-emission-permits scheme in the whole dynamic process and if it is allowed to control the target amount of emission permits to  $B^* \in E$  in the long-run, following adjustment formula (16.22), and choosing the parameters properly, then a short-run equilibrium always exists and it will converge to a steady-state equilibrium.

Finally, let us explain intuitively why the government can make a short-run equilibrium exist and lead an economy to a long-run equilibrium position. The supply formula of emission permits (16.22) imposes restriction on the use of the permits which comes from the two sectors. Due to this restriction, both sectors cannot realize the increase in inputs which *were* required without the restriction. This suggests us that the input coefficients can virtually be adjusted so that the existence condition be satisfied and the dynamic movement be stabilized according to the supply formula expressed by (16.22).

#### A case where emission permits do not expire

We have so far assumed that emission permits remain valid for a year and expire after that. Capitalists must, therefore, renew the permits every year. There is no stock of emission permits.

In this subsection, we discuss the possibility that emission permits do not expire and remain valid for ever. Thus, once issued, emission permits remain in capitalists' hands, and accumulate as stock in an economy. This alteration does not affect the above conclusion essentially: the stability condition remains the same, and the government can stabilize an economy by adjusting the amount of *newly issued emission permits*. One point which differs from the former analysis is the distributional relationship.

Let us assume that the government sells newly issued emission permits to capitalists. The proceeds of the sales of there permits are supposed to be transferred to workers through the government, as before. Conversely, if the government buys emission permits from capitalists, money must be collected, maybe in the form of tax, from workers by the government, and it will be transferred to capitalists as the proceeds of the sales.

But once issued emission permits are held by capitalists as stock, the value of the stock of emission permits accrues to capitalists, the owners of the permits. Hence, only the sales corresponding to a change in the total amount of emission permits are distributed by capitalists or workers.

Under these circumstances,  $B$  can be interpreted as the stock of emission permits, which has accumulated from the past. The amount of newly issued

{237}------------------------------------------------

emission permits is  $\dot{B}$ .<sup>13</sup> As far as the quantity system is concerned, the former analysis can be applied to this case, too. The existence and stability condition is exactly the same as before.

The distribution side is, however, affected. Capitalists' income consists of profits and rewards which comes from holding a stock of emission permits. Clearly, those rewards cannot be spent for investment, since they are implicit. The things are the same as before so far. Yet, capitalists have to spare profits for newly issued emission permits. On the other hand, if the government buys emission permits from capitalists, proceeds of the sales of the permits are obtained by capitalists.

Considering this, the formula of capital accumulation must be modified as follows:

$$p\dot{K} = px_1 = rpK - q\dot{B},$$

or

$$r = \frac{\dot{K}}{K} + \frac{q}{p} \frac{\dot{B}}{K}. \quad (16.28)$$

At a given moment, capital stock  $K$  and stock of emission permits are given, and  $\dot{K} (= x_1)$  is determined by  $K$ ,  $B$  and  $L$ . Since  $q/p$  is a function of  $r$ , as seen from (16.1), the rate of profit  $r$  is determined by (16.28), once a formula of  $\dot{B}$  such as (16.22) is given.

Although the distribution side is affected in a short-run equilibrium as shown in (16.28), it is unaffected in a steady state. Since  $\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \dot{B} = 0$  holds, the relationship between the rate of profit and the capital accumulation rate is the same as before:  $r = n$  holds.

### Conclusion

Let us summarize what we have discussed in the previous sections. First, we have shown the existence and stability condition both in a growing-emission-permits scheme and a constant-emission-permits scheme. At first glance, the condition looks similar to the existence/stability condition in the conventional two-sector analysis, although there is an essential difference. Particularly, the existence/stability condition may be incompatible with an arbitrarily given amount of emission permits.

Thus, we have explored whether the government can make a short-run equilibrium exist and lead it to a long-run equilibrium next. It has been shown that the government can control the amount of newly issued emission permits so that it may make a short-run equilibrium exist and stabilize an economy. Thus, a short-run equilibrium position will converge to a position in a steady state by means of a proper policy. This conclusion is valid whether we assume newly issued emission permits remain valid for a year or for ever. The length of validity of emission permits does not affect the conclusion on a stabilization policy, although it may change the relationship between the growth rate and the rate of profit in a short-run equilibrium.

{238}------------------------------------------------

This conclusion seems quite interesting, particularly when we consider a discussion of the feasibility of the trade of emission permits. It might be argued that, unless initial allocation of emission permits is proper, an economy may be disturbed by the trade of permits. According to our discussion, however, the initial allocation does not matter so much, insofar as an economy is in a short-run equilibrium. What is important is the government formula which adjusts the new issue of emission permits. An example of such a formula is equation (16.22). If the government sets the parameters in the formula properly, it can lead an economy to a steady-state equilibrium, in whatever proportion initial emission permits may be allocated to sectors, as far as an economy is in equilibrium at every moment. Thus, we can safely depend upon a tradeable emission permits scheme, one of the environmental policies based upon Coase's great insight.

### **Appendix A**

#### **A simple two-sector dynamics**

Let us review briefly an equilibrium and dynamics of a simple two-sector model, where there is neither environmental restriction nor an abatement sector.<sup>14</sup> In this case, the quantity system expressed by (16.2) is reduced to the following:

$$\begin{cases} K &= a_1 x_1 &+& a_2 x_2 \\ L &= l_1 x_1 &+& l_2 x_2 \\ x_1 &= \dot{K} \\ \dot{L}/L &= n \end{cases} \tag{16.A.1}$$

#### *A short-run equilibrium*

A short-run equilibrium is expressed as follows:

$$\begin{pmatrix} K \\ L \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_1 & a_2 \\ l_1 & l_2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus, we have

$$x = \frac{1}{\det A} \begin{pmatrix} l_2 K - a_2 L \\ -l_1 K + a_1 L \end{pmatrix},$$

where  $x \equiv \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix}$ , and  $A \equiv \begin{pmatrix} a_1 & a_2 \\ l_1 & l_2 \end{pmatrix}$ . If  $\det A < 0$ , then  $\frac{a_1}{l_1} < \frac{a_2}{l_2}$  holds. From this,

we know that if  $\frac{a_1}{l_1} < \frac{K(t)}{L(t)} < \frac{a_2}{l_2}$  holds, *a short-run equilibrium with*  $x_1 > 0$  *and*  $x_2 > 0$  *exits at*  $t$ .

{239}------------------------------------------------

#### **Dynamics**

Dynamics is expressed as follows:

$$\begin{cases} \dot{K} &= a_1 \dot{x}_1 + a_2 \dot{x}_2 \\ \dot{L} &= l_1 \dot{x}_1 + l_2 \dot{x}_2 \end{cases}$$

Defining  $y_i \equiv x_i e^{-nt} L_0$  and considering  $x_1 = \dot{K}$ , we can transform the above equations into the following:

$$A\dot{y} + nAy = \begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ n \end{pmatrix}$$

Defining  $I_1$  as  $I_1 \equiv \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ , we have

$$\dot{y} = -(nI - A^{-1}I_1)y + A^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ n \end{pmatrix}.$$

Let us define  $\Theta$  as  $\Theta \equiv -(nI - A^{-1}I_1)$ . Then, a particular solution is expressed as

$$y^* = -(A\Theta)^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ n \end{pmatrix}.$$

The general solution to a homogeneous part of the above differential equation is given as

$$y(t) = \alpha_1 v_1 e^{\lambda_1 t} + \alpha_2 v_2 e^{\lambda_2 t},$$

where  $v_i$  is an eigenvector corresponding to an eigenvalue  $\lambda_i$  ( $i = 1, 2$ ). The eigenvector and the eigenvalue are obtained by solving a characteristic equation of the differential equation as follows:

$$\det(\lambda I - \Theta) = 0.$$

Thus, we have

$$\lambda_1 = -n + \frac{1}{\det A} l_2 \quad \text{and} \quad \lambda_2 = -n$$

If  $\det A$  is positive, then  $-n + \frac{1}{\det A} l_2$  is positive due to the feasibility condition  $n < \frac{1}{a_1}$ . This means that the stability condition is  $\det A < 0$ . Let us summarize the results of existence of equilibrium and stability as follows:

{240}------------------------------------------------

*Proposition 6 (Shinkai and Uzawa)*

(i) *If*  $\frac{a_1}{l_1} < \frac{K(t)}{L(t)} < \frac{a_2}{l_2}$  *holds, a short-run equilibrium with*  $x_1(t) > 0$  *and*  $x_2(t) > 0$  *exits for*  $t$ . (ii) *If and only if*  $\det A < 0$  *holds, a short-run equilibrium, converges to a long-run equilibrium.*

Let us find eigenvectors  $v_1$  and  $v_2$ . Solve the following for each  $\lambda_i (i = 1, 2)$ , where  $\lambda_1 = -n + \frac{1}{\det A} l_2$  and  $\lambda_2 = -n$ :

$$(\lambda_i I - \Theta) v_i = 0.$$

From this, we have

$$v_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{l_2}{l_1} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad v_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.$$

Consequently, we have obtained the general solution of the dynamic system in the following form:

$$y(t) = \alpha_1 \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{l_2}{l_1} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} e^{\lambda_1 t} + \alpha_2 \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} e^{\lambda_2 t} - (A\Theta)^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ n \end{pmatrix}.$$

### **Appendix B**

#### **A three-sectoral dynamics 1**

In this section, let us prove Propositions 2 and 3.

##### ***Proof of Proposition 2***

*We show the following: An equilibrium vector*  $(x_1(t), x_2(t), x_3(t))$  *is positive for any*  $t$  *if*  $a_1^\dagger / l_1^\dagger < k_0^\dagger < a_2^\dagger / l_2^\dagger$  *holds, where*  $k^\dagger \equiv (k_0 + a_3 b_0)/(1 + a_3 b_0)$ .

*Proof.* Let us consider (16.18) with (16.19). Namely,

$$1 + l_3 b(t) = l_1^\dagger y_1(t) + l_2^\dagger y_2(t),$$

where  $b(t) = b_0$  or  $b_0 e^{-nt}$ .

The left-hand side of (16.18) is constant or decreasing monotonically. Notice

$$y_1(t) = -\alpha_1 \frac{l_2^\dagger}{l_1^\dagger} \exp(\lambda_1 t) + y_1^* \tag{16.A.2}$$

{241}------------------------------------------------

$$y_2(t) = \alpha_1 \exp(\lambda_1 t) + \alpha_2 \exp(\lambda_2 t) + y_2^*, \tag{16.A.3}$$

where  $\lambda_1 < \lambda_2 = -n < 0$ . Let us consider the following to cases:

- (i) Suppose  $\alpha_1 > 0$ . Then,  $y_1(t) \leq y_1^*$  and  $y_1(t)$  converges to  $y_1^*$  monotonically. Since  $y_1(t)$  increases and  $b(t)$  does not increase in (16.18),  $y_2(t)$  decreases monotonically. Since  $y_2(t) \rightarrow y_2^*$ , we have  $y_2(t) > 0$  for all  $t$ .
- (ii) Suppose  $\alpha_1 < 0$ . Notice that  $y_2(0) = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2 + y_2^*$  holds.

- (a) Suppose  $\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 > 0$ . Then,  $y_2(0) > y_2^*$ . And  $\alpha_2 > -\alpha_1 > 0$  and so  $-\frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2} < 1$  hold. If  $y_2(t') < y^*$  holds for some  $t'$ , then  $y_2(t) = y_2^*$  must hold for some  $t \leq t'$ . Then  $\alpha_1 \exp(\lambda_1 t) + \alpha_2 \exp(\lambda_2 t) = 0$  holds. This implies that

$$-\frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2} = \exp((\lambda_2 - \lambda_1)t) < 1$$

holds. But  $(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1)t \geq 0$ . A contradiction. Thus,  $y_2(t) > y_2^*$  for all  $t$ .

- (b) Suppose  $\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 < 0$ . Let us consider the following sub-cases.
  - (b-1) If  $\alpha_2 < 0$ , then  $y_2(t)$  converges to  $y_2^*$  monotonically. Thus,  $y_2(t) > 0$  for all  $t$ .
  - (b-2) If  $\alpha_2 > 0$ , then  $0 < \alpha_2 < -\alpha_1$  or equivalently  $|\alpha_2| < |\alpha_1|$ . Evaluating

$$\dot{y}_2(t) = \alpha_1 \lambda_1 \exp(\lambda_1 t) + \alpha_2 \lambda_2 \exp(\lambda_2 t)$$

at  $t = 0$ , we have

$$\dot{y}_2(0) = \alpha_1 \lambda_1 + \alpha_2 \lambda_2.$$

Since  $\lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < 0$  and  $0 < \alpha_2 < -\alpha_1$  hold,

$$\dot{y}_2(0) = \alpha_1 \lambda_1 + \alpha_2 \lambda_2 > 0.$$

By hypothesis  $y_2(0) - y_2^* = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2 < 0$  holds, we know that  $y_2(t)$  first increases. Notice  $\alpha_1 \exp(\lambda_1 t) + \alpha_2 \exp(\lambda_2 t) = 0$  holds for unique  $t$ . This means that  $\alpha_2 \exp(\lambda_2 t) = -\alpha_1 \exp(\lambda_1 t)$  holds, and thus we have

$$t = \ln \left( -\frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2} \right) / (\lambda_2 - \lambda_1) > 0.$$

Hence,  $y_2(t)$  first increases and goes beyond  $y_2^*$  and turns to decrease, converging to  $y_2^*$ . Consequently,  $y_2(t)$  cannot become non-positive. Therefore,  $(y_1(t), y_2(t))$  or  $(x_1(t), x_2(t))$  is positive. Positivity of  $y_3(t)$  (or  $x_3(t)$ ) is clear insofar as  $b_0 < b_0^*$  holds. ■

{242}------------------------------------------------

##### ***Proof of Proposition 3***

Notice that the stability condition is always satisfied in case (ii) and case (iii). Thus  $a_1^\dagger / l_1^\dagger < a_2^\dagger / l_2^\dagger$  holds in these cases. What matters is the existence condition in the short-run. The second the inequality of the existence condition, namely (16.20) is

$$\frac{a_2^\dagger}{l_2^\dagger} \equiv \frac{a_2 + b_2 a_3}{l_2 + b_2 l_3} > \frac{k_0 + a_3 b_0}{1 + l_3 b_0} \equiv k_0^\dagger,$$

which is equivalent to

$$(\theta_2 - \theta_3)b_0 > (k_0 - \theta_2) \frac{1}{l_3} + (k_0 - \theta_3) \frac{b_2}{l_2}.$$

Since  $\theta_2 > \theta_3$  holds by hypothesis, the above is equivalent to

$$b_0 > \frac{1}{\theta_2 - \theta_3} \left\{ (k_0 - \theta_2) \frac{1}{l_3} + (k_0 - \theta_3) \frac{b_2}{l_2} \right\}.$$

Similarly, the first inequality of the existence condition (16.20) implies

$$b_0 > \frac{1}{\theta_1 - \theta_3} \left\{ (k_0 - \theta_1) \frac{1}{l_3} + (k_0 - \theta_3) \frac{b_1}{l_1} \right\}.$$

Thus, the condition is equivalent to

$$b_0 > \max_{i=1,2} \frac{1}{\theta_i - \theta_3} \left\{ (k_0 - \theta_i) \frac{1}{l_3} + (k_0 - \theta_3) \frac{b_i}{l_i} \right\}$$

### **Appendix C**

#### **A three-sectoral dynamics 2**

In this Appendix, we consider mathematical deductions in the section on a stabilization policy.

#### ***A short-run equilibrium***

A short-run equilibrium in section on a stabilization policy is expressed as

$$A^\dagger x(t) = \begin{pmatrix} K(t) \\ L(t) \end{pmatrix} + B(t) \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix},$$

{243}------------------------------------------------

or

$$A^\dagger y(t) = \begin{pmatrix} k(t) \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + b(t) \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix},$$

where

$$b(t) = \beta_1 \{y_1(t) - y_1^*\} + \beta_2 \{y_2(t) - y_2^*\} + (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0)e^{-nt}.$$

Let us consider a short-run equilibrium at  $t = 0$ .

$$\hat{A}y(0) = \begin{pmatrix} k_0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + c_0 \begin{pmatrix} a_3 \\ l_3 \end{pmatrix}.$$

If

$$\frac{\hat{a}_1}{\hat{l}_1} < \frac{k_0 + c_0 a_3}{1 + c_0 l_3} < \frac{\hat{a}_2}{\hat{l}_2} \tag{16.A.4}$$

is satisfied,  $y(0)$  is positive, as we have shown in Appendix A. We will show, as before, that a short-run equilibrium always exists for non-negative  $t$  if the above inequality is satisfied.

#### ***Dynamics***

Notice that (16.24) is fundamentally the same as (16.12). Indeed, the general solution to (16.24) is, as we have already shown,

$$\begin{cases} y_1(t) &= \left( -\alpha_1 \frac{\hat{l}_2}{\hat{l}_1} e^{\mu_1 t} + y_1^* \right) \\ y_2(t) &= (\alpha_1 e^{\mu_1 t} + \alpha_2 e^{\mu_2 t} + y_2^*), \end{cases} \tag{16.A.5}$$

As we have shown in the main text,  $\mu_1$  and  $\mu_2$  are solutions to the characteristic equation

$$\det \{\mu I - (\hat{A}^{-1} I_1 - nI)\} = 0,$$

and the eigenvectors corresponding to  $\mu_1$  and  $\mu_2$  are expressed as

$$v_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{\hat{l}_2}{\hat{l}_1} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad v_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.$$

{244}------------------------------------------------

Notice that

$$1 + l_3 b(t) = \hat{l}_1 y_1(t) + \hat{l}_2 y_2(t) \tag{16.A.6}$$

holds and this is equivalent to

$$1 + l_3 \{(\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0) e^{-nt} - (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^*)\} = \hat{l}_1 y_1(t) + \hat{l}_2 y_2(t).$$

Since  $(\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0)$  is non-negative<sup>15</sup>, the left-hand side of the above inequality is a non-increasing function of  $t$ . Thus, completely the same argument as Appendix B. is applicable to this case by replacing  $\lambda_i$  with  $\mu_i$ . Therefore, if (16.A.4) holds, a short-run equilibrium exists and converges to a long-run equilibrium.

It is easy to see that  $y_3(t)$  (or  $x_3(t)$ ) is non-negative for small  $c_0$ . For  $B(t) \leq b_1 x_1(t) + b_2 x_2(t)$  holds when  $c_0$  is sufficiently small. (Notice  $b_i \geq \beta_i$ .)

#### ***The target amount of emission permits***

*Proof of (16.26).* From (16.A.5), we know that the following holds:

$$\hat{l}_1 y_1(t) + \hat{l}_2 y_2(t) = \hat{l}_1 y_1^* + \hat{l}_2 y_2^* + \hat{l}_2 \alpha_2 e^{\mu_2 t} \tag{16.A.7}$$

On the other hand, from (16.A.6) we obtain

$$\hat{l}_1 y_1(t) + \hat{l}_2 y_2(t) = 1 + \{(\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0) e^{-nt} - (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^*)\} l_3 \tag{16.A.8}$$

holds, taking  $t \rightarrow \infty$ , we have

$$\hat{l}_1 y_1^* + \hat{l}_2 y_2^* = 1 - (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^*) l_3.$$

Substituting this into (16.A.7), we have

$$\hat{l}_1 y_1(t) + \hat{l}_2 y_2(t) = 1 - (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^*) l_3 + \hat{l}_2 \alpha_2 e^{\mu_2 t}. \tag{16.A.9}$$

It follows from (16.A.8) and (16.A.9), evaluated at  $t = 0$  and from  $\mu_2 = -n$  that

$$l_3 (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0) = \hat{l}_2 \alpha_2.$$

Therefore,

$$\alpha_2 = \frac{l_3}{\hat{l}_2} (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0)$$

holds.

{245}------------------------------------------------

On the other hand, from (\*) in the subsection on Dynamics and considering  $x_i(t) = y_i e^{nt}$ , we have

$$\begin{aligned} & \beta_1 \{y_1(t)e^{nt} - y_1^* e^{nt}\} L_0 + \beta_2 \{y_2(t)e^{nt} - y_2^* e^{nt}\} L_0 \\ &= L_0 \left\{ -\alpha_1 \left( \beta_1 \frac{\hat{l}_2}{\hat{l}_1} e^{(\mu_1+n)t} \right) \right\} + \beta_2 \alpha_2 L_0 \\ &\rightarrow \beta_2 \alpha_2 L_0 \text{ as } t \rightarrow 0, \end{aligned}$$

since  $\mu_1 < \mu_2 = -n$  holds.

Hence,

$$\begin{aligned} \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} B(t) &= (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0) L_0 + \beta_2 \alpha_2 L_0 \\ &= L_0 \left( 1 + \beta_2 \frac{l_3}{\hat{l}_2} \right) (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0) = L_0 \frac{l_2^\dagger}{\hat{l}_2} (\beta_1 y_1^* + \beta_2 y_2^* + c_0) \blacksquare \end{aligned}$$

##### *The initial amount of emission permits*

Let us prove the following lemma:

##### *Lemma*

- 1 Suppose that (16.25) or (16.27) is satisfied as well as  $\beta_1 = b_1$  in cases (i) and (ii). Then, the initial amount of emission permits is non-negative for any  $\beta_2$ , if  $\theta_1^\dagger \geq k_0 (= K_0/L_0)$  holds.*
- 2 Suppose that (16.25) or (16.27) is satisfied as well as  $\beta_2 = b_2$  in cases (iii) and (iv). Then, the initial amount of emission permits is non-negative for any  $\beta_1$ , if  $\theta_2^\dagger \leq k_0$  holds.*

*Proof.* We assume here that  $c_0 = 0$  without loss of generality. Notice that the initial amount of emission permits  $B(0)$  is expressed as  $B(0) = \beta x(0)$ , where  $\beta \equiv (\beta_1, \beta_2)$ . Notice

$$\beta x(0) = \beta \hat{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \beta \begin{pmatrix} \hat{l}_2 & -\hat{a}_2 \\ -\hat{l}_1 & \hat{a}_1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix}.$$

Let  $\beta_2 \rightarrow -\infty$  with  $\beta_1 = b_1$  or  $\beta_1 \rightarrow -\infty$  with  $\beta_2 = b_2$ .

Since (16.25) or (16.27) is satisfied by hypothesis, we know that  $x(0)$  is positive for  $\beta_1 = b_1$  with any negative  $\beta_2$  or for  $\beta_2 = b_2$  with any negative  $\beta_1$ . Furthermore, it is easy to calculate

$$\lim_{\beta_2 \rightarrow -\infty} \beta x(0) = \frac{l_1^\dagger L_0 (\theta_1^\dagger - k_0)}{l_1 l_3 (\theta_3 - \theta_1)},$$

{246}------------------------------------------------

where  $\beta_1 = b_1$ . Since  $\theta_1 < k_0 < \beta_3$  holds in cases (i)–(ii), we know that

$$\lim_{\beta_2 \rightarrow -\infty} B(0) = \lim_{\beta_2 \rightarrow -\infty} \beta x(0) \geq 0$$

holds if  $\theta_1^\dagger \geq k_0$  is satisfied.

In the same way, we can easily show that, if  $\theta^\dagger \leq k_0$  is satisfied, we obtain

$$\lim_{\beta_1 \rightarrow -\infty} \beta x(0) = \frac{l_2^\dagger L_0 (k_0 - \theta_2^\dagger)}{l_2 l_3 (\theta_2 - \theta_3)} \geq 0,$$

in cases (iii)–(iv) where  $\beta_2 = b_2$ , since  $\theta_3 < k_0 < \theta_2$  holds.

Thus, we have shown that

$$\lim_{\beta_1 \rightarrow -\infty} B(0) = \lim_{\beta_1 \rightarrow -\infty} \beta x(0) \geq 0.$$

In any case, insofar as  $\beta_1 = b_1$  holds in cases (i)–(ii) or  $\beta_2 = b_2$  holds in cases (iii)–(iv),  $B(0)$  does not go to non-positive value as  $\beta_2$  or  $\beta_1$  goes to minus infinity.

Next, let us consider how  $B(0)$  changes corresponding to decrease in  $\beta_1$  or  $\beta_2$ :

$$\frac{\partial B(0)}{\partial \beta_2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_2} \left\{ \beta \hat{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} \right\} = (0, 1) \hat{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} + \beta \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_2} \left\{ \hat{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} \right\}. \quad (16.A.10)$$

Calculating the second term in the right-hand side of (16.A.10), we have

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_2} \left\{ \hat{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} \right\} &= \left\{ -\frac{\hat{a}_1 \frac{\partial \hat{l}_2}{\partial \beta_2} - \hat{l}_1 \frac{\partial \hat{a}_2}{\partial \beta_2}}{(\det \hat{A})^2} \begin{pmatrix} \hat{l}_2 & -\hat{a}_2 \\ -\hat{l}_1 & \hat{a}_1 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial \hat{l}_2}{\partial \beta_2} & -\frac{\partial \hat{a}_2}{\partial \beta_2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \right\} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \frac{\hat{a}_1 l_3 - \hat{l}_1 a_3}{\det \hat{A}} \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \begin{pmatrix} \hat{l}_2 & -\hat{a}_2 \\ -\hat{l}_1 & \hat{a}_1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \begin{pmatrix} a_3 L_0 - l_3 K_0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \frac{a_1 l_3 - l_1 a_3}{\det \hat{A}} x(0) + \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \begin{pmatrix} a_3 L_0 - l_3 K_0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \end{aligned}$$

where we have utilized  $\hat{a}_1 l_3 - \hat{l}_1 a_3 = a_1 l_3 - l_1 a_3$  and

$$x(0) = \hat{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \begin{pmatrix} \hat{l}_2 & -\hat{a}_2 \\ -\hat{l}_1 & \hat{a}_1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix}.$$

{247}------------------------------------------------

Thus, we have

$$\frac{\partial B(0)}{\partial \beta_2} = (0, 1) \hat{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{a_1 l_3 - l_1 a_3}{\det \hat{A}} \beta x(0) + \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \beta \begin{pmatrix} a_3 L_0 - l_3 K_0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$

Suppose that  $\partial B(0)/\partial \beta_2 = 0$  holds. Then, we have

$$\frac{l_1 l_3 (\theta_1 - \theta_3)}{\det \hat{A}} \beta x(0) = - \left\{ (0, 1) \hat{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \beta \begin{pmatrix} a_3 L_0 - l_3 K_0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \right\}, \quad (16.A.11)$$

where the right-hand side of (16.A.11) is calculated to be

$$- \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} l_1^\dagger L_0 \left( \frac{a_1^\dagger}{l_1^\dagger} - k_0 \right).$$

where  $k_0 \equiv K_0/L_0$ .

Since the stability condition is satisfied by hypothesis, we have  $\det \hat{A} < 0$ . Furthermore,  $\theta_1 < \theta_3$  holds in cases (i)–(ii). Hence,  $B(0) = \beta_x(0) \geq 0$  for  $\beta_2$  such that  $\partial B/\partial \beta_2 = 0$ .

Coupling this result with the  $B(0) > 0$  for  $\beta_1 = b_1$  with  $\beta_2 = 0$  and  $\lim_{\beta_2 \rightarrow -\infty} B(0) \geq 0$ , we can tell that  $B(0) \geq 0$  for any  $\beta_2$  and  $\beta_1 = b_1$  if  $a_1^\dagger/l_1^\dagger (\equiv \theta_1^\dagger) \geq k_0$  holds and the stability condition is satisfied.

In exactly the same way, we can show that

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial B(0)}{\partial \beta_1} &= (0, 1) \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \begin{pmatrix} \hat{l}_2 & -\hat{a}_2 \\ -\hat{l}_1 & \hat{a}_1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} K_0 \\ L_0 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{l_2 l_3 (\theta_3 - \theta_2)}{\det \hat{A}} \beta x(0) \\ &\quad + \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \beta_2 (l_3 K_0 - a_3 L_0). \end{aligned}$$

Then, if  $\partial B(0)/\partial \beta_1 = 0$  holds, we have

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{l_2 l_3 (\theta_3 - \theta_2)}{\det \hat{A}} \beta x(0) &= - \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} \left\{ (\hat{l}_2 K_0 - \hat{a}_2 L_0) + \beta_2 (l_3 K_0 - a_3 L_0) \right\} \\ &= - \frac{1}{\det \hat{A}} l_2^\dagger L_0 \left( k_0 - \frac{a_2^\dagger}{l_2^\dagger} \right). \end{aligned}$$

Hence, if  $k_0 (\equiv K_0/L_0) \geq a_2^\dagger/l_2^\dagger (\theta_2^\dagger)$  holds, then  $\beta x(0) \geq 0$  holds, since  $\det \hat{A} < 0$  by hypothesis and  $\theta_3 < k_0 < \theta_2$  in cases (iii)–(iv). Coupling this result with the fact that  $B(0) > 0$  for  $\beta_2 = b_2$  with  $\beta_1 = 0$  and  $\lim_{\beta_1 \rightarrow -\infty} B(0) \geq 0$ , we know that  $B(0) \geq 0$  for any negative  $\beta_1$  with  $\beta_2 = b_2$ , if  $\theta_2^\dagger \leq k_0$  holds and the stability condition is satisfied. ■
